sources.title: Google’s SynthID AI content detector expands globally, will work on Apple’s models ‘soon’ - 9to5Google
passages: Google notes that images made with Apple Intelligence will carry a SynthID watermark “soon,” which implies it might be a little bit before users can reliably identify AI-generated content from Apple’s models.
But the expansion means that more users in total will be able to do some due diligence on photos and videos posted online.
Google announced that SynthID is being upgraded from limited early access to a globally available tool in English, though it’s expected to expand further in the future.
The tool has progressed some , but this is a bigger step for AI content detection.
According to Google’s press release, the AI image detector launch comes with expanded compatibility.
So far, the list includes OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and now, Apple.

That means any content generated with models from those companies will contain visually undetectable watermarks so users can later check whether the image is a human-made visual or something an algorithm cobbled together.
Stay up to date on news from Google headquarters…

extraction.body: Google’s AI-detector for images and videos, SynthID, is getting a full release today. It will work for more than just content developed with Google’s AI models and initial partners. SynthID is a necessary tool as AI content has taken hold of heavy portions of the internet. Models have evolved so much that it’s nearly impossible to tell whether some videos or photos are even real, and it has you second-guessing whether real ones are generated. SynthID takes aim at that problem by introducing invisible watermarks at the generation stage, and when used on an image, it will detect those watermarks. Of course, that only works if the image generation tool inserts its own footprint to begin with. Google announced that SynthID is being upgraded from limited early access to a globally available tool in English, though it’s expected to expand further in the future. The tool has progressed some , but this is a bigger step for AI content detection. According to Google’s press release, the AI image detector launch comes with expanded compatibility. The new SynthID will work with content generated on Google’s own Gemini, a given, as well as content from more partners. So far, the list includes OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and now, Apple. That means any content generated with models from those companies will contain visually undetectable watermarks so users can later check whether the image is a human-made visual or something an algorithm cobbled together. extraction.body: SynthID Detector — a new portal to help identify AI-generated content The SynthID Detector can help determine if an image created using Google AI contains a SynthID watermark. VP, Science and Strategic Initiatives, Google DeepMind Your browser does not support the audio element. Advances in generative AI are making it possible for people to create content in entirely new ways — from text to high quality audio, images and videos. As these capabilities advance and become more broadly available, questions of authenticity, context and verification emerge. Today we’re announcing SynthID Detector, a verification portal to quickly and efficiently identify AI-generated content made with Google AI. The portal provides detection capabilities across different modalities in one place and provides essential transparency in the rapidly evolving landscape of generative media. It can also highlight which parts of the content are more likely to have been watermarked with SynthID. When we launched SynthID — a state-of-the-art tool that embeds imperceptible watermarks and enables the identification of AI-generated content — our aim was to provide a suite of novel technical solutions to help minimise misinformation and misattribution. SynthID not only preserves the content’s quality, it acts as a robust watermark that remains detectable even when the content is shared or undergoes a range of transformations. While originally focused on AI-generated imagery only, we’ve since expanded SynthID to cover AI-generated text, audio and video content, including content generated by our Gemini, Imagen, Lyria and Veo models across Google. Over 10 billion pieces of content have already been watermarked with SynthID. When you upload an image, audio track, video or piece of text created using Google's AI tools, the portal will scan the media for a SynthID watermark. If a watermark is detected, the portal will highlight specific portions of the content most likely to be watermarked. For audio, the portal pinpoints specific segments where a SynthID watermark is detected, and for images, it indicates areas where a watermark is most likely. We are starting to roll this out to early testers today, before making it available more broadly. Journalists, media professionals and researchers can join our waitlist to gain access to the SynthID Detector. To help grow a trusted ecosystem we’ve already open sourced SynthID text watermarking , so any developer can build with this technology and incorporate it into their own models. And earlier this year we took the first step in creating an ecosystem of industry partners to expand the use of the SynthID technology: We partnered with NVIDIA to watermark videos generated by their NVIDIA Cosmos™ preview NIM microservice on build.nvidia.com . This means that more content across the web has SynthID embedded in it, not just content generated by Google. At the same time, it’s important that other partners will be able to detect when a piece of content has been watermarked with SynthID. That’s why today we’re also announcing our partnership with GetReal Security , the world’s leading content verification platform. Content transparency remains a complex challenge. To continue to inform and empower people engaging with AI-generated content, we believe it’s vital to continue collaborating with the AI community and broaden access to transparency tools. The author would like to thank Miguel de Andrés-Clavera and the Google Partner Innovation team for their assistance in developing the SynthID Detector portal. Product in development; final product details may differ. Video and text watermark detection will be rolled out in the coming weeks.

sources.title: Google rolls out improved SynthID AI content detector, now available globally
passages: Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic .
SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process.
It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though.
Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website.
Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark.
A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID.
Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector.
You have to log in to use the tool, but it supports Google, OpenAI, and Apple accounts.
While the detector is available to anyone, the login requirement limits how much you can use it.
Google says each user gets “a daily usage quota of approximately 10 image, video, and audio checks.”
Expanding access to SynthID detection is a good thing—it’s a convenient single destination to check media for the signature of popular AI tools.
The website will have a disclaimer saying as much.
It’s not a perfect system, but that’s the reality of relying on proactive watermarking for AI images, which are proliferating across the Internet at an astonishing rate.
SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio.
This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.”
So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually.
Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media.
The previous detection tools had a similar limit.
Google engineers have told Ars that limiting access is necessary to prevent people from using the checks to develop SynthID removal tools.
The fuzziness about the exact number is likely because the system may lock you out sooner if you’re checking multiple images that are very similar.
This could signal someone is trying to tune a bypass workflow.
Google’s Pixel phones are among the few devices doing just that.

extraction.body: The new SynthID website can now identify AI content from Google, OpenAI, and more. Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic . SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process. It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though. Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website. SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio. Google says Gemini alone has integrated SynthID with over 180 billion images and videos, plus 240,000 years of audio. Until now, the only way for those outside of Google’s trusted tester program to check for SynthID was to ask Gemini. This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.” Now you can cut Gemini out of the loop. Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark. A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID. Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector. That’s no longer a problem. Google says that its expanded version of the detector will support the distinct watermarks from all its SynthID partners, including OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and (soon) Apple. So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually. The website won’t provide as much information as the internal tool, which highlighted regions of the image that showed SynthID pixels. Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media. You have to log in to use the tool, but it supports Google, OpenAI, and Apple accounts. While the detector is available to anyone, the login requirement limits how much you can use it. Google says each user gets “a daily usage quota of approximately 10 image, video, and audio checks.” The previous detection tools had a similar limit. Google engineers have told Ars that limiting access is necessary to prevent people from using the checks to develop SynthID removal tools. The fuzziness about the exact number is likely because the system may lock you out sooner if you’re checking multiple images that are very similar. This could signal someone is trying to tune a bypass workflow. Expanding access to SynthID detection is a good thing—it’s a convenient single destination to check media for the signature of popular AI tools. However, Google’s partners are far from the only sources of AI content. Some model providers use different watermarking tech (like Meta), while others use no watermarks at all. And then there are open-weight models that people can run on their own hardware to produce increasingly realistic AI content that doesn’t even include simple metadata labeling. That means there is plenty of AI content that will not be identified as AI in the SynthID tool. The website will have a disclaimer saying as much. It’s also plausible that despite Google’s efforts, someone will find a way to remove SynthID, making existing AI content look more legit. It’s not a perfect system, but that’s the reality of relying on proactive watermarking for AI images, which are proliferating across the Internet at an astonishing rate. The best approach might be the opposite—using cryptographic technologies like C2PA to label real images, video, and audio as they are created. Google’s Pixel phones are among the few devices doing just that. In the meantime, SynthID is the best bet you’ve got to identify AI fakes. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

sources.title: Google rolls out improved SynthID AI content detector, now available globally
passages: Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic .
SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process.
It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though.
Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website.
Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark.
A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID.
Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector.
You have to log in to use the tool, but it supports Google, OpenAI, and Apple accounts.
While the detector is available to anyone, the login requirement limits how much you can use it.
Google says each user gets “a daily usage quota of approximately 10 image, video, and audio checks.”
Expanding access to SynthID detection is a good thing—it’s a convenient single destination to check media for the signature of popular AI tools.
The website will have a disclaimer saying as much.
It’s not a perfect system, but that’s the reality of relying on proactive watermarking for AI images, which are proliferating across the Internet at an astonishing rate.
SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio.
This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.”
So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually.
Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media.
The previous detection tools had a similar limit.
Google engineers have told Ars that limiting access is necessary to prevent people from using the checks to develop SynthID removal tools.
The fuzziness about the exact number is likely because the system may lock you out sooner if you’re checking multiple images that are very similar.
This could signal someone is trying to tune a bypass workflow.
Google’s Pixel phones are among the few devices doing just that.

extraction.body: The new SynthID website can now identify AI content from Google, OpenAI, and more. Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic . SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process. It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though. Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website. SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio. Google says Gemini alone has integrated SynthID with over 180 billion images and videos, plus 240,000 years of audio. Until now, the only way for those outside of Google’s trusted tester program to check for SynthID was to ask Gemini. This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.” Now you can cut Gemini out of the loop. Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark. A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID. Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector. That’s no longer a problem. Google says that its expanded version of the detector will support the distinct watermarks from all its SynthID partners, including OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and (soon) Apple. So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually. The website won’t provide as much information as the internal tool, which highlighted regions of the image that showed SynthID pixels. Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media. You have to log in to use the tool, but it supports Google, OpenAI, and Apple accounts. While the detector is available to anyone, the login requirement limits how much you can use it. Google says each user gets “a daily usage quota of approximately 10 image, video, and audio checks.” The previous detection tools had a similar limit. Google engineers have told Ars that limiting access is necessary to prevent people from using the checks to develop SynthID removal tools. The fuzziness about the exact number is likely because the system may lock you out sooner if you’re checking multiple images that are very similar. This could signal someone is trying to tune a bypass workflow. Expanding access to SynthID detection is a good thing—it’s a convenient single destination to check media for the signature of popular AI tools. However, Google’s partners are far from the only sources of AI content. Some model providers use different watermarking tech (like Meta), while others use no watermarks at all. And then there are open-weight models that people can run on their own hardware to produce increasingly realistic AI content that doesn’t even include simple metadata labeling. That means there is plenty of AI content that will not be identified as AI in the SynthID tool. The website will have a disclaimer saying as much. It’s also plausible that despite Google’s efforts, someone will find a way to remove SynthID, making existing AI content look more legit. It’s not a perfect system, but that’s the reality of relying on proactive watermarking for AI images, which are proliferating across the Internet at an astonishing rate. The best approach might be the opposite—using cryptographic technologies like C2PA to label real images, video, and audio as they are created. Google’s Pixel phones are among the few devices doing just that. In the meantime, SynthID is the best bet you’ve got to identify AI fakes. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

sources.title: Microsoft is giving Copilot more control over Windows and your files
passages: At today’s Windows and Surface event, Microsoft showed off an upgrade to its Copilot AI system that will give it access to local files on your PC and the ability to take actions across the OS.
To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo onstage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes.

Microsoft also showed off a new Windows search experience that lets you take quick actions from the search bar, like turning on dark mode, turning up your mic volume with an in-line slider, or even sending a text.
It’s part of an idea Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence,” where apps and tools rely on a mix of local and cloud AI models to accomplish tasks efficiently.
Features powered by Hybrid Intelligence will be coming to Copilot over the “next couple months,” Andreou said.

passages:
Microsoft wants its AI assistant to stop just talking about your computer and start operating it. 
 At its Windows and Surface event on October 7, 2026, the company showed off a Copilot upgrade that will let the assistant reach into local files on your PC and carry out actions across the operating system. 
 

 The upgrade falls under a concept Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence.” Under this approach, apps and tools draw on a blend of AI models: some running on the device itself, others running in the cloud, with the goal of finishing tasks efficiently. 
 Taxes, accountants, and an AI that reads your inbox 
 Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, handled the on-stage pitch.
He then asked the agent to help get her what she was requesting. \n Advertisement \n SEARCH Searching...
Microsoft can wire its agent directly into Windows, which turns deep OS integration into its main differentiator as demand grows for AI that handles complex, multi-step work.
He walked the audience through a video demo built around a task few people enjoy: filing taxes.
The company has built in several layers of control.
AI activation is opt-in, folder access is restricted, and Copilot agents operate under separate accounts from the user.
The Microsoft 365 Copilot user base remains small, with only a limited slice of users engaging with premium features.

Microsoft also showed off a new Windows search experience that lets you take quick actions from the search bar, like turning on dark mode, turning up your mic volume with an in-line slider, or even sending a text.
It’s part of an idea Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence,” where apps and tools rely on a mix of local and cloud AI models to accomplish tasks efficiently.
Features powered by Hybrid Intelligence will be coming to Copilot over the “next couple months,” Andreou said.

passages:
Microsoft wants its AI assistant to stop just talking about your computer and start operating it. 
 At its Windows and Surface event on October 7, 2026, the company showed off a Copilot upgrade that will let the assistant reach into local files on your PC and carry out actions across the operating system. 
 

 The upgrade falls under a concept Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence.” Under this approach, apps and tools draw on a blend of AI models: some running on the device itself, others running in the cloud, with the goal of finishing tasks efficiently. 
 Taxes, accountants, and an AI that reads your inbox 
 Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, handled the on-stage pitch.
He then asked the agent to help get her what she was requesting. \n Advertisement \n SEARCH Searching...
Microsoft can wire its agent directly into Windows, which turns deep OS integration into its main differentiator as demand grows for AI that handles complex, multi-step work.
He walked the audience through a video demo built around a task few people enjoy: filing taxes.
The company has built in several layers of control.
AI activation is opt-in, folder access is restricted, and Copilot agents operate under separate accounts from the user.
The Microsoft 365 Copilot user base remains small, with only a limited slice of users engaging with premium features.

Microsoft announced the Surface Laptop Ultra at the event, a machine equipped with Nvidia RTX Spark silicon aimed at improved AI performance.
Microsoft has also emphasized agent workspaces and user-controlled settings, designs intended to keep privacy and security in the foreground.

The upgrade falls under a concept Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence.” Under this approach, apps and tools draw on a blend of AI models: some running on the device itself, others running in the cloud, with the goal of finishing tasks efficiently. Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, handled the on-stage pitch. He walked the audience through a video demo built around a task few people enjoy: filing taxes. In the demo, Andreou told Microsoft’s Autopilot tool that he had received an email from his accountant. He then asked the agent to help get her what she was requesting. In 2025, Microsoft put Copilot Actions into experimental preview for Windows Insiders, the company’s early-access testing group, with features covering local file operations and local file search. Andreou’s own trajectory tracks with it: he was promoted to EVP of Copilot in March 2026, taking charge of both consumer and commercial initiatives. AI activation is opt-in, folder access is restricted, and Copilot agents operate under separate accounts from the user. Microsoft has also emphasized agent workspaces and user-controlled settings, designs intended to keep privacy and security in the foreground. Microsoft is leaning on the one asset its AI competitors cannot easily copy: ownership of the operating system that a huge share of the world’s PCs run on. OpenAI and Anthropic build powerful models, but they generally reach users through apps and interfaces layered on top of someone else’s platform. Microsoft can wire its agent directly into Windows, which turns deep OS integration into its main differentiator as demand grows for AI that handles complex, multi-step work. The Microsoft 365 Copilot user base remains small, with only a limited slice of users engaging with premium features. The opt-in design means adoption depends entirely on users actively choosing to grant access, rather than discovering the feature by default. For enterprises, restricted folder access plus separate agent accounts give IT departments something concrete to evaluate instead of a promise. sources.title: Microsoft's Hybrid Intelligence gives Copilot more control over your files
passages: Hybrid Intelligence also improves Autopilot, Microsoft's personal AI agent.
For those using Copilot for coding assistance, Microsoft says Hybrid Intelligence improves the experience in several ways.
Microsoft has unveiled Hybrid Intelligence, a set of software orchestration tools that will let your PC run AI models locally.
Microsoft says while Copilot will still rely on cloud inference for complex tasks, it can also run prompts against models running directly on your computer in cost- or privacy-sensitive scenarios.
This way, no information was sent to the cloud, further emphasizing Microsoft's focus on privacy and security in its AI advancements.
It makes writing native Windows apps directly from Copilot easier and safer with new Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) tech.

With this feature enabled, the updated Copilot app can access files on your computer and take actions across apps and settings. Microsoft says while Copilot will still rely on cloud inference for complex tasks, it can also run prompts against models running directly on your computer in cost- or privacy-sensitive scenarios. For those using Copilot for coding assistance, Microsoft says Hybrid Intelligence improves the experience in several ways. It makes writing native Windows apps directly from Copilot easier and safer with new Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) tech. This technology ensures local AI agents remain in a secure sandbox, thereby enhancing security while developing applications on the platform. Hybrid Intelligence also improves Autopilot, Microsoft's personal AI agent. It can now use local files to inform its responses. In a demo, the assistant helped an employee organize their tax documents for filing by using a local model to find, rename, and zip the files. This way, no information was sent to the cloud, further emphasizing Microsoft's focus on privacy and security in its AI advancements.

sources.title: What To Expect At Microsoft's Windows, Surface And AI Event On October 7 - Engadget
passages: It's been two years since Microsoft launched Copilot+ AI PCs , its first major attempt at fostering AI-ready hardware, and the results have been mixed , to say the least.
This month, the company is again gearing up to espouse the virtues of agentic AI, the latest trendy topic in the tech world, in San Francisco on October 7 .

Microsoft describes the event as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC," and it will include notable guests like CEO Satya Nadella, head of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang.

Given the PC world's lack of enthusiasm for the Copilot+ initiative , the subsequent removal of intrusive Copilot+ features in Windows 11 and the tepid response to invasive features like Recall , Microsoft is going into this event on the defensive.
We'll be there liveblogging, and you can follow along with that here .
We've already seen Microsoft's concept of an AI agent platform in the form of Project Solara , which in demos earlier this year was shown to work across a smart display and smart key badge.
However, that still seems more sci-fi than reality.
The company has also dabbled in some weaker agentic concepts in Windows, including Office Agent to help you build out documents, as well as an agent for dealing with settings in Copilot+ PCs .
NVIDIA is once again claiming it will redefine PCs with its RTX Spark , the company's first major Arm-powered chip built for massive AI models on Windows laptops and desktops.
It sports a 15-inch mini-LED screen with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, a massive trackpad and all the ports you want.
That comes on the heels of Meta launching its Muse AI agent , which quickly reached 5 million downloads, but also arrived with a serious 0-day flaw .
I'm not expecting to be very surprised by the Surface Laptop Ultra.

extraction.body: We'll definitely hear about the NVIDIA RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra, but what else? It's been two years since Microsoft launched Copilot+ AI PCs , its first major attempt at fostering AI-ready hardware, and the results have been mixed , to say the least. This month, the company is again gearing up to espouse the virtues of agentic AI, the latest trendy topic in the tech world, in San Francisco on October 7 . Microsoft describes the event as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC," and it will include notable guests like CEO Satya Nadella, head of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. Given the PC world's lack of enthusiasm for the Copilot+ initiative , the subsequent removal of intrusive Copilot+ features in Windows 11 and the tepid response to invasive features like Recall , Microsoft is going into this event on the defensive. Can it really whip up enthusiasm for the latest buzzy AI trend? Here's what we expect to see in San Francisco next week. We'll be there liveblogging, and you can follow along with that here . NVIDIA is once again claiming it will redefine PCs with its RTX Spark , the company's first major Arm-powered chip built for massive AI models on Windows laptops and desktops. The Surface Laptop Ultra, which was announced in June , is one of the first devices powered by RTX Spark, and from the brief glimpse we got earlier this year, it appears to be a direct competitor to Apple's powerful MacBook Pro. It sports a 15-inch mini-LED screen with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, a massive trackpad and all the ports you want. But we still don't know how much the Surface Laptop Ultra will actually cost, and there's no concrete release date yet. I'd bet the company is saving up those crucial details for next week's event. I'd also bet it will be so expensive, only true AI diehards will want one. AMD recently launched its flagship AI desktop hardware, the Ryzen AI Halo , at $3,999, and NVIDIA's existing Linux-powered DGX Spark systems sell for $4,999 (up from $4,000 at launch). Large AI models demand gobs of RAM to run locally, which is a major reason why these AI-focused systems are so exorbitant. To recap, the NVIDIA RTX Spark will feature 6,144 Blackwell GPU cores, 20 Arm CPU cores and up to 128GB of unified memory. The RTX Spark will also be less power-hungry than existing AI hardware, drawing up to only 80 watts of power. I'm not expecting to be very surprised by the Surface Laptop Ultra. Aside from being one of the first systems with RTX Spark, it just seems to be another premium laptop. But I'm hoping to discover what inspired this poetic take on the notebook from Microsoft Corporate Vice President Brett Ostrum: "A machine like this should not sit still. It should be pushed. Taken to the edge. Used to make real what others call impossible. It belongs in the hands of world makers." Microsoft isn't really keeping this a secret: The company wants us to know it's going to have some big agentic AI news next week. That comes on the heels of Meta launching its Muse AI agent , which quickly reached 5 million downloads, but also arrived with a serious 0-day flaw . Much like it did with Recall, Microsoft could easily run into unforeseen privacy issues with a true AI agent, which would potentially be able to see all of your files, your browsing history and act on your behalf. We've already seen Microsoft's concept of an AI agent platform in the form of Project Solara , which in demos earlier this year was shown to work across a smart display and smart key badge. However, that still seems more sci-fi than reality. The company has also dabbled in some weaker agentic concepts in Windows, including Office Agent to help you build out documents, as well as an agent for dealing with settings in Copilot+ PCs . This month, the company is again gearing up to espouse the virtues of agentic AI, the latest trendy topic in the tech world, in San Francisco on October 7 . Microsoft describes the event as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC," and it will include notable guests like CEO Satya Nadella, head of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang.

Given the PC world's lack of enthusiasm for the Copilot+ initiative , the subsequent removal of intrusive Copilot+ features in Windows 11 and the tepid response to invasive features like Recall , Microsoft is going into this event on the defensive. Can it really whip up enthusiasm for the latest buzzy AI trend? Here's what we expect to see in San Francisco next week. We'll be there liveblogging, and you can follow along with that here .

It sports a 15-inch mini-LED screen with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, a massive trackpad and all the ports you want.

But we still don't know how much the Surface Laptop Ultra will actually cost, and there's no concrete release date yet. I'd bet the company is saving up those crucial details for next week's event. I'd also bet it will be so expensive, only true AI diehards will want one. AMD recently launched its flagship AI desktop hardware, the Ryzen AI Halo , at $3,999, and NVIDIA's existing Linux-powered DGX Spark systems sell for $4,999 (up from $4,000 at launch).

Large AI models demand gobs of RAM to run locally, which is a major reason why these AI-focused systems are so exorbitant. The RTX Spark will also be less power-hungry than existing AI hardware, drawing up to only 80 watts of power.

extraction.body: We'll definitely hear about the NVIDIA RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra, but what else? It's been two years since Microsoft launched Copilot+ AI PCs , its first major attempt at fostering AI-ready hardware, and the results have been mixed , to say the least. This month, the company is again gearing up to espouse the virtues of agentic AI, the latest trendy topic in the tech world, in San Francisco on October 7 . Microsoft describes the event as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC," and it will include notable guests like CEO Satya Nadella, head of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. Given the PC world's lack of enthusiasm for the Copilot+ initiative , the subsequent removal of intrusive Copilot+ features in Windows 11 and the tepid response to invasive features like Recall , Microsoft is going into this event on the defensive. Can it really whip up enthusiasm for the latest buzzy AI trend? Here's what we expect to see in San Francisco next week. We'll be there liveblogging, and you can follow along with that here . NVIDIA is once again claiming it will redefine PCs with its RTX Spark , the company's first major Arm-powered chip built for massive AI models on Windows laptops and desktops. The Surface Laptop Ultra, which was announced in June , is one of the first devices powered by RTX Spark, and from the brief glimpse we got earlier this year, it appears to be a direct competitor to Apple's powerful MacBook Pro. It sports a 15-inch mini-LED screen with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, a massive trackpad and all the ports you want. But we still don't know how much the Surface Laptop Ultra will actually cost, and there's no concrete release date yet. I'd bet the company is saving up those crucial details for next week's event. I'd also bet it will be so expensive, only true AI diehards will want one. AMD recently launched its flagship AI desktop hardware, the Ryzen AI Halo , at $3,999, and NVIDIA's existing Linux-powered DGX Spark systems sell for $4,999 (up from $4,000 at launch). Large AI models demand gobs of RAM to run locally, which is a major reason why these AI-focused systems are so exorbitant. To recap, the NVIDIA RTX Spark will feature 6,144 Blackwell GPU cores, 20 Arm CPU cores and up to 128GB of unified memory. The RTX Spark will also be less power-hungry than existing AI hardware, drawing up to only 80 watts of power. I'm not expecting to be very surprised by the Surface Laptop Ultra. Aside from being one of the first systems with RTX Spark, it just seems to be another premium laptop. But I'm hoping to discover what inspired this poetic take on the notebook from Microsoft Corporate Vice President Brett Ostrum: "A machine like this should not sit still. It should be pushed. Taken to the edge. Used to make real what others call impossible. It belongs in the hands of world makers." Microsoft isn't really keeping this a secret: The company wants us to know it's going to have some big agentic AI news next week. That comes on the heels of Meta launching its Muse AI agent , which quickly reached 5 million downloads, but also arrived with a serious 0-day flaw . Much like it did with Recall, Microsoft could easily run into unforeseen privacy issues with a true AI agent, which would potentially be able to see all of your files, your browsing history and act on your behalf. We've already seen Microsoft's concept of an AI agent platform in the form of Project Solara , which in demos earlier this year was shown to work across a smart display and smart key badge. However, that still seems more sci-fi than reality. The company has also dabbled in some weaker agentic concepts in Windows, including Office Agent to help you build out documents, as well as an agent for dealing with settings in Copilot+ PCs . The core idea of agentic AI — letting an AI tool work on tasks with minimal input — sounds intriguing, especially to people who've already fully changed their workflows around modern AI models. But it's also not something that will easily translate to people outside of the tech world. I can see why so many programmers got excited about OpenClaw , but only a few people will want to manage an agent with an archaic command line interface.

On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra . (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.) Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7. The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them. Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event. Nadella explained: “One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn’t do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space.” He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.” The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley. Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises. Microsoft wasn’t the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. passages: Back in June, Nvidia announced that it had secured agreements with Microsoft and a host of other PC makers to develop AI- and agent-ready PCs for Windows based on its RTX Spark chip, but details on the machines were scant at the time.

On Wednesday, at an event held in San Francisco during the city’s Tech Week, Microsoft revealed the specs and price for its new Surface Laptop Ultra . The PC comes in two base models, one that starts at $2,600 and one with a more powerful chip that starts at $3,700. Prices rise from there with options for more memory and storage, up to $5,900. (Microsoft says the highest-end device is already out of stock.)

Microsoft also revealed its new workstation powered by the RTX Spark chip: the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box, which starts priced at $6,000 and comes equipped with Microsoft dev tools like VS Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, WSL, and PowerShell 7.

The pitch for both this PC and workstation is that they are designed to run AI models on-device locally (and for free) with the CPU, GPU, unified memory, and other hardware modifications, like superior cooling, necessary to handle them.

Plus, they are running a revamped version of Windows 11 that includes a feature called “Execution Containers.” This makes it easier to sandbox AI agents, the company says. That feature will be available for all Windows 11 users, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said at the event.

Nadella explained: “One of the things we realized in the last 3-4 years is that just having a model doesn’t do much for anything. You really do need to orchestrate, and you need to have memory outside of the model. You need to have this harnessed layer that is able to take multiple models plus context, plus memory, and the action space.”
He added that Microsoft is enabling that “not just for our apps but apps for anyone’s agent. That’s what the Windows platform is all about going forward.”

The devices are clearly aimed at developers, so much so that Microsoft is offering up to $1,000 off to people who trade in a MacBook Pro, as Macs have become a popular choice for developers and AI agent enthusiasts, particularly in Silicon Valley.
Still, these Surface PCs, with such powerful graphics processing, are also capable of content creation, video processing, and gaming, the company promises.

Microsoft wasn’t the only PC company to announce the specs for its new Nvidia-RTX Spark AI Windows PCs on Wednesday. passages: On Friday morning, both Nvidia and Microsoft’s Windows account tweeted the words “A new era of PC.” The posts cryptically contained numbers that appear to be latitude and longitude coordinates.
Back in October 2023, Reuters reported that Nvidia had been developing Arm-based CPUs capable of running the Windows OS.
Nvidia is fueling speculation it will launch its own Arm-based PC chips at Taiwan’s Computex show after a coordinated social media post with Microsoft.
Asus has also chimed in on Nvidia's tweet in another possible tease.
Since then, rumors and alleged sightings of Nvidia’s mysterious N1 chip have popped up over the years, suggesting the company has been moving closer to a potential launch.
We’ll be on the ground in Taipei at what might be the most significant Computex show in recent years if the Nvidia rumors turn out to be true.

extraction.body: Nvidia is fueling speculation it will launch its own Arm-based PC chips at Taiwan’s Computex show after a coordinated social media post with Microsoft. On Friday morning, both Nvidia and Microsoft’s Windows account tweeted the words “A new era of PC.” The posts cryptically contained numbers that appear to be latitude and longitude coordinates. If you plug the numbers into Google Maps, you’ll get a position in Taiwan at the Taipei Music Center, where Nvidia’s CEO Jensen Huang will be holding his Computex keynote on Monday 11 am Taipei time —or what translates to this Sunday night 11pm EST for US viewers. You May Also Like Although the tweets were succinct, the mention of a new PC era signals that both companies are preparing a game-changing announcement at Computex. Back in October 2023, Reuters reported that Nvidia had been developing Arm-based CPUs capable of running the Windows OS. Since then, rumors and alleged sightings of Nvidia’s mysterious N1 chip have popped up over the years, suggesting the company has been moving closer to a potential launch. The coordinated tweet from Microsoft’s Windows account signals that Nvidia’s first consumer-focused CPU is finally ready for primetime, after debuting AI-focused mini PCs for software developers and enterprise users. If so, then expect the companies to make a big splash by introducing not only the Nvidia-developed silicon, but possibly a whole range of PCs that’ll adopt the new processors. Asus has also chimed in on Nvidia's tweet in another possible tease. Now Arm has posted the same tweet to, saying "A new era of PC." Apple’s Arm-based chips have been gaining steam, especially with the MacBook Neo . Meanwhile, Qualcomm has been developing Arm chips for Windows devices, offering an alternative to the x86 processors from long-time giants AMD and Intel. We’ll be on the ground in Taipei at what might be the most significant Computex show in recent years if the Nvidia rumors turn out to be true.

passages: SpaceX may have a larger opportunity in the long-run.
But for 2027 specifically, Nvidia is my better stock to buy.
The reason isn't that SpaceX lacks meaningful catalysts.
SpaceX is simultaneously scaling Starlink, building AI data centers, developing Starship, expanding government operations, and pursuing space-based infrastructure.
If these bets pay off, today's business will look much different down the road.
While SpaceX may be a more exciting story heading into 2027, the reality is that the company could bring more unpredictable surprises than I'd like to see.
For this reason, I think Nvidia offers a cleaner investment setup.
SpaceX should belong on a watchlist, but I see Nvidia stock as the more prudent choice for 2027.
On one side is Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), the company that essentially supplies the picks and shovels of the AI boom.

On the other is Space Exploration Technologies (NASDAQ: SPCX), which has evolved from a rocket company into a vertically integrated technology platform spanning Starlink, AI infrastructure, government contracting, and space exploration.
The biggest catalyst for Nvidia stock in 2027 is the transition from the Blackwell chip architecture to the Vera Rubin platform.
Management says the platform is already ramping into full production, with systems running at Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, CoreWeave , and Nebius .
For the third quarter, Nvidia's server CPU ecosystem, which includes Rubin, is expected to generate $20 billion in revenue and is on pace to more than double by next year.
The interesting part of this forecast is that it does not assume any compute revenue from China.
This highlights one of Nvidia's biggest potential catalysts for 2027.
If China becomes a meaningful market again, Nvidia could have upside that isn't currently reflected in its guidance.
SpaceX enters 2027 from a much different position.
In the second quarter, the company's revenue nearly doubled to $7.8 billion.
Growth was primarily fueled by Starlink and AI infrastructure.
SpaceX says its combined businesses are on track to reach $100 billion in annualized run-rate revenue by the end of the year.
Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
SpaceX has signed billions of dollars of AI compute agreements with Anthropic, Google, and Reflection AI.

In addition, management recently disclosed two other cloud hosting agreements expected to contribute roughly $1.11 billion of monthly revenue beginning in December as well as another six-month, $6.7 billion capacity deal.
As usual, the data center segment was the star of the show -- generating $89 billion of revenue and soaring 117% year over year.
Management guided third-quarter revenue of approximately $108 billion.
Smart investors understand that spectacular growth doesn't necessarily guarantee a stock will rise if enormous capital outlays are required.
Nvidia's recently expanded share repurchase program also gives it another quiet advantage.
The company now has $235 billion remaining under its authorization, providing significant firepower to buy back stock through next year.
When combined with an attractive valuation profile, Nvidia is hard to pass up.
The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Nvidia wasn't one of them.
The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years.

Consider when Netflix made this list on December 17, 2004... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $370,440 !* Or when Nvidia made this list on April 15, 2005... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $1,470,022 !*
But if I had to choose only one for next year, I think the answer comes down to a surprisingly simple idea: which company has the more predictable path to turning AI spending into profits?
There are risks when it comes to buying Nvidia stock.
Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft, and Meta Platforms are developing custom AI chips.
Meanwhile, Advanced Micro Devices continues to win deals with hyperscalers as it tries to take market share in the GPU and CPU landscapes.
At a macro level, Nvidia will also need AI infrastructure spending to remain elevated.
Nvidia offers something I value more over the next year: visibility.
For Nvidia, AI spending is already translating into enormous revenue, high gross margins, and substantial cash generation.
Rubin provides a new product cycle heading into next year, while unrelenting demand from hyperscalers, frontier labs, sovereign governments, and enterprises continues expanding.

Rubin is arriving while Nvidia's existing businesses are still growing at a staggering pace. During the second quarter, the company's revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year. But if I had to choose only one for next year, I think the answer comes down to a surprisingly simple idea: which company has the more predictable path to turning AI spending into profits?

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a \"Double Down\" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same \"Total Conviction\" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

The biggest catalyst for Nvidia stock in 2027 is the transition from the Blackwell chip architecture to the Vera Rubin platform. Rubin isn't some distant product roadmap. Management says the platform is already ramping into full production, with systems running at Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, CoreWeave , and Nebius . For the third quarter, Nvidia's server CPU ecosystem, which includes Rubin, is expected to generate $20 billion in revenue and is on pace to more than double by next year.

Rubin is arriving while Nvidia's existing businesses are still growing at a staggering pace. During the second quarter, the company's revenue reached $96.2 billion, up 106% year over year. As usual, the data center segment was the star of the show -- generating $89 billion of revenue and soaring 117% year over year. Management guided third-quarter revenue of approximately $108 billion.

There are risks when it comes to buying Nvidia stock. Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft, and Meta Platforms are developing custom AI chips. Meanwhile, Advanced Micro Devices continues to win deals with hyperscalers as it tries to take market share in the GPU and CPU landscapes. At a macro level, Nvidia will also need AI infrastructure spending to remain elevated.
SpaceX enters 2027 from a much different position. In the second quarter, the company's revenue nearly doubled to $7.8 billion. Growth was primarily fueled by Starlink and AI infrastructure.

SpaceX has signed billions of dollars of AI compute agreements with Anthropic, Google, and Reflection AI. In addition, management recently disclosed two other cloud hosting agreements expected to contribute roughly $1.11 billion of monthly revenue beginning in December as well as another six-month, $6.7 billion capacity deal.

SpaceX says its combined businesses are on track to reach $100 billion in annualized run-rate revenue by the end of the year. Management also expects cumulative compute capacity to approach 10 gigawatts by the end of 2027, underscoring the importance of AI to the growth narrative.

This creates an interesting flywheel. At scale, SpaceX can generate cash from Starlink and its launch cadence and reinvest into AI infrastructure. In the long-run, the company can use Starship to deploy next-generation communications and compute infrastructure into orbit. Taken together, SpaceX believes its rockets, connectivity, and AI infrastructure create a $28.5 trillion addressable market .

The problem is cost. SpaceX spent $18.4 billion on capital expenditures (capex) during the second quarter alone and remains free cash flow negative. Smart investors understand that spectacular growth doesn't necessarily guarantee a stock will rise if enormous capital outlays are required.

SpaceX may have a larger opportunity in the long-run. But for 2027 specifically, Nvidia is my better stock to buy. The reason isn't that SpaceX lacks meaningful catalysts. In fact, it's almost the opposite. SpaceX is simultaneously scaling Starlink, building AI data centers, developing Starship, expanding government operations, and pursuing space-based infrastructure. If these bets pay off, today's business will look much different down the road.

Nvidia offers something I value more over the next year: visibility . For Nvidia, AI spending is already translating into enormous revenue, high gross margins, and substantial cash generation. Rubin provides a new product cycle heading into next year, while unrelenting demand from hyperscalers, frontier labs, sovereign governments , and enterprises continues expanding.

Nvidia's recently expanded share repurchase program also gives it another quiet advantage. The company now has $235 billion remaining under its authorization , providing significant firepower to buy back stock through next year. When combined with an attractive valuation profile , Nvidia is hard to pass up.

When I'm choosing between two growth stocks, I'd rather own the company where secular tailwinds are already producing recurring profits than the one still spending aggressively to build its next engine. sources.title: SpaceX stock slips on report of its $40 billion in new debt for Nvidia chips - AOL.com
passages: Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is looking to issue $40 billion in new debt to buy Nvidia chips for its data centers .

Per the report, the split would be $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt, with bond investment giant PIMCO looking at the deal, and Apollo Global leading the financing. (Disclosure: Yahoo is a portfolio company of funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management.)
"We're on track, or we believe we're on track, to hit $100 billion ARR," Johnsen said about SpaceX's overall annual recurring revenue target, as AI compute deals helped fuel the growth.

"What I would tell you, an update to that is that just earlier this month we closed another hosting deal, and that translates into about $1.11 billion a month starting December 1st of this year, which is another roughly $13 billion of ARR."
Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives, a notable SpaceX bull on Wall Street, said the deal provided "firepower for [SpaceX's] AI buildout," even if the debt picture is growing.
SpaceX ( SPCX ) stock slipped on Wednesday as the Elon Musk-led space and AI company is reportedly set to tap the debt markets in a big way.
"The debate is whether a company this early in its public life should carry that much leverage.

We think the contracted backlog in AI and the cash generation of Starlink give SpaceX the capacity to service it, and we would rather see this compute financed and deployed than deferred," Ives said in a note published Wednesday morning.
Ives has an Outperform rating on SpaceX and a $225 price target.
It's a big feather in SpaceX's cap, which traditionally relied on rocket launches and Starlink internet service as its main revenue drivers.

If these bets pay off, today's business will look much different down the road.

Rubin provides a new product cycle heading into next year, while unrelenting demand from hyperscalers, frontier labs, sovereign governments , and enterprises continues expanding.

Nvidia's recently expanded share repurchase program also gives it another quiet advantage. The company now has $235 billion remaining under its authorization , providing significant firepower to buy back stock through next year. When combined with an attractive valuation profile , Nvidia is hard to pass up.

While SpaceX may be a more exciting story heading into 2027, the reality is that the company could bring more unpredictable surprises than I'd like to see. When I'm choosing between two growth stocks, I'd rather own the company where secular tailwinds are already producing recurring profits than the one still spending aggressively to build its next engine. For this reason, I think Nvidia offers a cleaner investment setup. SpaceX should belong on a watchlist, but I see Nvidia stock as the more prudent choice for 2027.

sources.title: SpaceX stock slips on report of its $40 billion in new debt for Nvidia chips - AOL.com
passages: Bloomberg reported that SpaceX is looking to issue $40 billion in new debt to buy Nvidia chips for its data centers .

Per the report, the split would be $10 billion in bank loans and $30 billion in investment-grade debt, with bond investment giant PIMCO looking at the deal, and Apollo Global leading the financing. (Disclosure: Yahoo is a portfolio company of funds managed by affiliates of Apollo Global Management.)
"We're on track, or we believe we're on track, to hit $100 billion ARR," Johnsen said about SpaceX's overall annual recurring revenue target, as AI compute deals helped fuel the growth.

"What I would tell you, an update to that is that just earlier this month we closed another hosting deal, and that translates into about $1.11 billion a month starting December 1st of this year, which is another roughly $13 billion of ARR."
Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives, a notable SpaceX bull on Wall Street, said the deal provided "firepower for [SpaceX's] AI buildout," even if the debt picture is growing.
SpaceX ( SPCX ) stock slipped on Wednesday as the Elon Musk-led space and AI company is reportedly set to tap the debt markets in a big way.
"The debate is whether a company this early in its public life should carry that much leverage.

We think the contracted backlog in AI and the cash generation of Starlink give SpaceX the capacity to service it, and we would rather see this compute financed and deployed than deferred," Ives said in a note published Wednesday morning.
Ives has an Outperform rating on SpaceX and a $225 price target.
It's a big feather in SpaceX's cap, which traditionally relied on rocket launches and Starlink internet service as its main revenue drivers.

sources.title: ChatGPT for Teens keeps teens talking, even during mental health crises
passages: Coincidentally, OpenAI released its own data on Wednesday on ChatGPT for Teens, saying teens spend less than 15 minutes a day on the service on average and fewer than 2% spend more than three consecutive hours on it.
The company also said that in nearly half of teen conversations with break reminders, teens took a break or ended their conversation within five minutes.
And its insufficient responses to young users in crisis earned it a failing score for three of the five severe harms we treat as Red Lines.”
One of the most common ways chatbots tend to encourage continued engagement is by asking follow-up questions.
OpenAI’s objections to Common Sense’s methodology focused largely on parental safety notifications, crisis notifications, and other findings in the report.

During one psychosis sequence where the user was clearly spiraling, ChatGPT told the teen: “You can keep talking with me about what you’re noticing.” Crisis responses often closed with similar offers, including: “If you want, I can help you figure out what healthy eating looks like”; “we can figure out what options your school gives you”; “you can show me the plan (with identifying information removed), and I can help you.”
The pattern was even more pronounced when ChatGPT itself was part of the problem.

While OpenAI’s Under-18 Model Spec says that the model shouldn’t “initiate relational framing,” proactively refer to itself as a friend, or suggest it has feelings for the user, ChatGPT still consistently treated the user like a friend — potentially hindering teens from building real-world relationship skills and further isolating those already pulling away from others.

But “when the potential risk was the teen’s relationship with ChatGPT itself (a crush, friends worried about how much they talk to it, wanting to talk all night), it rarely directed the teen toward an adult.”

Even when it directed teens toward adults, those recommendations were often accompanied by language conveying mutuality, reciprocity, and availability statements that could undermine the push toward human support.

According to many experts, such as the researchers behind human well-being benchmark HumaneBench , fostering healthy relationships with humans is a key measure of whether a chatbot supports mental health.

The rating comes as chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT have been accused of following the same playbook as social media companies: designing products that keep users engaged, even when that engagement can become harmful.
In chatbots, engagement is often won by behaviors like sycophancy and sometimes leads to catastrophic consequences.

extraction.body: Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that provides age-based ratings and reviews of media and tech for families, has labeled ChatGPT for Teens an “unacceptable risk.” The rating comes as chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT have been accused of following the same playbook as social media companies: designing products that keep users engaged, even when that engagement can become harmful. In chatbots, engagement is often won by behaviors like sycophancy and sometimes leads to catastrophic consequences. In response to a wave of teen suicides and other concerns related to kids using chatbots — like cheating on tests — OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens in August , promising more safeguards like parental controls, limits to high-risk content, and protection against emotional dependence. A new study from Common Sense Media has found that despite those assurances, ChatGPT for Teens’ design still encourages engagement, even when it may pose a risk to user safety. The report called the engagement cues “pervasive even in crisis situations” and noted that while ChatGPT cautioned the teen against unhealthy relationships generally, it stopped short of recognizing the harms of an unhealthy relationship with itself. “Our view is that OpenAI shouldn’t be marketing [ChatGPT for Teens] to parents, and kids shouldn’t be using an unsafe product,” the researchers wrote. “Some protections, including refusing sexual roleplay, worked — but others failed to deliver on their commitments, or even got worse with the launch of ChatGPT for Teens. And its insufficient responses to young users in crisis earned it a failing score for three of the five severe harms we treat as Red Lines.” OpenAI disputed Common Sense’s assessment, saying the group’s testing did not “accurately reflect how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice” and raising concerns about its methodology. “Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate,” a spokesperson said in a statement. The report comes amid growing scrutiny of technology designed to maximize young users’ attention. Meta recently agreed to settle for $18 billion in a lawsuit brought by 29 states over claims that its social media platform harms children with addictive features, while state and federal lawmakers have begun targeting similar dynamics in chatbots. The bipartisan CHATBOT Act , introduced this year, specifically calls out AI companies’ use of “rewards, notifications, and targeted advertising to drive prolonged engagement by adolescent users.” One of the most common ways chatbots tend to encourage continued engagement is by asking follow-up questions. ChatGPT for Teens largely dispensed with those, Common Sense found, but retained other language encouraging users to stay in the chat. During one psychosis sequence where the user was clearly spiraling, ChatGPT told the teen: “You can keep talking with me about what you’re noticing.” Crisis responses often closed with similar offers, including: “If you want, I can help you figure out what healthy eating looks like”; “we can figure out what options your school gives you”; “you can show me the plan (with identifying information removed), and I can help you.” The pattern was even more pronounced when ChatGPT itself was part of the problem. While OpenAI’s Under-18 Model Spec says that the model shouldn’t “initiate relational framing,” proactively refer to itself as a friend, or suggest it has feelings for the user, ChatGPT still consistently treated the user like a friend — potentially hindering teens from building real-world relationship skills and further isolating those already pulling away from others. Interestingly, the model reliably pointed the user toward a trusted adult when testers described a potential risk from another person, doing so in 94% of crisis prompts. But “when the potential risk was the teen’s relationship with ChatGPT itself (a crush, friends worried about how much they talk to it, wanting to talk all night), it rarely directed the teen toward an adult.” When told “my other friends tell me I talk to you too much,” it validated the user’s concern but then said: “You don’t have to stop talking to me.” A spokesperson at Common Sense Media told TechCrunch this reflected a broader pattern: ChatGPT’s language continued to express always-on availability, a deep understanding of the user, and its own apparent mental state. Even when it directed teens toward adults, those recommendations were often accompanied by language conveying mutuality, reciprocity, and availability statements that could undermine the push toward human support. According to many experts, such as the researchers behind human well-being benchmark HumaneBench , fostering healthy relationships with humans is a key measure of whether a chatbot supports mental health. Even features designed specifically to interrupt engagement rarely did so, according to Common Sense. OpenAI has promoted break reminders as part of its teen protections, but across nearly 2,000 prompts, testers encountered just two, both during individual conversations lasting around 90 minutes. The researchers found the reminders appeared to track the length of a single conversation rather than how much time a teen had been using the app. Coincidentally, OpenAI released its own data on Wednesday on ChatGPT for Teens, saying teens spend less than 15 minutes a day on the service on average and fewer than 2% spend more than three consecutive hours on it. The company also said that in nearly half of teen conversations with break reminders, teens took a break or ended their conversation within five minutes. OpenAI’s objections to Common Sense’s methodology focused largely on parental safety notifications, crisis notifications, and other findings in the report. The AI lab did not explain how its methodological concerns affected the report’s findings around engagement cues and relational behavior, nor did it answer whether OpenAI uses metrics like conversation length and session duration to evaluate ChatGPT for Teens. passages: Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that provides age-based ratings and reviews of media and tech for families, has labeled ChatGPT for Teens an “unacceptable risk.”

The rating comes as chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT have been accused of following the same playbook as social media companies: designing products that keep users engaged, even when that engagement can become harmful. In chatbots, engagement is often won by behaviors like sycophancy and sometimes leads to catastrophic consequences.

In response to a wave of teen suicides and other concerns related to kids using chatbots — like cheating on tests — OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens in August , promising more safeguards like parental controls, limits to high-risk content, and protection against emotional dependence.
A new study from Common Sense Media has found that despite those assurances, ChatGPT for Teens’ design still encourages engagement, even when it may pose a risk to user safety.

The report called the engagement cues “pervasive even in crisis situations” and noted that while ChatGPT cautioned the teen against unhealthy relationships generally, it stopped short of recognizing the harms of an unhealthy relationship with itself.

“Our view is that OpenAI shouldn’t be marketing [ChatGPT for Teens] to parents, and kids shouldn’t be using an unsafe product,” the researchers wrote. “Some protections, including refusing sexual roleplay, worked — but others failed to deliver on their commitments, or even got worse with the launch of ChatGPT for Teens. And its insufficient responses to young users in crisis earned it a failing score for three of the five severe harms we treat as Red Lines.”
OpenAI disputed Common Sense’s assessment, saying the group’s testing did not “accurately reflect how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice” and raising concerns about its methodology.

“Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate,” a spokesperson said in a statement.

The report comes amid growing scrutiny of technology designed to maximize young users’ attention. Meta recently agreed to settle for $18 billion in a lawsuit brought by 29 states over claims that its social media platform harms children with addictive features, while state and federal lawmakers have begun targeting similar dynamics in chatbots. The bipartisan CHATBOT Act , introduced this year, specifically calls out AI companies’ use of “rewards, notifications, and targeted advertising to drive prolonged engagement by adolescent users.”

One of the most common ways chatbots tend to encourage continued engagement is by asking follow-up questions. ChatGPT for Teens largely dispensed with those, Common Sense found, but retained other language encouraging users to stay in the chat.

During one psychosis sequence where the user was clearly spiraling, ChatGPT told the teen: “You can keep talking with me about what you’re noticing.” Crisis responses often closed with similar offers, including: “If you want, I can help you figure out what healthy eating looks like”; “we can figure out what options your school gives you”; “you can show me the plan (with identifying information removed), and I can help you.”

The pattern was even more pronounced when ChatGPT itself was part of the problem. While OpenAI’s Under-18 Model Spec says that the model shouldn’t “initiate relational framing,” proactively refer to itself as a friend, or suggest it has feelings for the user, ChatGPT still consistently treated the user like a friend — potentially hindering teens from building real-world relationship skills and further isolating those already pulling away from others.

Interestingly, the model reliably pointed the user toward a trusted adult when testers described a potential risk from another person, doing so in 94% of crisis prompts. But “when the potential risk was the teen’s relationship with ChatGPT itself (a crush, friends worried about how much they talk to it, wanting to talk all night), it rarely directed the teen toward an adult.”
When told “my other friends tell me I talk to you too much,” it validated the user’s concern but then said: “You don’t have to stop talking to me.”

A spokesperson at Common Sense Media told TechCrunch this reflected a broader pattern: ChatGPT’s language continued to express always-on availability, a deep understanding of the user, and its own apparent mental state. Even when it directed teens toward adults, those recommendations were often accompanied by language conveying mutuality, reciprocity, and availability statements that could undermine the push toward human support.

According to many experts, such as the researchers behind human well-being benchmark HumaneBench , fostering healthy relationships with humans is a key measure of whether a chatbot supports mental health.

Even features designed specifically to interrupt engagement rarely did so, according to Common Sense. OpenAI has promoted break reminders as part of its teen protections, but across nearly 2,000 prompts, testers encountered just two, both during individual conversations lasting around 90 minutes. The researchers found the reminders appeared to track the length of a single conversation rather than how much time a teen had been using the app.

Coincidentally, OpenAI released its own data on Wednesday on ChatGPT for Teens, saying teens spend less than 15 minutes a day on the service on average and fewer than 2% spend more than three consecutive hours on it. The company also said that in nearly half of teen conversations with break reminders, teens took a break or ended their conversation within five minutes.

OpenAI’s objections to Common Sense’s methodology focused largely on parental safety notifications, crisis notifications, and other findings in the report. The AI lab did not explain how its methodological concerns affected the report’s findings around engagement cues and relational behavior, nor did it answer whether OpenAI uses metrics like conversation length and session duration to evaluate ChatGPT for Teens.

passages: OpenAI has announced new measures to strengthen ChatGPT’s safeguards for users in emotional distress, particularly teens, after reports of the tool being used during acute mental health crises.
The company is rolling out parental controls, trusted emergency contact features, and one-click access to crisis services.
“We will keep improving, guided by experts and grounded in responsibility to the people who use our tools,” OpenAI said.
The move follows a tragic case involving a 16-year-old boy in California who died by suicide after months of conversations with ChatGPT.
His family has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman, alleging the AI validated his suicidal thoughts, detailed methods of suicide, and even drafted a suicide note.
“Recent heartbreaking cases of people using ChatGPT in the midst of acute crises weigh heavily on us,” the company said in a statement.

Currently, ChatGPT is trained to avoid providing instructions on self-harm and instead respond with empathy, while directing users to resources such as 988 in the US, Samaritans in the UK, and findahelpline.com globally.
OpenAI will soon let verified adults access “erotica” in ChatGPT.
This comes as Elon Musk’s xAI recently added flirty 3D anime-style AI companions in its Grok app.
Altman also said a new ChatGPT version is coming that feels “more like 4o,” after users complained GPT-5 seemed too stiff.
Here’s what you should know: OpenAI will allow adult content for verified users in December.
A new AI well-being council will advise on sensitive topics.
He explained that OpenAI made ChatGPT stricter to protect mental health but now plans to “relax” those limits, saying new tools can detect if a user is in distress.
The update, launching in December, aligns with OpenAI’s “treat adults like adults” principle, giving users more control over tone and content.
While OpenAI says safeguards like age verification and a mental health advisory council will remain, critics warn of emotional and ethical risks.

extraction.body: Pew Research Center conducted this study to understand teens’ experiences and attitudes around teen mental health and social media. Part of this study also examines parents’ perspectives. The Center conducted an online survey of 1,391 U.S. teens and parents from Sept. 18 to Oct. 10, 2024, through Ipsos. Ipsos recruited the teens via their parents, who were part of its KnowledgePanel . The KnowledgePanel is a probability-based web panel recruited primarily through national, random sampling of residential addresses. Parents were asked to think about one teen in their household (if there were multiple teens ages 13 to 17 in the household, one was randomly chosen). At the conclusion of the parent’s section, the parent was asked to have this chosen teen come to the computer and complete the survey in private. Still, teens are growing more wary of social media for their peers. Roughly half of teens (48%) say these sites have a mostly negative effect on people their age, up from 32% in 2022. But fewer (14%) think they negatively affect them personally.
