coreStoryFacts.text: Robinhood has added approximately $25 million worth of bitcoin to its corporate balance sheet, marking a significant step in its growing involvement in cryptocurrency.
This move, confirmed by Robinhood's senior VP Johann Kerbrat, reflects the company's deep commitment to bitcoin and the crypto ecosystem.
Robinhood continues to expand its crypto offerings, including launching an Ethereum-compatible network and tokenized stock products, indicating ongoing growth in its crypto business.

The posture is.As recently as November 2025, at Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call, incoming CFO Shiv Verma said the company was "still thinking about" the move, weighing the community-alignment benefit against the cost of tying up capital, and raising the question of whether adding Bitcoin to the balance sheet makes any decision for shareholders who can already buy BTC directly through the Robinhood platform.

Robinhood's first balance sheet purchase came roughly nine months after the rule took effect for most companies.What a HOOD Shareholder Actually FacesHere is the structural consequence the headline dollar amount does not fully communicate.Robinhood's revenue is already substantially correlated with Bitcoin prices.

More than 140 publicly traded companies had adopted Bitcoin treasury positions in the first quarter of 2026 alone, with corporate treasuries collectively adding roughly 62,000 BTC in that quarter.Robinhood has not disclosed a formal BTC accumulation policy, and Kerbrat's language — emphasizing conviction over capital deployment — signals the company is not attempting to replicate Strategy's leveraged, all-in approach.Why Robinhood Chain Makes This More Than SymbolicRobinhood's Bitcoin balance sheet purchase did not arrive in isolation.

Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy), which had already adopted the standard early, described it in its Q1 2025 filing as likely to "have a material impact on our financial results, increase the volatility of our financial results and affect the carrying value of our bitcoin on our balance sheet."The ASU 2023-08 fair-value rule removed the structural disincentive for operating companies to hold BTC.

When prices rise, the reverse applies, but the point stands structurally: HOOD shareholders face Bitcoin price exposure on two separate lines of the income statement simultaneously, and neither exposure hedges the other.This makes Robinhood's position categorically different from both ends of the corporate Bitcoin spectrum.
In Q4 2024, crypto trading accounted for 53% of Robinhood's transaction-based revenue — then fell to 12.88% in Q2 2026 when Bitcoin's price declined.

Robinhood has made its first proprietary Bitcoin purchase, putting approximately $25 million of company money into BTC — crossing a threshold that separates platforms that merely facilitate Bitcoin trading from companies that actually hold it.

Standard Chartered's Global Head of Digital Assets Research, Geoffrey Kendrick, has raised related concerns about the broader corporate treasury trend, warning that "Bitcoin treasuries are adding to Bitcoin buying pressure for now, but we see a risk that this may reverse over time."Neither warning is directed at Robinhood specifically.

Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy), which holds approximately 848,000 BTC as of early October 2026 — roughly 69% of all Bitcoin owned by listed companies — is a leveraged BTC pure-play; its equity is designed to move with Bitcoin, and shareholders self-select for that risk.
A post circulating on social media before Wednesday's DAS Asia disclosure cited this figure and claimed Robinhood was a massive Bitcoin holder.
Under the old US GAAP model for crypto assets, companies could only write down Bitcoin holdings when prices fell — but could never recognize gains when prices rose.
But both apply with particular force to an operating company that already earns substantially from Bitcoin trading activity.Custody vs.
Robinhood had 27.4 million funded customers and held $307 billion in platform assets as of Q1 2026.

Those $25 billion in crypto assets spread across Robinhood's customer custody wallets belong entirely to Robinhood's customers — Robinhood holds the private keys, but the coins are not on Robinhood's own books.The $25 million corporate BTC purchase is a different category.

The distinction matters for both accounting and risk: customer custody creates zero direct P&L exposure for Robinhood (it earns custody-related revenue from fees and services, not from BTC price movements).
MARA Holdings and other Bitcoin miners hold substantial secondary positions.

Among traditional, non-Bitcoin-native operating companies, Robinhood joins Tesla and Block (the payments company founded by Jack Dorsey) in what analysts describe as symbolic or diversification allocations rather than primary treasury strategies.The corporate treasury trend has also been bolstered by the FASB accounting shift.

Robinhood has taken a direct stake in bitcoin, adding roughly $25 million of the cryptocurrency to its corporate balance sheet and joining a growing list of public companies treating the token as a treasury asset rather than merely a product for customers.
Bitcoin traded near $84,000 at the time of the disclosure, having closed around $85,540 on Oct.
The move marks a shift in tone from the company's posture just under a year ago, when executives had expressed caution about holding volatile crypto assets on the corporate books.
Robinhood has for years facilitated customer trading in digital tokens, but those holdings are segregated from company treasury assets and do not expose the firm to bitcoin's price swings.

sources.title: Robinhood Puts $25M Bitcoin on Its Balance Sheet; HOOD Now Has Double BTC Exposure
passages: The posture is.As recently as November 2025, at Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call, incoming CFO Shiv Verma said the company was "still thinking about" the move, weighing the community-alignment benefit against the cost of tying up capital, and raising the question of whether adding Bitcoin to the balance sheet makes any decision for shareholders who can already buy BTC directly through the Robinhood platform.

Robinhood's first balance sheet purchase came roughly nine months after the rule took effect for most companies.What a HOOD Shareholder Actually FacesHere is the structural consequence the headline dollar amount does not fully communicate.Robinhood's revenue is already substantially correlated with Bitcoin prices.

More than 140 publicly traded companies had adopted Bitcoin treasury positions in the first quarter of 2026 alone, with corporate treasuries collectively adding roughly 62,000 BTC in that quarter.Robinhood has not disclosed a formal BTC accumulation policy, and Kerbrat's language — emphasizing conviction over capital deployment — signals the company is not attempting to replicate Strategy's leveraged, all-in approach.Why Robinhood Chain Makes This More Than SymbolicRobinhood's Bitcoin balance sheet purchase did not arrive in isolation.

Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy), which had already adopted the standard early, described it in its Q1 2025 filing as likely to "have a material impact on our financial results, increase the volatility of our financial results and affect the carrying value of our bitcoin on our balance sheet."The ASU 2023-08 fair-value rule removed the structural disincentive for operating companies to hold BTC.

When prices rise, the reverse applies, but the point stands structurally: HOOD shareholders face Bitcoin price exposure on two separate lines of the income statement simultaneously, and neither exposure hedges the other.This makes Robinhood's position categorically different from both ends of the corporate Bitcoin spectrum.
In Q4 2024, crypto trading accounted for 53% of Robinhood's transaction-based revenue — then fell to 12.88% in Q2 2026 when Bitcoin's price declined.

Robinhood has made its first proprietary Bitcoin purchase, putting approximately $25 million of company money into BTC — crossing a threshold that separates platforms that merely facilitate Bitcoin trading from companies that actually hold it.

Standard Chartered's Global Head of Digital Assets Research, Geoffrey Kendrick, has raised related concerns about the broader corporate treasury trend, warning that "Bitcoin treasuries are adding to Bitcoin buying pressure for now, but we see a risk that this may reverse over time."Neither warning is directed at Robinhood specifically.

Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy), which holds approximately 848,000 BTC as of early October 2026 — roughly 69% of all Bitcoin owned by listed companies — is a leveraged BTC pure-play; its equity is designed to move with Bitcoin, and shareholders self-select for that risk.
A post circulating on social media before Wednesday's DAS Asia disclosure cited this figure and claimed Robinhood was a massive Bitcoin holder.
Under the old US GAAP model for crypto assets, companies could only write down Bitcoin holdings when prices fell — but could never recognize gains when prices rose.
But both apply with particular force to an operating company that already earns substantially from Bitcoin trading activity.Custody vs.
Robinhood had 27.4 million funded customers and held $307 billion in platform assets as of Q1 2026.

Those $25 billion in crypto assets spread across Robinhood's customer custody wallets belong entirely to Robinhood's customers — Robinhood holds the private keys, but the coins are not on Robinhood's own books.The $25 million corporate BTC purchase is a different category.

The distinction matters for both accounting and risk: customer custody creates zero direct P&L exposure for Robinhood (it earns custody-related revenue from fees and services, not from BTC price movements).
MARA Holdings and other Bitcoin miners hold substantial secondary positions.

Among traditional, non-Bitcoin-native operating companies, Robinhood joins Tesla and Block (the payments company founded by Jack Dorsey) in what analysts describe as symbolic or diversification allocations rather than primary treasury strategies.The corporate treasury trend has also been bolstered by the FASB accounting shift.

extraction.body: Robinhood has made its first proprietary Bitcoin purchase, putting approximately $25 million of company money into BTC — crossing a threshold that separates platforms that merely facilitate Bitcoin trading from companies that actually hold it. He framed the purchase as conviction, not capital reallocation — "it represents how deeply we care about bitcoin and the ecosystem around it" — and was direct about the scale relative to the company: "Robinhood is a massive company at this point, with a market cap in the $100 billion range. So the $25 million worth of bitcoin is not going to change a lot of the current trajectory of the company."The gap between the $25 million purchase and the $100 billion valuation is deliberate. Robinhood had 27.4 million funded customers and held $307 billion in platform assets as of Q1 2026. A $25 million BTC position is 0.025% of its market cap. The posture is.As recently as November 2025, at Robinhood's third-quarter earnings call, incoming CFO Shiv Verma said the company was "still thinking about" the move, weighing the community-alignment benefit against the cost of tying up capital, and raising the question of whether adding Bitcoin to the balance sheet makes any decision for shareholders who can already buy BTC directly through the Robinhood platform. That deliberation about Bitcoin treasury has now closed.What Changed — and Why It Required an Accounting Rule to Change FirstRobinhood did not buy Bitcoin in 2024 or early 2025 even as corporate BTC adoption accelerated around it. The accounting environment is part of the reason. Under the old US GAAP model for crypto assets, companies could only write down Bitcoin holdings when prices fell — but could never recognize gains when prices rose. A corporate Bitcoin position in 2023 created asymmetric accounting punishment: losses hit the income statement, gains were invisible until the asset was sold. That model made holding BTC on an operating company's books artificially punitive.That changed with FASB Accounting Standards Update 2023-08, issued December 13, 2023 and effective for fiscal years beginning after December 15, 2024. Under ASU 2023-08, in-scope crypto assets — Bitcoin included — must be measured at fair value at every reporting date, with gains and losses flowing through net income each quarter. Strategy (formerly MicroStrategy), which had already adopted the standard early, described it in its Q1 2025 filing as likely to "have a material impact on our financial results, increase the volatility of our financial results and affect the carrying value of our bitcoin on our balance sheet."The ASU 2023-08 fair-value rule removed the structural disincentive for operating companies to hold BTC. Robinhood's first balance sheet purchase came roughly nine months after the rule took effect for most companies.What a HOOD Shareholder Actually FacesHere is the structural consequence the headline dollar amount does not fully communicate.Robinhood's revenue is already substantially correlated with Bitcoin prices. In Q4 2024, crypto trading accounted for 53% of Robinhood's transaction-based revenue — then fell to 12.88% in Q2 2026 when Bitcoin's price declined. When BTC drops, Robinhood's trading volumes compress and its crypto transaction revenue contracts. This has been true since the company launched crypto trading.What is new is that the $25 million corporate Bitcoin position is now marked to market every quarter under ASU 2023-08. When Bitcoin prices fall, Robinhood's quarterly earnings will now reflect unrealized losses on its corporate BTC holding — in addition to the revenue contraction from lower trading volumes. When prices rise, the reverse applies, but the point stands structurally: HOOD shareholders face Bitcoin price exposure on two separate lines of the income statement simultaneously, and neither exposure hedges the other.This makes Robinhood's position categorically different from both ends of the corporate Bitcoin spectrum. Strategy (the company formerly known as MicroStrategy), which holds approximately 848,000 BTC as of early October 2026 — roughly 69% of all Bitcoin owned by listed companies — is a leveraged BTC pure-play; its equity is designed to move with Bitcoin, and shareholders self-select for that risk. Robinhood sits in a new category: an operating company whose revenue is already Bitcoin-correlated and whose balance sheet is now also Bitcoin-marked-to-market."Cryptocurrencies' high volatility and uncertain regulatory landscape are misaligned with the fundamental goals of treasury management — stability, liquidity, and capital preservation," David Krause, a finance professor at Marquette University, noted in a January 2026 research publication on corporate Bitcoin holdings. Standard Chartered's Global Head of Digital Assets Research, Geoffrey Kendrick, has raised related concerns about the broader corporate treasury trend, warning that "Bitcoin treasuries are adding to Bitcoin buying pressure for now, but we see a risk that this may reverse over time."Neither warning is directed at Robinhood specifically. But both apply with particular force to an operating company that already earns substantially from Bitcoin trading activity.Custody vs. Corporate: Why the Numbers Look ConfusingRobinhood controls approximately $25 billion in crypto assets across approximately 1.7 million wallet addresses on 12 different blockchains. A post circulating on social media before Wednesday's DAS Asia disclosure cited this figure and claimed Robinhood was a massive Bitcoin holder. Those $25 billion in crypto assets spread across Robinhood's customer custody wallets belong entirely to Robinhood's customers — Robinhood holds the private keys, but the coins are not on Robinhood's own books.The $25 million corporate BTC purchase is a different category. It sits on Robinhood's own balance sheet, subject to FASB ASU 2023-08 quarterly fair-value measurement. The distinction matters for both accounting and risk: customer custody creates zero direct P&L exposure for Robinhood (it earns custody-related revenue from fees and services, not from BTC price movements). The corporate position creates direct earnings exposure every quarter.Bitcoin was trading near $83,360 at the time of the DAS Asia disclosure, per CoinDesk market data.Robinhood's Position in the Corporate Bitcoin LandscapeWith the purchase, Robinhood joins a cohort that has expanded dramatically since Strategy made its initial $250 million BTC purchase in August 2020. More than 170 publicly traded companies worldwide now hold Bitcoin on their balance sheets, with combined corporate holdings exceeding 1.2 million BTC — representing more than 6% of Bitcoin's hard-capped supply of 21 million coins.Strategy remains the dominant holder by orders of magnitude. At approximately 848,000 BTC, it accounts for roughly 69% of all corporate-held Bitcoin globally. MARA Holdings and other Bitcoin miners hold substantial secondary positions. Among traditional, non-Bitcoin-native operating companies, Robinhood joins Tesla and Block (the payments company founded by Jack Dorsey) in what analysts describe as symbolic or diversification allocations rather than primary treasury strategies.The corporate treasury trend has also been bolstered by the FASB accounting shift. More than 140 publicly traded companies had adopted Bitcoin treasury positions in the first quarter of 2026 alone, with corporate treasuries collectively adding roughly 62,000 BTC in that quarter.Robinhood has not disclosed a formal BTC accumulation policy, and Kerbrat's language — emphasizing conviction over capital deployment — signals the company is not attempting to replicate Strategy's leveraged, all-in approach.Why Robinhood Chain Makes This More Than SymbolicRobinhood's Bitcoin balance sheet purchase did not arrive in isolation. It follows 98 days after Robinhood Chain — the company's permissionless Ethereum Layer 2 network built on Arbitrum's Orbit stack — went live on mainnet on July 1, 2026. The chain carries chain ID 4663, processes transactions off the Ethereum mainchain in rollup batches before settling back to Ethereum for security, and uses ETH as its native gas token.Since its mainnet debut, Robinhood Chain has added tokenized stock and ETF products (Stock Tokens), a US dollar stablecoin (USDG), and a yield-bearing lending product called Robinhood Earn.

passages: Robinhood has taken a direct stake in bitcoin, adding roughly $25 million of the cryptocurrency to its corporate balance sheet and joining a growing list of public companies treating the token as a treasury asset rather than merely a product for customers.
Bitcoin traded near $84,000 at the time of the disclosure, having closed around $85,540 on Oct.
The move marks a shift in tone from the company's posture just under a year ago, when executives had expressed caution about holding volatile crypto assets on the corporate books.
Robinhood has for years facilitated customer trading in digital tokens, but those holdings are segregated from company treasury assets and do not expose the firm to bitcoin's price swings.
That brings its total holdings to 848,000 bitcoin, far eclipsing any other corporate treasury.

Robinhood's $25 million allocation is modest by comparison, but it carries outsized symbolic weight given the brokerage's visibility among retail investors and its more than 28 million funded customers globally.

extraction.body: Robinhood has taken a direct stake in bitcoin, adding roughly $25 million of the cryptocurrency to its corporate balance sheet and joining a growing list of public companies treating the token as a treasury asset rather than merely a product for customers. The purchase was disclosed Wednesday by Johann Kerbrat, Robinhood's senior vice president and general manager of crypto and international, during an interview with The Block's Starting Block program at the Digital Asset Summit Asia conference in Singapore. The company has not separately confirmed the transaction through a press release or regulatory filing. "We care deeply about bitcoin and the ecosystem around it," Kerbrat said. "For us, it's more aligning our company and our vision with the crypto community." The executive was careful to frame the allocation as a strategic signal rather than a financial bet that would reshape the company's trajectory. With Robinhood's market capitalization hovering around $100 billion, he noted, a $25 million bitcoin position "is not going to change a lot of the current trajectory of the company." The move marks a shift in tone from the company's posture just under a year ago, when executives had expressed caution about holding volatile crypto assets on the corporate books. Robinhood has for years facilitated customer trading in digital tokens, but those holdings are segregated from company treasury assets and do not expose the firm to bitcoin's price swings. The new allocation changes that dynamic, giving Robinhood direct exposure to the cryptocurrency's market value. Robinhood now stands alongside more than 170 publicly traded companies worldwide that hold bitcoin as a corporate asset, a trend that Strategy (NASDAQ:MSTR) initiated in 2020 when it began converting cash reserves into the cryptocurrency. Current corporate holders include Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA), Block (NYSE:XYZ), MARA Holdings (NASDAQ:MARA), CleanSpark (NASDAQ:CLSK) and Riot Platforms (NASDAQ:RIOT). Together, those firms and others account for well over 1.2 million bitcoin on their balance sheets. Strategy continues to add to its position. The company disclosed this week that it purchased an additional 334 bitcoin between Sept. 28 and Oct. 4 for roughly $28.7 million, at an average price of $85,838.80 per coin. That brings its total holdings to 848,000 bitcoin, far eclipsing any other corporate treasury. Robinhood's $25 million allocation is modest by comparison, but it carries outsized symbolic weight given the brokerage's visibility among retail investors and its more than 28 million funded customers globally. The company has been methodically expanding its crypto footprint beyond simple spot trading. In July, it launched Robinhood Chain, an Ethereum-compatible Layer 2 network built on Arbitrum and designed for tokenized real-world assets and decentralized finance. Since the mainnet went live, the chain has rolled out tokenized stock products, a stablecoin called USDG, and yield-bearing lending through Robinhood Earn, while integrating DeFi protocols such as Uniswap and infrastructure from Chainlink, Alchemy and BitGo. The network has already reached $1.05 billion in total value locked, according to earlier reporting. Kerbrat said trading volume for stock tokens on the chain has grown to the point where it is approaching limits set by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's innovation exemption for tokenized U.S. equities. Robinhood has also signaled plans to launch perpetual futures trading for eligible U.S. customers, covering eight assets. Chief Executive Officer Vlad Tenev has described the offering as "America's first true perps," with no expiry and profit and loss settled every 15 minutes. The company reported 28.6 million funded customers and $384 billion in total platform assets for August. Crypto notional trading volume reached $17.5 billion during that month, underscoring why the bitcoin treasury position is viewed more as an alignment of corporate identity with the asset class than as a meaningful capital allocation. The cryptocurrency has remained below recent local highs, and a $25 million purchase is unlikely to move its price in any meaningful way given the asset's overall market size. Robinhood shares were down roughly 3% in premarket trading, extending a pullback from a recent high of $125. The stock has broken below its 20-day exponential moving average at $114 and is testing the 50-day exponential moving average near $109, with the relative strength index at 48.75 indicating fading momentum. The shares still hold above the 100-day and 200-day exponential moving averages, suggesting the longer-term uptrend remains intact. For investors, the more significant implication lies in signaling. A consumer-facing brokerage with millions of users formalizing a direct bitcoin position reinforces the narrative that the cryptocurrency is becoming a standard corporate treasury consideration, particularly for companies with crypto-adjacent business lines. It also invites scrutiny of how such holdings will be valued and disclosed in future financial reporting. Robinhood has not detailed a long-term target size for its bitcoin holdings, nor has it indicated whether additional allocations or other digital assets might follow. The company's press team did not immediately respond to inquiries about potential future purchases. The disclosure arrives amid continued competition among brokerages, exchanges and fintech platforms to capture crypto-focused customers. Firms are increasingly differentiating themselves not just through trading fees, but through the depth of their underlying commitment to digital assets. passages: ChatGPT is about to get a lot more visual, thanks to a new feature that OpenAI calls Intelligent UI.
The new interface, which is being rolled out Wednesday with a new GPT-6 model, will integrate a significant amount of visuals into users’ conversations.

Aarush Selvan, a product manager at the company, said that while “ChatGPT has predominantly been a text-based interface,” the company really wants to help users “get things done — from everyday things like planning a recipe or a trip or even trying to learn something — the most helpful answers aren’t just text.”
Selvan gave the example of a college student wanting to know how an airplane wing functions.
As with other aspects of ChatGPT’s personality, if users don’t want so many visuals in their responses, they’ll be able to dial them back.
Intelligent UI rolls out globally with GPT-6 for Pro, Plus, Business, and Enterprise users, and arrives Thursday for users of the free and lower-cost Go tiers.

The big goal here, according to OpenAI, is to make “learning complex topics easier.” It may also make ChatGPT friendlier and more accessible and help bring in a wider audience, though OpenAI didn’t say so directly.

extraction.body: ChatGPT is about to get a lot more visual, thanks to a new feature that OpenAI calls Intelligent UI. The new interface, which is being rolled out Wednesday with a new GPT-6 model, will integrate a significant amount of visuals into users’ conversations. OpenAI says many of those visuals will be interactive. In other words, instead of just flat, cartoonish pictures, the chatbot will frequently include things like tappable buttons, a customized calculator for a specific task, interactive charts, editable graphs, and other elements the user can work with directly. The big goal here, according to OpenAI, is to make “learning complex topics easier.” It may also make ChatGPT friendlier and more accessible and help bring in a wider audience, though OpenAI didn’t say so directly. In a call with journalists, OpenAI staff gave a brief demonstration of Intelligent UI’s capabilities, showing how the new chatbot can instantly whip up various diagrams and visuals that help users understand more abstract topics. Aarush Selvan, a product manager at the company, said that while “ChatGPT has predominantly been a text-based interface,” the company really wants to help users “get things done — from everyday things like planning a recipe or a trip or even trying to learn something — the most helpful answers aren’t just text.” Selvan gave the example of a college student wanting to know how an airplane wing functions. He asked ChatGPT to “explore how an airplane wing generates lift” and the chatbot quickly spun up a number of diagrams designed to show how planes stay in the air. Other examples from the company included things like visuals for recipes, a diagram explaining bicycle mechanics, a map for a multi-day hiking excursion, a personal savings calculator, and more. This new feature will be customizable. As with other aspects of ChatGPT’s personality, if users don’t want so many visuals in their responses, they’ll be able to dial them back. In other words, instead of just flat, cartoonish pictures, the chatbot will frequently include things like tappable buttons, a customized calculator for a specific task, interactive charts, editable graphs, and other elements the user can work with directly.

The big goal here, according to OpenAI, is to make “learning complex topics easier.” It may also make ChatGPT friendlier and more accessible and help bring in a wider audience, though OpenAI didn’t say so directly.

In a call with journalists, OpenAI staff gave a brief demonstration of Intelligent UI’s capabilities, showing how the new chatbot can instantly whip up various diagrams and visuals that help users understand more abstract topics.

Aarush Selvan, a product manager at the company, said that while “ChatGPT has predominantly been a text-based interface,” the company really wants to help users “get things done — from everyday things like planning a recipe or a trip or even trying to learn something — the most helpful answers aren’t just text.”

Selvan gave the example of a college student wanting to know how an airplane wing functions. He asked ChatGPT to “explore how an airplane wing generates lift” and the chatbot quickly spun up a number of diagrams designed to show how planes stay in the air.
Other examples from the company included things like visuals for recipes, a diagram explaining bicycle mechanics, a map for a multi-day hiking excursion, a personal savings calculator, and more.

This new feature will be customizable. As with other aspects of ChatGPT’s personality, if users don’t want so many visuals in their responses, they’ll be able to dial them back. Intelligent UI rolls out globally with GPT-6 for Pro, Plus, Business, and Enterprise users, and arrives Thursday for users of the free and lower-cost Go tiers.

sources.title: OpenAI Launches Visual Ads in ChatGPT with New Measurement Tools
passages: OpenAI has quietly launched a sophisticated visual ad format within ChatGPT, complete with expanded measurement tools and attribution partnerships that could fundamentally change how brands reach consumers in the age of conversational AI.

Unlike traditional search or social media advertising, these new visual ads integrate directly into AI conversations, creating what industry insiders are calling "contextual advertising 2.0." What makes this launch particularly significant is OpenAI's approach to measurement and attribution.
With ChatGPT now processing over 100 million weekly active users, OpenAI is sitting on one of the most engaged digital audiences in history.
The measurement tools represent perhaps the most sophisticated attribution system ever built for conversational interfaces.

OpenAI's move into visual advertising represents more than just a new revenue stream - it's a fundamental shift in how AI companies will sustain their massive operational costs while scaling globally.
Rather than interrupting conversations with jarring display ads, OpenAI's visual format seems designed to integrate seamlessly into the chat experience.

OpenAI has quietly launched a sophisticated visual ad format within ChatGPT, complete with expanded measurement tools and attribution partnerships that could fundamentally change how brands reach consumers in the age of conversational AI. With ChatGPT now processing over 100 million weekly active users, OpenAI is sitting on one of the most engaged digital audiences in history. Unlike traditional search or social media advertising, these new visual ads integrate directly into AI conversations, creating what industry insiders are calling "contextual advertising 2.0." What makes this launch particularly significant is OpenAI's approach to measurement and attribution. The company isn't just throwing ads into chat windows and hoping for the best. According to the announcement, they're building comprehensive tracking capabilities that let advertisers understand how AI-powered conversations actually drive purchasing decisions. This represents a massive departure from OpenAI's subscription-only revenue model. While the company has been generating substantial income from ChatGPT Plus and enterprise subscriptions, advertising opens up an entirely new revenue stream that could dwarf subscription income within months. When users are having natural language conversations with AI, traditional keyword-based advertising becomes obsolete. OpenAI's new framework addresses this head-on, implementing controls that ensure ads only appear alongside appropriate content. The measurement tools represent perhaps the most sophisticated attribution system ever built for conversational interfaces. For marketers, this launch signals the beginning of a new era. Rather than interrupting conversations with jarring display ads, OpenAI's visual format seems designed to integrate seamlessly into the chat experience. What's particularly interesting is how this positions OpenAI against other AI companies. While Anthropic and others have focused purely on AI safety and capabilities, OpenAI is aggressively building the commercial infrastructure needed to sustain long-term development. The implications extend far beyond OpenAI itself. Every major tech company is now racing to integrate conversational AI into their products. Microsoft with Copilot, Google with Bard, and Meta with various AI initiatives all need sustainable monetization strategies. OpenAI's move into visual advertising represents more than just a new revenue stream - it's a fundamental shift in how AI companies will sustain their massive operational costs while scaling globally. As conversational AI becomes the primary interface between humans and digital services, traditional advertising models will need complete reinvention.

facts.text: ChatGPT is about to get a lot more visual, thanks to a new feature that OpenAI calls Intelligent UI.
The new interface, which is being rolled out Wednesday with a new GPT-6 model, will integrate a significant amount of visuals into users’ conversations.

Aarush Selvan, a product manager at the company, said that while “ChatGPT has predominantly been a text-based interface,” the company really wants to help users “get things done — from everyday things like planning a recipe or a trip or even trying to learn something — the most helpful answers aren’t just text.”
Selvan gave the example of a college student wanting to know how an airplane wing functions.
As with other aspects of ChatGPT’s personality, if users don’t want so many visuals in their responses, they’ll be able to dial them back.
Intelligent UI rolls out globally with GPT-6 for Pro, Plus, Business, and Enterprise users, and arrives Thursday for users of the free and lower-cost Go tiers.

extraction.body: ChatGPT is about to get a lot more visual, thanks to a new feature that OpenAI calls Intelligent UI. The new interface, which is being rolled out Wednesday with a new GPT-6 model, will integrate a significant amount of visuals into users’ conversations. OpenAI says many of those visuals will be interactive. In other words, instead of just flat, cartoonish pictures, the chatbot will frequently include things like tappable buttons, a customized calculator for a specific task, interactive charts, editable graphs, and other elements the user can work with directly. The big goal here, according to OpenAI, is to make “learning complex topics easier.” It may also make ChatGPT friendlier and more accessible and help bring in a wider audience, though OpenAI didn’t say so directly. In a call with journalists, OpenAI staff gave a brief demonstration of Intelligent UI’s capabilities, showing how the new chatbot can instantly whip up various diagrams and visuals that help users understand more abstract topics. Aarush Selvan, a product manager at the company, said that while “ChatGPT has predominantly been a text-based interface,” the company really wants to help users “get things done — from everyday things like planning a recipe or a trip or even trying to learn something — the most helpful answers aren’t just text.” Selvan gave the example of a college student wanting to know how an airplane wing functions. He asked ChatGPT to “explore how an airplane wing generates lift” and the chatbot quickly spun up a number of diagrams designed to show how planes stay in the air. Other examples from the company included things like visuals for recipes, a diagram explaining bicycle mechanics, a map for a multi-day hiking excursion, a personal savings calculator, and more. This new feature will be customizable. As with other aspects of ChatGPT’s personality, if users don’t want so many visuals in their responses, they’ll be able to dial them back. Intelligent UI rolls out globally with GPT-6 for Pro, Plus, Business, and Enterprise users, and arrives Thursday for users of the free and lower-cost Go tiers. According to the announcement, they're building comprehensive tracking capabilities that let advertisers understand how AI-powered conversations actually drive purchasing decisions. This represents a massive departure from OpenAI's subscription-only revenue model. While the company has been generating substantial income from ChatGPT Plus and enterprise subscriptions, advertising opens up an entirely new revenue stream that could dwarf subscription income within months. When users are having natural language conversations with AI, traditional keyword-based advertising becomes obsolete. OpenAI's new framework addresses this head-on, implementing controls that ensure ads only appear alongside appropriate content. The measurement tools represent perhaps the most sophisticated attribution system ever built for conversational interfaces. For marketers, this launch signals the beginning of a new era. Rather than interrupting conversations with jarring display ads, OpenAI's visual format seems designed to integrate seamlessly into the chat experience. extraction.body: Teenage Engineering founder and CEO Jesper Kouthoofd told Highsnobiety that it plans to stop making synths. And yes, that includes the iconic OP-1, which put the company on the map. But almost everything the company makes itself — the OP-1, the OP-XY, EP-133, TP-7, et cetera — is music or audio-focused. Here’s the relevant quote from Highsnobiety: > Kouthoofd tells me that, as part of a reorganization last fall, he announced to his team he is planning to stop making synthesizers altogether. sources.title: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 Instrument: Hands-on, Videos, Why it’s Different - CDM Create Digital Music
passages: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware.
It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths .
It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique.

It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.)

I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design.
The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly.
Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise.
I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now.
The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator.
The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage.
A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport.
But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away.
Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback .
And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced .
Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware.
Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special.
Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM :
The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way.
Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible.
Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing.
There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating.
I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real.
Some of the little touches I was able to glean:
Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results.

extraction.body: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware. It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths . It’s a sampler. It’s a synth. It has an FM radio. It will have a variety of sequencers. It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique. It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.) I got to spend some hands-on time with the current prototype of the OP-1, and hanging out with the guys from Teenage Engineering. I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design. The OP-1 is real, it’s coming, and it’s far enough along in the prototyping phase that I think we’ll see real details on getting one soon. Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing. There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating. I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real. I am surprised, though, that people are now complaining that the OP-1 is taking a long time – I think some people don’t realize how time-consuming hardware development really is, and we only just saw an under-glass prototype last spring. The fact that the OP-1 does integrate hardware and onboard software tightly and does do things in new ways is a testament to having a single, small team that works on the whole product. Teenage Engineering – OP-1 @ NAMM 2010 from Neil Bufkin on Vimeo . In the din of the NAMM hall, some people didn’t seem to “get” the OP-1. The prototypes available aren’t entirely refined in regards to the sound engine, so it’s too soon to judge sound quality, and some functionality was missing from the units on display. And it’d be easy to see this its collection of synthesis and sampling tricks as nothing new. (In fact, I get the sense that some people dialed up essentially an init preset and judged the sound quality based on that.) But look closer, and even prior to the finished product, there’s real design genius here. Some of the little touches I was able to glean: You can record backwards, an idea so simple in sampling, but also powerful, it’s a wonder it’s not widespread. Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results. It’s not hard to imagine putting an OP-1 alongside a computer, and using it alternatively as a hardware synth and a tool for resampling the output of a live computer mix. It’s a four-track virtual tape recorder, complete with virtual splicing. The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage. The OP-1 is the most convincing adaptation of that idea I’ve ever seen. A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport. But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away. Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback . And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced . Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware. Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special. Whereas clunky hardware designs from mainstream manufacturers have typically treated tape recording as something you do to record an arrangement, the OP-1’s tape recorder is one you can play as an instrument. (See our video of one of the Teenage Engineers jamming with this feature, which I smuggled off one of their Mac laptops.) And it’s finally a sampling feature that functions on recording like tape, not just on playback. That sound you heard all around NAMM was the sound of developers and engineers collectively saying to themselves, “why didn’t I do this myself, first?” (Okay, knowing this site, I’m sure we’ll get someone on comments who has done this first, so do speak up.) Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM : The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly. To me, the greatest accomplishment of the OP-1 is making a small screen seem integral to a hardware design, rather than a concession to practicality. Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise. I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now. The design of the OP-1’s interface is so minimal, however, that the onboard screen seems perfect. The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator. It’s finally a small screen that seems ideal for its purpose – maybe even better than looking at a computer-sized screen. And that’s not just because it’s pretty; it’s because it’s functional. For a look at some of these beautiful design ideas in motion, here’s a video from a hands-on (more with sound yet to come): The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way. In keeping with some of the most fun instruments of all time, the OP-1 is something people will want to play. Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible. There’s nothing revolutionary in the synth or sampler; it just takes the 90% of sound-making techniques most people use and makes them more immediate. All of these things are wonderful, and clearly it’s a gorgeous little device. And it’s impossible, as always, to judge a design that isn’t finished. I have a suspicion, however, that some of the most important magic of the OP-1 lies in what the impishly-secretive Teenage Engineers aren’t saying: The OP-1 is definitely one I’ll be following; it’s at the top of my list for the year. And it’s about time we got some really significant new hardware. For more information… Teenage has a lovely set of photos on their blog – and yes, that’s me, by coincidence amidst a crew from Hispasonic: NAMM Photo Bananza And don’t miss the product page, which now has a lot of detail on it: Teenage Engineering OP-1 Among the juicy specs: how about an onboard accelerometer, Li-Ion rechargeable battery, a 60-fps display, and a powerful (for this kind of gear) 400MHz processor core? Just please, please, don’t judge the sound quality of a non-shipping synth based on YouTube videos. I’ll be sure to report back on final sound quality before you unload your hard-earned change. CDM is a home for people who make and play music and motion.

The design of the OP-1’s interface is so minimal, however, that the onboard screen seems perfect. The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator.

It’s finally a small screen that seems ideal for its purpose – maybe even better than looking at a computer-sized screen. And that’s not just because it’s pretty; it’s because it’s functional. For a look at some of these beautiful design ideas in motion, here’s a video from a hands-on (more with sound yet to come):

The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way. In keeping with some of the most fun instruments of all time, the OP-1 is something people will want to play. Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible. There’s nothing revolutionary in the synth or sampler; it just takes the 90% of sound-making techniques most people use and makes them more immediate.

All of these things are wonderful, and clearly it’s a gorgeous little device. And it’s impossible, as always, to judge a design that isn’t finished. I have a suspicion, however, that some of the most important magic of the OP-1 lies in what the impishly-secretive Teenage Engineers aren’t saying:
The OP-1 is definitely one I’ll be following; it’s at the top of my list for the year. And it’s about time we got some really significant new hardware. For more information…
Teenage has a lovely set of photos on their blog – and yes, that’s me, by coincidence amidst a crew from Hispasonic: NAMM Photo Bananza

And don’t miss the product page, which now has a lot of detail on it: Teenage Engineering OP-1 Among the juicy specs: how about an onboard accelerometer, Li-Ion rechargeable battery, a 60-fps display, and a powerful (for this kind of gear) 400MHz processor core?
Just please, please, don’t judge the sound quality of a non-shipping synth based on YouTube videos. I’ll be sure to report back on final sound quality before you unload your hard-earned change.
CDM is a home for people who make and play music and motion.

extraction.body: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware. It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths . It’s a sampler. It’s a synth. It has an FM radio. It will have a variety of sequencers. It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique. It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.) I got to spend some hands-on time with the current prototype of the OP-1, and hanging out with the guys from Teenage Engineering. I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design. The OP-1 is real, it’s coming, and it’s far enough along in the prototyping phase that I think we’ll see real details on getting one soon. Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing. There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating. I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real. I am surprised, though, that people are now complaining that the OP-1 is taking a long time – I think some people don’t realize how time-consuming hardware development really is, and we only just saw an under-glass prototype last spring. The fact that the OP-1 does integrate hardware and onboard software tightly and does do things in new ways is a testament to having a single, small team that works on the whole product. Teenage Engineering – OP-1 @ NAMM 2010 from Neil Bufkin on Vimeo . In the din of the NAMM hall, some people didn’t seem to “get” the OP-1. The prototypes available aren’t entirely refined in regards to the sound engine, so it’s too soon to judge sound quality, and some functionality was missing from the units on display. And it’d be easy to see this its collection of synthesis and sampling tricks as nothing new. (In fact, I get the sense that some people dialed up essentially an init preset and judged the sound quality based on that.) But look closer, and even prior to the finished product, there’s real design genius here. Some of the little touches I was able to glean: You can record backwards, an idea so simple in sampling, but also powerful, it’s a wonder it’s not widespread. Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results. It’s not hard to imagine putting an OP-1 alongside a computer, and using it alternatively as a hardware synth and a tool for resampling the output of a live computer mix. It’s a four-track virtual tape recorder, complete with virtual splicing. The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage. The OP-1 is the most convincing adaptation of that idea I’ve ever seen. A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport. But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away. Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback . And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced . Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware. Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special. Whereas clunky hardware designs from mainstream manufacturers have typically treated tape recording as something you do to record an arrangement, the OP-1’s tape recorder is one you can play as an instrument. (See our video of one of the Teenage Engineers jamming with this feature, which I smuggled off one of their Mac laptops.) And it’s finally a sampling feature that functions on recording like tape, not just on playback. That sound you heard all around NAMM was the sound of developers and engineers collectively saying to themselves, “why didn’t I do this myself, first?” (Okay, knowing this site, I’m sure we’ll get someone on comments who has done this first, so do speak up.) Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM : The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly. To me, the greatest accomplishment of the OP-1 is making a small screen seem integral to a hardware design, rather than a concession to practicality. Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise. I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now. The design of the OP-1’s interface is so minimal, however, that the onboard screen seems perfect. The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator. It’s finally a small screen that seems ideal for its purpose – maybe even better than looking at a computer-sized screen. And that’s not just because it’s pretty; it’s because it’s functional. For a look at some of these beautiful design ideas in motion, here’s a video from a hands-on (more with sound yet to come): The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way. In keeping with some of the most fun instruments of all time, the OP-1 is something people will want to play. Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible. There’s nothing revolutionary in the synth or sampler; it just takes the 90% of sound-making techniques most people use and makes them more immediate. All of these things are wonderful, and clearly it’s a gorgeous little device. And it’s impossible, as always, to judge a design that isn’t finished. I have a suspicion, however, that some of the most important magic of the OP-1 lies in what the impishly-secretive Teenage Engineers aren’t saying: The OP-1 is definitely one I’ll be following; it’s at the top of my list for the year. And it’s about time we got some really significant new hardware. For more information… Teenage has a lovely set of photos on their blog – and yes, that’s me, by coincidence amidst a crew from Hispasonic: NAMM Photo Bananza And don’t miss the product page, which now has a lot of detail on it: Teenage Engineering OP-1 Among the juicy specs: how about an onboard accelerometer, Li-Ion rechargeable battery, a 60-fps display, and a powerful (for this kind of gear) 400MHz processor core? Just please, please, don’t judge the sound quality of a non-shipping synth based on YouTube videos. I’ll be sure to report back on final sound quality before you unload your hard-earned change. CDM is a home for people who make and play music and motion.

It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.)

I got to spend some hands-on time with the current prototype of the OP-1, and hanging out with the guys from Teenage Engineering. I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design.

The OP-1 is real, it’s coming, and it’s far enough along in the prototyping phase that I think we’ll see real details on getting one soon. Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing. There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating. I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real. sources.title: Why Packaging Is Now a Frontline Issue in Pharma Supply Chains
passages: This is why packaging is now a frontline issue — not because it has become less important, but because it has become more exposed.
Pharmaceutical supply chains are being pushed into a level of coordination and control they were not originally designed to handle.
Traditional cold chain models detect issues after delivery, but modern cold chains require decisions during transit.
There are few places where that progress is more evident than in cold chain packaging.
These assumptions are breaking more frequently as variability becomes the new supply chain norm.
The shift underway in the cold chain is not about improving packaging performance; it is about redefining control.

extraction.body: Pharmaceutical supply chains are being pushed into a level of coordination and control they were not originally designed to handle. At the same time, the logistics environments they move through are becoming less stable. On the surface, many of these challenges appear to be logistics problems. Protecting high-value medications, biologics and personalized medicines goes beyond packaging alone. The cold chain is no longer a controlled environment; it is a dynamic system operating under constant disruption. Packaging Is No Longer a Passive Layer — It Requires Oversight In the 100 years since the dawn of electric refrigeration, humans' ability to keep things cool has advanced significantly. There are few places where that progress is more evident than in cold chain packaging. The problem is that these systems were built on assumptions. Their success assumes that a shipment will move within a defined transit window, that exposure conditions will stay within tested ranges, or that handoffs between partners will happen as planned. These assumptions are breaking more frequently as variability becomes the new supply chain norm. Here’s what those breakdowns can look like in practice: A biologic shipment delayed at an airport transfer hub can sit on a tarmac for hours in high heat. A shipment flagged for inspection may experience temperature fluctuations that packaging was never designed to absorb. In each case, the shipment's packaging still does exactly what it was designed to do. But ultimately, packaging can only perform within its limits, and those limits are often pushed to the edge of what they can withstand. This is why packaging is now a frontline issue — not because it has become less important, but because it has become more exposed. How Are Advanced Therapies Exposing Blind Spots in Cold Chain Control? The shift in cold chain risk starts with the shipments themselves. Biologics, cell and gene therapies and personalized medicine have redefined acceptable risk in pharmaceutical logistics. Many require strict temperature control at minus 20 C, minus 80 C or below. For logistics providers handling advanced therapies at scale, this risk profile leaves no margin for error. One operator managing tens of thousands of life sciences shipments annually ultimately moved to real-time monitoring across all shipments because, in their mind, there is simply no option for failure when transporting cell and gene therapies. The difference between product loss and recovery is timing. Traditional cold chain models detect issues after delivery, but modern cold chains require decisions during transit. Packaging is designed to protect within expected conditions; it cannot adapt to compounded delays, exposure or handling variability. This assumes that what happens during shipping (and between actual checkpoints) is stable — and if it’s not, there’s no way to adapt. Continuous monitoring of temperature, location and environmental conditions enables teams to see where risk is developing, not just that it occurred. For example, when a shipment is delayed at a transfer hub, real-time data can show both the current temperature and the rate of change. Teams can estimate how much thermal protection remains and determine whether intervention is required. With visibility, teams can act while a shipment is still recoverable. One company noted that before implementing real-time tracking, “we had no real way to understand what happened” when shipments were delayed. With full visibility, teams can now trace exactly where and how disruptions occur — and intervene accordingly. When analyzed over time, shipment data reveal patterns. Addressing them often reduces risk more effectively than changing packaging alone. Why Does Control Now Depend on Visibility, Response and System Design? The shift underway in the cold chain is not about improving packaging performance; it is about redefining control. For years, protection was measured by whether packaging could hold temperature under expected conditions.

extraction.body: Staff at the Warfield say that about 15 minutes before a security guard was fatally shot, a chemical irritant was sprayed inside the venue, sending a crowd of people rushing out while coughing and struggling to breathe. The San Francisco Police Department is investigating the death of Warfield security guard Ulysses Tykee Davis, 47, who was shot outside the theater around 1 am Saturday. As KTVU reports , Davis’s wife and two of his six children witnessed the shooting. His brother-in-law, Terrance Cooper, said Davis had been helping remove a disruptive woman from the theater when she allegedly shot him in the back. The Warfield Theatre had been hosting an 18-and-over event on Friday night featuring the cast of “ Baddies USA Chapter 3 ,” which was scheduled to end at midnight. According to Mission Local , filming for the show's new season had taken place that night, and bartenders estimated that the venue was less than half full. Staff told Mission Local that a chemical irritant described as bear mace was released inside the theater at 12:45 am, sending a large crowd rushing into the lobby. Bartenders described people coughing, with red eyes and tears streaming down their faces, while others covered their faces and shouted that they could not breathe. One bartender said people were jumping over the bar as they fled, with some taking items and one person swinging at a coworker. Another bartender told the paper that a security guard pulled an attacker away before she was struck. Per Mission Local, staff were still cleaning up when two gunshots were heard near the lobby. Several workers reportedly hid in an office and locked the door. A witness who was near the box office told Mission Local that he saw a woman take a handgun from another woman before someone yelled “Gun!” He said the woman pointed the gun in his direction before he ran and heard several shots. When he looked back, he saw a security guard had been shot near the theater entrance. Police have not confirmed that account. Friends and coworkers described Davis as a longtime Bayview-Hunters Point resident who was well-liked by the people who worked alongside him, as KTVU reports. “Bear was just doing his job. He was at work, doing security,” said Terrance Silas, a friend who works next door to the theater. Police have not released information about a suspect or said whether anyone has been arrested. Per KTVU, SFPD spokesman Officer Robert Rueca said investigators are examining what happened before the shooting, including whether the Warfield had the proper permits for the event and was operating within their restrictions. passages: San Francisco police have arrested a woman in the fatal shooting of a security guard over the weekend at the Warfield on Market Street.
sources.body: San Francisco police have arrested a woman in the fatal shooting of a security guard over the weekend at the Warfield on Market Street.

extraction.body: San Francisco police have arrested a woman in the fatal shooting of a security guard over the weekend at the Warfield on Market Street. Shakia Vanderbilt of San Francisco was taken into custody Tuesday, the San Francisco Police Department said Wednesday. District Attorney Brooke Jenkins said Vanderbilt is charged with murder with a firearm enhancement, a count of intentionally discharging a firearm in an occupied building and a count of being a felon in possession of a firearm. The victim was identified by the office of the chief medical examiner as Ulysses Tykee Davis, 47. His wife and two of his six children were present at the Mid-Market theater when he was gunned down, according to reports . Davis had been working at the Warfield, which was hosting the “Baddies USA: Chapter Three” tour, a reality TV series known for arguing, shouting, and fighting. Police Chief Derrick Lew said Vanderbilt was escorted outside the Warfield following a disruption and that a dispute ensued, culminating in the shooting at approximately 1 a.m Saturday. Lew declined to say if Vanderbilt targeted Davis, but added that there is footage of the shooting. Vanderbilt possibly brought a gun inside the Warfield despite their screening process for attendees, Jenkins said. “Nobody should worry that if they go watch a show at a venue that somebody is armed inside,” Jenkins said. “We want to hold those accountable who think that gun violence is okay in our city.” Davis died in a hospital, police said. Prosecutors will seek to have her held without bail, Jenkins said. According to Mission Local , Warfield staffers said Davis, nicknamed “Bear,” was working at the event as a security guard. Bartenders told Mission Local that during the event, a chemical irritant, possibly bear mace, was released, sending a swarm of panicked attendees toward the exits. The Warfield’s management did not respond to requests for comment. There have been 21 homicides in San Francisco this year through Sunday, according to police statistics . “We have made great strides as a city in reducing gun violence and homicides, and we will continue to devote resources into preventing violence of this kind,” Lew said.

passages: Bitmine's Relentless Ethereum Buying Is About to End, Tom Lee Says

Bitmine Immersion Technologies is about to take its foot off the gas. Chairman Tom Lee said the company will halt its Ethereum buying once its holdings reach 5% of the token's circulating supply, drawing a hard line under one of the market's steadiest sources of demand.

Speaking Wednesday at the Token2049 conference in Singapore, Lee said the company is roughly 100,000 ETH away from the threshold. At last week's pace, that's about six to seven more weeks of accumulation before Bitmine stops.
"We thought this would take five years," Lee said on stage. "It took us a little over a year. More importantly, we did this all in the middle of a bear market,” he said. “Now we’re going to stop.”

The NYSE-listed firm is the world's largest Ethereum treasury company, holding 6,016,414 ETH, or about 4.9% of supply, as of its latest disclosure. Bitmine added roughly $41 million in ETH just last week as it closed in on the goal it brands the " Alchemy of 5% ." (Disclosure: Tom Lee is one of several investors in Dastan, Decrypt ’s parent company.)
🚨BREAKING: Tom Lee says BitMine will "STOP" buying ETH at 5% "hard cap."
"We only need to get another 100,000 ETH to get to 5%," Lee said on stage at Token2049.
Lee called 5% BitMine’s “hard cap,” saying it optimizes shareholder value. pic.twitter.com/mm0WYnv4Z0
The company has bought Ethereum every week since launching its treasury strategy in June 2025, providing a reliable bid that helped underpin the token through a choppy stretch.

That makes the coming stop notable for the broader market. Bitmine's weekly purchases have been a persistent source of demand, and their end removes a buyer that has absorbed a steady stream of ETH for more than a year.
Lee has previously signaled the company could even sell Ethereum earned through staking to keep its share of supply from drifting above the 5% cap.

The milestone arrives with Bitmine deep underwater on paper. Because much of its accumulation happened last year at higher prices during the bull market, the firm's ETH holdings carry roughly $4.5 billion in unrealized losses, according to tracking data, with Ethereum trading near $2,570 on Wednesday.
Ethereum is down 5.5% today, outpacing losses across most major crypto assets, dropping sharply during Asia trading hours, coinciding with Lee’s remarks.

Still, Lee framed the achievement as a point of pride, having compressed a five-year plan into just over a year. Once the 5% ceiling is reached, Bitmine's defining buying spree, and the market demand it generated, will come to a close.

passages: Bitmine's Relentless Ethereum Buying Is About to End, Tom Lee Says

Bitmine Immersion Technologies is about to take its foot off the gas. Chairman Tom Lee said the company will halt its Ethereum buying once its holdings reach 5% of the token's circulating supply, drawing a hard line under one of the market's steadiest sources of demand.

Speaking Wednesday at the Token2049 conference in Singapore, Lee said the company is roughly 100,000 ETH away from the threshold. At last week's pace, that's about six to seven more weeks of accumulation before Bitmine stops.
"We thought this would take five years," Lee said on stage. "It took us a little over a year. More importantly, we did this all in the middle of a bear market,” he said. “Now we’re going to stop.”

The NYSE-listed firm is the world's largest Ethereum treasury company, holding 6,016,414 ETH, or about 4.9% of supply, as of its latest disclosure. Bitmine added roughly $41 million in ETH just last week as it closed in on the goal it brands the " Alchemy of 5% ." (Disclosure: Tom Lee is one of several investors in Dastan, Decrypt ’s parent company.)
🚨BREAKING: Tom Lee says BitMine will "STOP" buying ETH at 5% "hard cap."
"We only need to get another 100,000 ETH to get to 5%," Lee said on stage at Token2049.
Lee called 5% BitMine’s “hard cap,” saying it optimizes shareholder value. pic.twitter.com/mm0WYnv4Z0
The company has bought Ethereum every week since launching its treasury strategy in June 2025, providing a reliable bid that helped underpin the token through a choppy stretch.

That makes the coming stop notable for the broader market. Bitmine's weekly purchases have been a persistent source of demand, and their end removes a buyer that has absorbed a steady stream of ETH for more than a year.
Lee has previously signaled the company could even sell Ethereum earned through staking to keep its share of supply from drifting above the 5% cap.

The milestone arrives with Bitmine deep underwater on paper. Because much of its accumulation happened last year at higher prices during the bull market, the firm's ETH holdings carry roughly $4.5 billion in unrealized losses, according to tracking data, with Ethereum trading near $2,570 on Wednesday.
Ethereum is down 5.5% today, outpacing losses across most major crypto assets, dropping sharply during Asia trading hours, coinciding with Lee’s remarks.

Still, Lee framed the achievement as a point of pride, having compressed a five-year plan into just over a year. Once the 5% ceiling is reached, Bitmine's defining buying spree, and the market demand it generated, will come to a close.

In July, Thielen expanded his analysis by incorporating Elliott Wave theory, which interprets price charts as repeating wave patterns. He identified a first wave down to around $63,000 in February, followed by a rebound to between $82,000 and $83,000, and concluded with a final wave (Wave C) that would see prices drop to $46,000 to $47,000. Between mid-May and July, US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw around $7 billion in net outflows, and Strategy, the year's largest buyer with about $13 billion in purchases, slowed its buying.
