Understanding exactly where that bear case broke down reveals something crucial about who is now quietly controlling… This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. Markus Thielen of 10x Research made two forecasts about a potential Bitcoin bottom during the summer of 2026, but Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) never dipped to those levels. On June 24, he suggested that Bitcoin could drop to $55,000 between late August and October. Just ten days later, on July 4, he revised his forecast, calling for a fall to between $46,000 and $47,000 before anticipating a 30% bounce back to $60,000 to $65,000 by year-end. However, Bitcoin hit its 2026 low at $57,717 on June 30, just six days after the first forecast and four days before the second. Since then, it has surged nearly 49%, trading around $86,000 as of October 7—significantly above the $55,000 target and 85% higher than the middle of the lower range Thielen proposed. The current rally does have its limitations. Bitcoin has risen about 8% in the past month but is still down roughly 30% from the previous year and trades about 32% below its record high of $126,080 from October 2025. So, where did Thielen’s bear case go wrong? Thielen’s June forecast was based on a strong US dollar and a hawkish Federal Reserve, which was expected to keep interest rates high to combat inflation. A stronger dollar makes Bitcoin more expensive for investors using other currencies, while higher interest rates can make cash and bonds more appealing to investors. At the time, traders debated whether the Fed’s next move under Chair Kevin Warsh would be a rate hike rather than a cut. In July, Thielen expanded his analysis by incorporating Elliott Wave theory, which interprets price charts as repeating wave patterns. He identified a first wave down to around $63,000 in February, followed by a rebound to between $82,000 and $83,000, and concluded with a final wave (Wave C) that would see prices drop to $46,000 to $47,000. Market evidence supported his earlier claims. Between mid-May and July, US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw around $7 billion in net outflows, and Strategy, the year’s largest buyer with about $13 billion in purchases, slowed its buying. As Thielen noted in July, “there’s no real buyer in the market right now.” However, that claim about a lack of buyers was the one aspect of the forecast that was quickly tested, and the data soon contradicted it. Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which allow everyday investors to gain exposure to Bitcoin through regular brokerage accounts, attracted about $6.3 billion in the third quarter, including $2.3 billion in just four days at the end of September. This influx of funds correlated directly with Bitcoin’s performance. Thielen had forecast that the bottom would occur between late August and October, but instead, Bitcoin rose from its June low during that timeframe. The influx of ETF dollars also explains why his July wave count forecast failed. Wave C required active selling to push prices lower, but ETF investors were buying up the coins being sold instead. By late September, these funds controlled about 6.3% of all Bitcoin in circulation. On the macroeconomic side, we still need to evaluate Thielen’s calls about the dollar and the Federal Reserve. Bitcoin’s price rise alone doesn’t conclusively indicate whether his analysis of these factors was accurate. The Fed’s decision on rates during its September meeting was held on September 16, with another meeting slated for October 27 and 28. These outcomes will clarify whether rates have moved in line with Thielen’s expectations. Moreover, his end-of-year range now looks different. Initially, Thielen projected Bitcoin would rebound to $60,000 to $65,000 from $46,000. With Bitcoin currently around $86,000, achieving that target would require a drop of roughly 24% to 30% by December 31—a very different scenario from his initial forecast. The main flaw in the bear case was the misunderstanding of demand. Thielen’s outlook was predicated on the belief that buyers had exited the market, but ETF investors contributed $6.3 billion to Bitcoin funds in the same quarter he expected the bottom to form. Those who sold their Bitcoin near $59,000 around the time of his first forecast have missed out on about a 45% increase in value. Nonetheless, the bear case could still make a return. If Bitcoin drops below its 2026 low of $57,717 before December 31, and if ETF outflows resume in the fourth quarter, Thielen’s lower price targets could come back into play. As long as Bitcoin stays above that critical level and demand from fund buyers remains strong, the assertion that there is “no real buyer” will continue to prove incorrect. Markus Thielen of 10x Research made two forecasts about a potential Bitcoin bottom during the summer of 2026, but Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) never dipped to those levels. On June 24, he suggested that Bitcoin could drop to $55,000 between late August and October. Just ten days later, on July 4, he revised his forecast, calling for a fall to between $46,000 and $47,000 before anticipating a 30% bounce back to $60,000 to $65,000 by year-end.

However, Bitcoin hit its 2026 low at $57,717 on June 30, just six days after the first forecast and four days before the second. Since then, it has surged nearly 49%, trading around $86,000 as of October 7—significantly above the $55,000 target and 85% higher than the middle of the lower range Thielen proposed.

The current rally does have its limitations. Bitcoin has risen about 8% in the past month but is still down roughly 30% from the previous year and trades about 32% below its record high of $126,080 from October 2025. So, where did Thielen’s bear case go wrong?

Thielen’s June forecast was based on a strong US dollar and a hawkish Federal Reserve, which was expected to keep interest rates high to combat inflation. A stronger dollar makes Bitcoin more expensive for investors using other currencies, while higher interest rates can make cash and bonds more appealing to investors. At the time, traders debated whether the Fed’s next move under Chair Kevin Warsh would be a rate hike rather than a cut.

In July, Thielen expanded his analysis by incorporating Elliott Wave theory, which interprets price charts as repeating wave patterns. He identified a first wave down to around $63,000 in February, followed by a rebound to between $82,000 and $83,000, and concluded with a final wave (Wave C) that would see prices drop to $46,000 to $47,000.

Market evidence supported his earlier claims. Between mid-May and July, US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw around $7 billion in net outflows, and Strategy, the year’s largest buyer with about $13 billion in purchases, slowed its buying. As Thielen noted in July, “there’s no real buyer in the market right now.”

However, that claim about a lack of buyers was the one aspect of the forecast that was quickly tested, and the data soon contradicted it. Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which allow everyday investors to gain exposure to Bitcoin through regular brokerage accounts, attracted about $6.3 billion in the third quarter, including $2.3 billion in just four days at the end of September.

This influx of funds correlated directly with Bitcoin’s performance. Thielen had forecast that the bottom would occur between late August and October, but instead, Bitcoin rose from its June low during that timeframe.

The influx of ETF dollars also explains why his July wave count forecast failed. Wave C required active selling to push prices lower, but ETF investors were buying up the coins being sold instead. By late September, these funds controlled about 6.3% of all Bitcoin in circulation.

On the macroeconomic side, we still need to evaluate Thielen’s calls about the dollar and the Federal Reserve. Bitcoin’s price rise alone doesn’t conclusively indicate whether his analysis of these factors was accurate. The Fed’s decision on rates during its September meeting was held on September 16, with another meeting slated for October 27 and 28. These outcomes will clarify whether rates have moved in line with Thielen’s expectations.

Moreover, his end-of-year range now looks different. Initially, Thielen projected Bitcoin would rebound to $60,000 to $65,000 from $46,000. With Bitcoin currently around $86,000, achieving that target would require a drop of roughly 24% to 30% by December 31—a very different scenario from his initial forecast.

The main flaw in the bear case was the misunderstanding of demand. Thielen’s outlook was predicated on the belief that buyers had exited the market, but ETF investors contributed $6.3 billion to Bitcoin funds in the same quarter he expected the bottom to form. Those who sold their Bitcoin near $59,000 around the time of his first forecast have missed out on about a 45% increase in value.

Nonetheless, the bear case could still make a return. If Bitcoin drops below its 2026 low of $57,717 before December 31, and if ETF outflows resume in the fourth quarter, Thielen’s lower price targets could come back into play. As long as Bitcoin stays above that critical level and demand from fund buyers remains strong, the assertion that there is “no real buyer” will continue to prove incorrect.

facts.text: Markus Thielen of 10x Research made two forecasts about a potential Bitcoin bottom during the summer of 2026, but Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) never dipped to those levels.
On June 24, he suggested that Bitcoin could drop to $55,000 between late August and October.
Just ten days later, on July 4, he revised his forecast, calling for a fall to between $46,000 and $47,000 before anticipating a 30% bounce back to $60,000 to $65,000 by year-end.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Moreover, his end-of-year range now looks different.
With Bitcoin currently around $86,000, achieving that target would require a drop of roughly 24% to 30% by December 31—a very different scenario from his initial forecast.
In July, Thielen expanded his analysis by incorporating Elliott Wave theory, which interprets price charts as repeating wave patterns.
Bitcoin's 2026 low hit $57,717 on June 30, then surged 49% to $86,000, a level far above Thielen's $46,000 bear target.
Those who sold their Bitcoin near $59,000 around the time of his first forecast have missed out on about a 45% increase in value.

At the time, traders debated whether the Fed's next move under Chair Kevin Warsh would be a rate hike rather than a cut.

In July, Thielen expanded his analysis by incorporating Elliott Wave theory, which interprets price charts as repeating wave patterns. He identified a first wave down to around $63,000 in February, followed by a rebound to between $82,000 and $83,000, and concluded with a final wave (Wave C) that would see prices drop to $46,000 to $47,000.

Market evidence supported his earlier claims. Between mid-May and July, US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw around $7 billion in net outflows, and Strategy, the year's largest buyer with about $13 billion in purchases, slowed its buying. As Thielen noted in July, "there's no real buyer in the market right now."

However, that claim about a lack of buyers was the one aspect of the forecast that was quickly tested, and the data soon contradicted it. Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which allow everyday investors to gain exposure to Bitcoin through regular brokerage accounts, attracted about $6.3 billion in the third quarter, including $2.3 billion in just four days at the end of September.

This influx of funds correlated directly with Bitcoin's performance. Thielen had forecast that the bottom would occur between late August and October, but instead, Bitcoin rose from its June low during that timeframe.

The influx of ETF dollars also explains why his July wave count forecast failed. Wave C required active selling to push prices lower, but ETF investors were buying up the coins being sold instead. By late September, these funds controlled about 6.3% of all Bitcoin in circulation.

On the macroeconomic side, we still need to evaluate Thielen's calls about the dollar and the Federal Reserve. Bitcoin's price rise alone doesn't conclusively indicate whether his analysis of these factors was accurate. The Fed's decision on rates during its September meeting was held on September 16, with another meeting slated for October 27 and 28. These outcomes will clarify whether rates have moved in line with Thielen's expectations.

Moreover, his end-of-year range now looks different. Initially, Thielen projected Bitcoin would rebound to $60,000 to $65,000 from $46,000. With Bitcoin currently around $86,000, achieving that target would require a drop of roughly 24% to 30% by December 31—a very different scenario from his initial forecast.

The main flaw in the bear case was the misunderstanding of demand. Thielen's outlook was predicated on the belief that buyers had exited the market, but ETF investors contributed $6.3 billion to Bitcoin funds in the same quarter he expected the bottom to form. Those who sold their Bitcoin near $59,000 around the time of his first forecast have missed out on about a 45% increase in value.

Nonetheless, the bear case could still make a return. If Bitcoin drops below its 2026 low of $57,717 before December 31, and if ETF outflows resume in the fourth quarter, Thielen's lower price targets could come back into play. As long as Bitcoin stays above that critical level and demand from fund buyers remains strong, the assertion that there is "no real buyer" will continue to prove incorrect.

Markus Thielen of 10x Research made two forecasts about a potential Bitcoin bottom during the summer of 2026, but Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) never dipped to those levels. On June 24, he suggested that Bitcoin could drop to $55,000 between late August and October. Just ten days later, on July 4, he revised his forecast, calling for a fall to between $46,000 and $47,000 before anticipating a 30% bounce back to $60,000 to $65,000 by year-end.

However, Bitcoin hit its 2026 low at $57,717 on June 30, just six days after the first forecast and four days before the second. Since then, it has surged nearly 49%, trading around $86,000 as of October 7—significantly above the $55,000 target and 85% higher than the middle of the lower range Thielen proposed.

The current rally does have its limitations. Bitcoin has risen about 8% in the past month but is still down roughly 30% from the previous year and trades about 32% below its record high of $126,080 from October 2025. So, where did Thielen’s bear case go wrong?

Thielen’s June forecast was based on a strong US dollar and a hawkish Federal Reserve, which was expected to keep interest rates high to combat inflation. A stronger dollar makes Bitcoin more expensive for investors using other currencies, while higher interest rates can make cash and bonds more appealing to investors. At the time, traders debated whether the Fed’s next move under Chair Kevin Warsh would be a rate hike rather than a cut.

In July, Thielen expanded his analysis by incorporating Elliott Wave theory, which interprets price charts as repeating wave patterns. He identified a first wave down to around $63,000 in February, followed by a rebound to between $82,000 and $83,000, and concluded with a final wave (Wave C) that would see prices drop to $46,000 to $47,000.

Market evidence supported his earlier claims. Between mid-May and July, US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw around $7 billion in net outflows, and Strategy, the year’s largest buyer with about $13 billion in purchases, slowed its buying. As Thielen noted in July, “there’s no real buyer in the market right now.”

However, that claim about a lack of buyers was the one aspect of the forecast that was quickly tested, and the data soon contradicted it. Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which allow everyday investors to gain exposure to Bitcoin through regular brokerage accounts, attracted about $6.3 billion in the third quarter, including $2.3 billion in just four days at the end of September.

This influx of funds correlated directly with Bitcoin’s performance. Thielen had forecast that the bottom would occur between late August and October, but instead, Bitcoin rose from its June low during that timeframe.

The influx of ETF dollars also explains why his July wave count forecast failed. Wave C required active selling to push prices lower, but ETF investors were buying up the coins being sold instead. By late September, these funds controlled about 6.3% of all Bitcoin in circulation.

On the macroeconomic side, we still need to evaluate Thielen’s calls about the dollar and the Federal Reserve. Bitcoin’s price rise alone doesn’t conclusively indicate whether his analysis of these factors was accurate. The Fed’s decision on rates during its September meeting was held on September 16, with another meeting slated for October 27 and 28. These outcomes will clarify whether rates have moved in line with Thielen’s expectations.

Moreover, his end-of-year range now looks different. Initially, Thielen projected Bitcoin would rebound to $60,000 to $65,000 from $46,000. With Bitcoin currently around $86,000, achieving that target would require a drop of roughly 24% to 30% by December 31—a very different scenario from his initial forecast.

The main flaw in the bear case was the misunderstanding of demand. Thielen’s outlook was predicated on the belief that buyers had exited the market, but ETF investors contributed $6.3 billion to Bitcoin funds in the same quarter he expected the bottom to form. Those who sold their Bitcoin near $59,000 around the time of his first forecast have missed out on about a 45% increase in value.

Nonetheless, the bear case could still make a return. If Bitcoin drops below its 2026 low of $57,717 before December 31, and if ETF outflows resume in the fourth quarter, Thielen’s lower price targets could come back into play. As long as Bitcoin stays above that critical level and demand from fund buyers remains strong, the assertion that there is “no real buyer” will continue to prove incorrect.

passages: Investors in Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC), Ethereum (CRYPTO:ETH), XRP (CRYPTO:XRP), and Solana (CRYPTO:SOL) often hear predictions that their coins could 10x by 2030.
However, what a 10x increase means varies greatly between these cryptocurrencies.
For Solana, it would mean growing from a market cap of approximately $70 billion to $700 billion.
For Bitcoin, it would need to rise from $1.69 trillion to nearly $17 trillion—almost three times the value of Nvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA ), currently around $6 trillion.
However, its demand must outpace the growth of its token supply.
XRP follows closely, though potential escrow releases could add more coins as prices rise.
Ethereum ranks third, while Bitcoin sits at the bottom of the list, needing to grow nearly three times as much as Nvidia for a successful 10x.
The cryptocurrency with the easiest math—Solana—has a smaller pool of large buyers.
Solana's market cap would first need to surpass XRP's $93 billion, then Ethereum's $320 billion.
If Solana's price exceeds $1,189 before Ethereum reaches $26,169, the ranking holds.
But if Ethereum hits its target first, it suggests larger investors' buying power outweighs starting size, making the order potentially inaccurate.
Expanding token supplies in Solana and XRP could dilute gains, while Bitcoin's 21M cap and Ethereum's fee-burning mechanism favor long-term price.

However, both cryptocurrencies do have increasing supplies.
Solana rewards holders (stakers) with new tokens for helping secure its network, while Ripple can release up to 1 billion XRP each month from an escrow account.
If their supplies increase significantly, the same market values could result in lower prices than expected.
Bitcoin's 10x demands a $16.9T market cap, which would be nearly 60% of all gold ever mined, making it the least likely to achieve the milestone.
Bitcoin and Ethereum benefit from greater demand.
They have larger investor bases, more established ETF markets, and better access for institutional investors like banks and pension funds, making them more attractive for big-money investments.
That would place it among the few assets valued over $3 trillion.

Investors in Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ), and Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) often hear predictions that their coins could 10x by 2030. However, what a 10x increase means varies greatly between these cryptocurrencies. For Solana, it would mean growing from a market cap of approximately $70 billion to $700 billion. For Bitcoin, it would need to rise from $1.69 trillion to nearly $17 trillion—almost three times the value of Nvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ), currently around $6 trillion.
So which crypto stands the best chance of achieving a 10x increase by 2030, and what would each need to do to make that leap?

A coin’s price alone doesn’t provide much information, especially since these four cryptocurrencies have different token supplies. Market cap is the key metric here. It calculates a cryptocurrency’s total value by multiplying the price of one coin by the number of coins in circulation. This figure determines how much new investment is required for a 10x increase. Investors must be willing to pay the higher price for every circulating coin, so a larger starting market cap requires significantly more total investment.
Here’s a table comparing the four cryptocurrencies, ranked by their targets for a 10x increase as of October 7, 2026:

Solana and XRP have the smallest market cap targets for achieving a 10x increase. For instance, reaching $700 billion for Solana and $930 billion for XRP would not require the creation of a new market, as these values are comparable to some of the largest U.S. tech companies.

However, both cryptocurrencies do have increasing supplies. Solana rewards holders (stakers) with new tokens for helping secure its network, while Ripple can release up to 1 billion XRP each month from an escrow account. If their supplies increase significantly, the same market values could result in lower prices than expected.

Bitcoin and Ethereum benefit from greater demand. They have larger investor bases, more established ETF markets , and better access for institutional investors like banks and pension funds, making them more attractive for big-money investments.

Nevertheless, their targets are quite high. For Ethereum to reach a 10x increase, it would need a market cap of about $3.2 trillion, corresponding to a price per coin of $26,000. That would place it among the few assets valued over $3 trillion. Bitcoin, on the other hand, would need to surge to about $16.9 trillion or roughly $842,000 per coin. This equates to nearly 60% of the total value of all gold ever mined, estimated around $29 trillion at a price of $4,133 per ounce.

Supply dynamics could work in Bitcoin and Ethereum’s favor. Bitcoin’s maximum supply is capped at 21 million coins , while Ethereum’s protocol burns a portion of its transaction fees, which offsets much of its new issuance over time.

Based on our analysis, Solana appears to have the highest chance of achieving a 10x increase by 2030, primarily because it has the smallest target. However, its demand must outpace the growth of its token supply. XRP follows closely, though potential escrow releases could add more coins as prices rise. Ethereum ranks third, while Bitcoin sits at the bottom of the list, needing to grow nearly three times as much as Nvidia for a successful 10x.

This ranking has important implications. The cryptocurrency with the easiest math—Solana—has a smaller pool of large buyers . Solana’s market cap would first need to surpass XRP’s $93 billion, then Ethereum’s $320 billion. If Solana’s price exceeds $1,189 before Ethereum reaches $26,169, the ranking holds. But if Ethereum hits its target first, it suggests larger investors’ buying power outweighs starting size, making the order potentially inaccurate.

Investors in Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ), and Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) often hear predictions that their coins could 10x by 2030. However, what a 10x increase means varies greatly between these cryptocurrencies. For Solana, it would mean growing from a market cap of approximately $70 billion to $700 billion. For Bitcoin, it would need to rise from $1.69 trillion to nearly $17 trillion—almost three times the value of Nvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ), currently around $6 trillion.
So which crypto stands the best chance of achieving a 10x increase by 2030, and what would each need to do to make that leap?

A coin’s price alone doesn’t provide much information, especially since these four cryptocurrencies have different token supplies. Market cap is the key metric here. It calculates a cryptocurrency’s total value by multiplying the price of one coin by the number of coins in circulation. This figure determines how much new investment is required for a 10x increase. Investors must be willing to pay the higher price for every circulating coin, so a larger starting market cap requires significantly more total investment.
Here’s a table comparing the four cryptocurrencies, ranked by their targets for a 10x increase as of October 7, 2026:

Solana and XRP have the smallest market cap targets for achieving a 10x increase. For instance, reaching $700 billion for Solana and $930 billion for XRP would not require the creation of a new market, as these values are comparable to some of the largest U.S. tech companies.

However, both cryptocurrencies do have increasing supplies. Solana rewards holders (stakers) with new tokens for helping secure its network, while Ripple can release up to 1 billion XRP each month from an escrow account. If their supplies increase significantly, the same market values could result in lower prices than expected.

Bitcoin and Ethereum benefit from greater demand. They have larger investor bases, more established ETF markets , and better access for institutional investors like banks and pension funds, making them more attractive for big-money investments.

Nevertheless, their targets are quite high. For Ethereum to reach a 10x increase, it would need a market cap of about $3.2 trillion, corresponding to a price per coin of $26,000. That would place it among the few assets valued over $3 trillion. Bitcoin, on the other hand, would need to surge to about $16.9 trillion or roughly $842,000 per coin. This equates to nearly 60% of the total value of all gold ever mined, estimated around $29 trillion at a price of $4,133 per ounce.

Supply dynamics could work in Bitcoin and Ethereum’s favor. Bitcoin’s maximum supply is capped at 21 million coins , while Ethereum’s protocol burns a portion of its transaction fees, which offsets much of its new issuance over time.

Based on our analysis, Solana appears to have the highest chance of achieving a 10x increase by 2030, primarily because it has the smallest target. However, its demand must outpace the growth of its token supply. XRP follows closely, though potential escrow releases could add more coins as prices rise. Ethereum ranks third, while Bitcoin sits at the bottom of the list, needing to grow nearly three times as much as Nvidia for a successful 10x.

This ranking has important implications. The cryptocurrency with the easiest math—Solana—has a smaller pool of large buyers . Solana’s market cap would first need to surpass XRP’s $93 billion, then Ethereum’s $320 billion. If Solana’s price exceeds $1,189 before Ethereum reaches $26,169, the ranking holds. But if Ethereum hits its target first, it suggests larger investors’ buying power outweighs starting size, making the order potentially inaccurate.

In a blog post explaining the change, OpenAI says it trained GPT-6 when to generate interactive visuals over text, as well as how to format them in its response. You can also ask ChatGPT to generate tools for different tasks, such as a retirement savings calculator, retro game, or bill splitter. It will then generate the tool in-line with its response. OpenAI announced its first GPT-6 models last month, but now it’s bringing the Sol and Luna versions to ChatGPT. In addition to enabling Intelligent UI, OpenAI says its GPT-6 allows ChatGPT to perform better web searches and provide quicker, partial answers to users while it gathers information. The company notes that GPT-6 “showed stronger resistance to attempts to bypass its safety training” as well. While higher-tier subscribers will gain access to the mid-range GPT-6 Sol model, Go and free users will get to use the more efficient GPT-6 Luna.

extraction.body: When Justin Kosmides co-founded Bloom in 2023, his goal was to create a savior for the mobility industry . He had seen many e-bike and e-scooter companies fail because of an inability — or an unwillingness — to outsource some of the hardest problems, like logistics, manufacturing, or building a supply chain. He wanted to convince survivors and new entrants to let Bloom handle that work for them. Then Donald Trump got re-elected and started shotgun-blasting tariffs on dozens of countries, partially to jump-start U.S. manufacturing. This accelerated a hardware scene that was already heating up in this country and, suddenly, it was more than just mobility companies looking to beef up their domestic supply chain. Robotics startups, drone-makers, and many more started to pop up. That was an opportunity for Bloom, which is based in Detroit, but to tackle it, the startup had to partially reinvent itself. Instead of performing some of those harder, behind-the-scenes tasks, which was a big part of the original plan, Bloom shifted to a pure marketplace model, in which it connects buyers and sellers. It’s now focused on making, essentially, supply chain AI agents that Bloom’s customers use to find specific types of suppliers, parts, or manufacturing and engineering services. The reinvention slowed Bloom’s fundraising plans. But the company has now made over 2,000 matches for more than 140 companies, and it wants to grow faster. In an interview earlier this year, Kosmides, who is Bloom’s CEO, said his startup is like what an AI-driven version of Alibaba did in China, where it created a marketplace for contract manufacturers. Investors are finally buying in. On Wednesday, Bloom announced a $3.6 million seed round led by SNAK Venture Partners , a marketplace-focused investment firm. Also joining were Flyover Capital (an early-stage investor that focuses on flyover states), and deep tech firm Mana Ventures. Local backers include Detroit Venture Partners, Invest Detroit Ventures, and the Michigan Outdoor Innovation Fund. Kosmides, sounding relieved, said in the interview that he’s “excited to be done with fundraising and get back to building.” SNAK first met with Bloom in April of last year, in the early stages of this reinvention. So early, in fact, that the firm passed on the chance to invest in the startup’s pre-seed round. “We liked the founder and the thesis and passed anyway: we wanted to see more traction,” the firm wrote in a blog post. “We said so plainly and kept tracking the company.” Bloom kept in touch with SNAK as it worked through becoming a more software-focused startup. By May of this year, Bloom had made as much revenue in five months as it did in all of 2025. SNAK also said the number of memberships on its platform had grown fivefold “with low churn,” meaning few customers were canceling. “This is meant to reiterate that for us, a pass on pre-seed is not always a pass forever. We are fortunate to have a super focused thesis that allows us to track a small set of interesting early stage companies and build a relationship over time,” the firm wrote. Kosmides said the fundraising scene has been a bit ruthless for startups like Bloom. Proving your value to investors in a world where the leading AI models keep improving can be an uphill battle. “To find investors to actually write a term sheet, not follow one, is getting harder and harder,” he said. “That’s just this new era that we’re in, with everyone trying to figure out what’s real and what’s not, what to invest in.” Bloom did court other term sheets, Kosmides said. But SNAK, which was founded by longtime retail executive Sonia Nagar, is “who you want in your camp” to “build a hopefully category-defining marketplace for mobility, and drones, and all this hardware.” Bloom’s platform handles both sides of a supplier relationship. Some customers use the platform to post contract opportunities, while others use it to bid on those opportunities. Bloom handles quoting, booking, and payment all on its platform, and it now helps match companies with suppliers that can do contract manufacturing, assembly, design and engineering, freight, warehousing, repairs, and even hazardous-materials shipping. “Our friends at the parts marketplaces like Fictiv, Xometry, MacroFab, and others are really good yesteryear marketplaces for finding one particular part,” Kosmides said. “But when you’re XYZ Drone Company, or an electric motorcycle company, and you need to find a provider that meets all these requirements, have them all bid on this opportunity, that’s a lot more complicated than finding a CNC part.” Making this system work well is a big part of Bloom’s reinvention, and it involved ingesting a lot of data about each provider on the platform. A lot of that was public data — how a company describes itself on its website, for instance. But around 30-40% of that data is coming directly from the companies, Kosmides said. Add in the data being generated as the startup onboards more customers and makes more matches, and you have Bloom’s edge, he said. “You can build the craziest model for scraping data but you would never get to that accuracy,” he said. “We started with manually booking services, and then built in layers and pieces and understanding as we built up the provider network, as we built out more and more transactions, and so it’s only getting better and better.” Kosmides believes this is all a better way to strike up supplier relationships, and that it also makes it easier for startups to get off the ground. But he also thinks Bloom’s platform will help create opportunities for small manufacturers who may not have big marketing budgets or sales teams. He gave an example of one Michigan-based contract manufacturer that, until it started working with Bloom, was taking on odd jobs like refurbishing Nest thermostats and Bird scooters, or working with Chick-fil-A displays. That same company is now bidding on drone assembly contracts. “The ability to discover, and the ability to do matchmaking, that is what I think is truly missing” from U.S. manufacturing, he said. “That just doesn’t exist electronically.” Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. passages: When Justin Kosmides co-founded Bloom in 2023, his goal was to create a savior for the mobility industry . He had seen many e-bike and e-scooter companies fail because of an inability — or an unwillingness — to outsource some of the hardest problems, like logistics, manufacturing, or building a supply chain. He wanted to convince survivors and new entrants to let Bloom handle that work for them.

Then Donald Trump got re-elected and started shotgun-blasting tariffs on dozens of countries, partially to jump-start U.S. manufacturing. This accelerated a hardware scene that was already heating up in this country and, suddenly, it was more than just mobility companies looking to beef up their domestic supply chain. Robotics startups, drone-makers, and many more started to pop up.

That was an opportunity for Bloom, which is based in Detroit, but to tackle it, the startup had to partially reinvent itself. Instead of performing some of those harder, behind-the-scenes tasks, which was a big part of the original plan, Bloom shifted to a pure marketplace model, in which it connects buyers and sellers. It’s now focused on making, essentially, supply chain AI agents that Bloom’s customers use to find specific types of suppliers, parts, or manufacturing and engineering services.

The reinvention slowed Bloom’s fundraising plans. But the company has now made over 2,000 matches for more than 140 companies, and it wants to grow faster. In an interview earlier this year, Kosmides, who is Bloom’s CEO, said his startup is like what an AI-driven version of Alibaba did in China, where it created a marketplace for contract manufacturers.

Investors are finally buying in. On Wednesday, Bloom announced a $3.6 million seed round led by SNAK Venture Partners , a marketplace-focused investment firm. Also joining were Flyover Capital (an early-stage investor that focuses on flyover states), and deep tech firm Mana Ventures. Local backers include Detroit Venture Partners, Invest Detroit Ventures, and the Michigan Outdoor Innovation Fund.
Kosmides, sounding relieved, said in the interview that he’s “excited to be done with fundraising and get back to building.”
SNAK first met with Bloom in April of last year, in the early stages of this reinvention. So early, in fact, that the firm passed on the chance to invest in the startup’s pre-seed round.
“We liked the founder and the thesis and passed anyway: we wanted to see more traction,” the firm wrote in a blog post. “We said so plainly and kept tracking the company.”

Bloom kept in touch with SNAK as it worked through becoming a more software-focused startup. By May of this year, Bloom had made as much revenue in five months as it did in all of 2025. SNAK also said the number of memberships on its platform had grown fivefold “with low churn,” meaning few customers were canceling.

“This is meant to reiterate that for us, a pass on pre-seed is not always a pass forever. We are fortunate to have a super focused thesis that allows us to track a small set of interesting early stage companies and build a relationship over time,” the firm wrote.
Kosmides said the fundraising scene has been a bit ruthless for startups like Bloom. Proving your value to investors in a world where the leading AI models keep improving can be an uphill battle.

“To find investors to actually write a term sheet, not follow one, is getting harder and harder,” he said. “That’s just this new era that we’re in, with everyone trying to figure out what’s real and what’s not, what to invest in.”

Bloom did court other term sheets, Kosmides said. But SNAK, which was founded by longtime retail executive Sonia Nagar, is “who you want in your camp” to “build a hopefully category-defining marketplace for mobility, and drones, and all this hardware.”

Bloom’s platform handles both sides of a supplier relationship. Some customers use the platform to post contract opportunities, while others use it to bid on those opportunities. Bloom handles quoting, booking, and payment all on its platform, and it now helps match companies with suppliers that can do contract manufacturing, assembly, design and engineering, freight, warehousing, repairs, and even hazardous-materials shipping.

“Our friends at the parts marketplaces like Fictiv, Xometry, MacroFab, and others are really good yesteryear marketplaces for finding one particular part,” Kosmides said. “But when you’re XYZ Drone Company, or an electric motorcycle company, and you need to find a provider that meets all these requirements, have them all bid on this opportunity, that’s a lot more complicated than finding a CNC part.”

Making this system work well is a big part of Bloom’s reinvention, and it involved ingesting a lot of data about each provider on the platform. A lot of that was public data — how a company describes itself on its website, for instance. But around 30-40% of that data is coming directly from the companies, Kosmides said. Add in the data being generated as the startup onboards more customers and makes more matches, and you have Bloom’s edge, he said.

“You can build the craziest model for scraping data but you would never get to that accuracy,” he said. “We started with manually booking services, and then built in layers and pieces and understanding as we built up the provider network, as we built out more and more transactions, and so it’s only getting better and better.”

Kosmides believes this is all a better way to strike up supplier relationships, and that it also makes it easier for startups to get off the ground. But he also thinks Bloom’s platform will help create opportunities for small manufacturers who may not have big marketing budgets or sales teams.

He gave an example of one Michigan-based contract manufacturer that, until it started working with Bloom, was taking on odd jobs like refurbishing Nest thermostats and Bird scooters, or working with Chick-fil-A displays. That same company is now bidding on drone assembly contracts.
“The ability to discover, and the ability to do matchmaking, that is what I think is truly missing” from U.S. manufacturing, he said. “That just doesn’t exist electronically.”

Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane.

sources.title: X expands its ‘Gametime’ sports hub beyond the NFL, starting with MLB
passages: X is doubling down on sports, with Wednesday’s news that it’s expanding its “Gametime” feature on the social media site to go beyond tracking the NFL alone.

“In just six weeks, Gametime has evolved from a football-focused product into a scalable destination for sports, attracting strong demand across major advertisers from payments to consumer goods looking to engage highly attentive fans from the pregame conversation through the biggest moments of the game,” said SpaceXAI’s head of Global Advertising, Monique Pintarelli, in an announcement.
First announced in August, NFL Gametime is X’s new project that offers a single hub for tracking live scores, getting play-by-play updates, tuning into game feeds, and more.
The move wasn’t meant to be useful only to X users who like to congregate on the platform to discuss live sporting events, but to woo brands and advertisers looking to reach passionate sports fans.
At Advertising Week New York, X said Gametime will become a year-round destination spanning “all professional sports.”
However, that full expansion isn’t yet live as of today.
Instead, X announced its second league partnership with Major League Baseball (MLB).

Arriving this month, the new MLB experience will allow baseball fans to follow and engage in postseason discussions and will organize things like scores and stats, team and league content, plus news, creator content, and real-time discussions.

The expansion of the Gametime feature comes as X continues its efforts to win back advertisers — in this case by leveraging live sports and their highly engaged fans as a way to draw brands back to X.

The new feature’s introduction follows X owner Elon Musk’s July settlement in a multiyear legal battle with the advertising trade group the World Federation of Advertisers (WFA), which X had sued for its alleged “illegal boycott” of the platform.
Musk believed the WFA’s guidelines had steered brands and ad agencies away from X, suggesting it was a place where their ads could appear next to harmful online content.

sources.title: Google’s new SynthID website can identify AI-generated media
passages: Google is using SynthID, which it introduced in 2023 , to identify whether media is AI-generated.
The company’s Nano Banana, Veo, and Lyria models, as well as tools with generation capabilities, like Gemini, Flow, ProducerAI, and Vids, all use SynthID to watermark any media they generate.
Google has baked SynthID verification into the Gemini app and Google Chrome.
The company said people currently make 1 million requests to verify content every day.
Google on Tuesday launched a new site that lets anyone verify whether a piece of media, be it an image, a video, or an audio clip, is generated using AI.
Microsoft and Meta have their own standards for watermarking and verifying content.
However, these tools are not infallible, often failing to identify content created by their makers’ models.
OpenAI, Nvidia, and Kakao also support SynthID, and OpenAI maintains its own site for checking content.
Apple is said to be adding support soon, too.
The company made this tool available to select journalists, media professionals, and researchers for testing at Google I/O last year, and is now opening up access to the tool to everyone.

The site supports JPG, JPEG, PNG, BMP, WEBP, AVIF, HEIC, HEIF, TIFF, TIF, and GIF formats for images; MP4, MOV, and WEBM for videos; and WAV, MP3, OGG, FLAC, AAC, and M4A for audio.

Google is using SynthID, which it introduced in 2023 , to identify whether media is AI-generated. The company’s Nano Banana, Veo, and Lyria models, as well as tools with generation capabilities, like Gemini, Flow, ProducerAI, and Vids, all use SynthID to watermark any media they generate.
OpenAI, Nvidia, and Kakao also support SynthID, and OpenAI maintains its own site for checking content. Apple is said to be adding support soon, too.
Google has baked SynthID verification into the Gemini app and Google Chrome. The company said people currently make 1 million requests to verify content every day.
Microsoft and Meta have their own standards for watermarking and verifying content. However, these tools are not infallible, often failing to identify content created by their makers’ models.

That’s the question Tanvi Thombre and Lakshya Saraf began investigating when they were engineering students who worked in their university makerspace. In fact, Thombre said via email that, while working in the space, they were “unknowingly exposed to toxic fumes from laser cutters, 3D printers, and soldering irons,” but they didn’t realize it until Thombre’s best friend fainted and had to go to the hospital. After that, Thombre said, “We began investigating indoor air pollution and realized it was an invisible but dangerous health risk — especially in schools, offices, hotels, salons, and any commercial buildings where air-conditioning prevents windows from being opened.” Those issues persist even when a building is equipped with air purifiers, as their makerspace was. The problem, according to Saraf, is that although purifiers are good at cleaning out particulate matter like dust and pollen, they are less effective at removing toxic gases such as carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, and benzine (many of which are classified as volatile organic compounds, or VOCs — chemicals that evaporate easily into the air). Thombre said that VOCs are linked to chronic disease and “ sick building syndrome ,” a condition in which occupants experience health effects and discomfort after spending time in a building, even though no specific cause or illness has been identified. She also pointed to Harvard research showing that improving indoor air quality improved cognitive function and productivity as well. That’s why the pair is targeting toxic gases in the workplace with their startup Greenairy , which will be part of Startup Battlefield 200 at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt . Greenairy’s approach centers on building plant towers that are supposed to draw in air, break down toxic gases, and then release the purified air. As Saraf put it, “A plant in a pot cleans air slowly. But, when we change the conditions around the plant, it cleans air much faster and better than these conventional methods.” Saraf also said that while some air purifier filters can remove “a narrow range of VOCs,” those filters need to be changed frequently to be effective. In contrast, plants are “a natural solution, no harmful by-products are formed, and no filter replacement is required.” Greenairy has already conducted short-term pilots at locations around Singapore. Saraf said that in the startup’s own testing using RESET-certified air monitors, it compared three offices: one with Greenairy plant towers, one that had a medical-grade ionizer (a device that uses an electrical charge to make dust and other particles clump together and fall out of the air), and a third with a HEPA air purifier that traps very small particles. “Our tower had the lowest VOC levels and removed VOCs the fastest,” she said. “The office staff also grew fond of the natural ‘fresh’ aroma of the tower and the natural vibe it brought.” Thombre added that they saw an “immediate” improvement within regular office hours, with a 50% reduction in both the daily VOC average and peak levels. She said the results improved even more “as the plants and microbes mature and the gases are prevented from accumulating.” Greenairy has also had its results validated by the German testing and certification firm TÜV SÜD and will be publishing them soon. (Results are available upon request in the meantime.) The pair plans to begin large-scale manufacturing after the results are certified. The startup’s founders are currently based on opposite sides of the world, with Saraf in Berkeley, California, and Thombre in Singapore. It’s an arrangement that Saraf said “works well at this stage,” allowing one founder to focus on testing in Singapore while the other can fundraise in the Bay Area. “If things go to plan, both of us will be in Singapore by the first half of 2027,” she added. “That’s when we expect to launch our first mass-produced towers and install them for our first customers” in Singapore. VP, Science and Strategic Initiatives, Google DeepMind Your browser does not support the audio element. Advances in generative AI are making it possible for people to create content in entirely new ways — from text to high quality audio, images and videos. As these capabilities advance and become more broadly available, questions of authenticity, context and verification emerge. Today we’re announcing SynthID Detector, a verification portal to quickly and efficiently identify AI-generated content made with Google AI. The portal provides detection capabilities across different modalities in one place and provides essential transparency in the rapidly evolving landscape of generative media. It can also highlight which parts of the content are more likely to have been watermarked with SynthID. When we launched SynthID — a state-of-the-art tool that embeds imperceptible watermarks and enables the identification of AI-generated content — our aim was to provide a suite of novel technical solutions to help minimise misinformation and misattribution. SynthID not only preserves the content’s quality, it acts as a robust watermark that remains detectable even when the content is shared or undergoes a range of transformations. While originally focused on AI-generated imagery only, we’ve since expanded SynthID to cover AI-generated text, audio and video content, including content generated by our Gemini, Imagen, Lyria and Veo models across Google. Over 10 billion pieces of content have already been watermarked with SynthID. When you upload an image, audio track, video or piece of text created using Google's AI tools, the portal will scan the media for a SynthID watermark. If a watermark is detected, the portal will highlight specific portions of the content most likely to be watermarked. For audio, the portal pinpoints specific segments where a SynthID watermark is detected, and for images, it indicates areas where a watermark is most likely. We are starting to roll this out to early testers today, before making it available more broadly. Journalists, media professionals and researchers can join our waitlist to gain access to the SynthID Detector. To help grow a trusted ecosystem we’ve already open sourced SynthID text watermarking , so any developer can build with this technology and incorporate it into their own models. And earlier this year we took the first step in creating an ecosystem of industry partners to expand the use of the SynthID technology: We partnered with NVIDIA to watermark videos generated by their NVIDIA Cosmos™ preview NIM microservice on build.nvidia.com . This means that more content across the web has SynthID embedded in it, not just content generated by Google. Today we’re announcing SynthID Detector, a verification portal to quickly and efficiently identify AI-generated content made with Google AI. The portal provides detection capabilities across different modalities in one place and provides essential transparency in the rapidly evolving landscape of generative media. It can also highlight which parts of the content are more likely to have been watermarked with SynthID.

When we launched SynthID — a state-of-the-art tool that embeds imperceptible watermarks and enables the identification of AI-generated content — our aim was to provide a suite of novel technical solutions to help minimise misinformation and misattribution.

sources.title: Google rolls out improved SynthID AI content detector, now available globally
passages: Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic .
SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process.
It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though.
Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website.
Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark.
A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID.
Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector.
You have to log in to use the tool, but it supports Google, OpenAI, and Apple accounts.
While the detector is available to anyone, the login requirement limits how much you can use it.
Google says each user gets “a daily usage quota of approximately 10 image, video, and audio checks.”
Expanding access to SynthID detection is a good thing—it’s a convenient single destination to check media for the signature of popular AI tools.
The website will have a disclaimer saying as much.
It’s not a perfect system, but that’s the reality of relying on proactive watermarking for AI images, which are proliferating across the Internet at an astonishing rate.
SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio.
This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.”
So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually.
Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media.
The previous detection tools had a similar limit.
Google engineers have told Ars that limiting access is necessary to prevent people from using the checks to develop SynthID removal tools.
The fuzziness about the exact number is likely because the system may lock you out sooner if you’re checking multiple images that are very similar.
This could signal someone is trying to tune a bypass workflow.
Google’s Pixel phones are among the few devices doing just that.

So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually. SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process.
It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though.
Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website.
Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark.
A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID.
Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector.
You have to log in to use the tool, but it supports Google, OpenAI, and Apple accounts.
While the detector is available to anyone, the login requirement limits how much you can use it.
Google says each user gets “a daily usage quota of approximately 10 image, video, and audio checks.”
Expanding access to SynthID detection is a good thing—it’s a convenient single destination to check media for the signature of popular AI tools.
The website will have a disclaimer saying as much.
It’s not a perfect system, but that’s the reality of relying on proactive watermarking for AI images, which are proliferating across the Internet at an astonishing rate.
SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio.
This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.”
So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually.
Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media.
The previous detection tools had a similar limit.
Google engineers have told Ars that limiting access is necessary to prevent people from using the checks to develop SynthID removal tools.
The fuzziness about the exact number is likely because the system may lock you out sooner if you’re checking multiple images that are very similar.
This could signal someone is trying to tune a bypass workflow.
Google’s Pixel phones are among the few devices doing just that.

extraction.body: The new SynthID website can now identify AI content from Google, OpenAI, and more. Every piece of AI content from Google’s Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic . SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process. It’s going to be a little easier going forward, though. Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it’s available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website. SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio. Google says Gemini alone has integrated SynthID with over 180 billion images and videos, plus 240,000 years of audio. Until now, the only way for those outside of Google’s trusted tester program to check for SynthID was to ask Gemini. This is rather clunky, and the model’s output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple “yes” or “no.” Now you can cut Gemini out of the loop. Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark. A major limitation of Google’s previous detector was that it only checked for Google’s version of SynthID. Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn’t be flagged in Google’s detector. That’s no longer a problem. Google says that its expanded version of the detector will support the distinct watermarks from all its SynthID partners, including OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and (soon) Apple. So you’ll be able to go there and check a file for the involvement of all those AI systems instead of accessing their detectors individually. The website won’t provide as much information as the internal tool, which highlighted regions of the image that showed SynthID pixels. Instead, you’ll just get a message telling you whether SynthID was used to produce or edit the media. You have to log in to use the tool, but it supports Google, OpenAI, and Apple accounts. While the detector is available to anyone, the login requirement limits how much you can use it. Google says each user gets “a daily usage quota of approximately 10 image, video, and audio checks.” The previous detection tools had a similar limit. Google engineers have told Ars that limiting access is necessary to prevent people from using the checks to develop SynthID removal tools. The fuzziness about the exact number is likely because the system may lock you out sooner if you’re checking multiple images that are very similar. This could signal someone is trying to tune a bypass workflow. Expanding access to SynthID detection is a good thing—it’s a convenient single destination to check media for the signature of popular AI tools. However, Google’s partners are far from the only sources of AI content. Some model providers use different watermarking tech (like Meta), while others use no watermarks at all. And then there are open-weight models that people can run on their own hardware to produce increasingly realistic AI content that doesn’t even include simple metadata labeling. That means there is plenty of AI content that will not be identified as AI in the SynthID tool. The website will have a disclaimer saying as much. It’s also plausible that despite Google’s efforts, someone will find a way to remove SynthID, making existing AI content look more legit. It’s not a perfect system, but that’s the reality of relying on proactive watermarking for AI images, which are proliferating across the Internet at an astonishing rate. The best approach might be the opposite—using cryptographic technologies like C2PA to label real images, video, and audio as they are created. Google’s Pixel phones are among the few devices doing just that. In the meantime, SynthID is the best bet you’ve got to identify AI fakes. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

story.title: Google rolls out improved SynthID AI content detector, now available globally

facts.text: Google notes that images made with Apple Intelligence will carry a SynthID watermark “soon,” which implies it might be a little bit before users can reliably identify AI-generated content from Apple’s models.
But the expansion means that more users in total will be able to do some due diligence on photos and videos posted online.
Google announced that SynthID is being upgraded from limited early access to a globally available tool in English, though it’s expected to expand further in the future.
The tool has progressed some , but this is a bigger step for AI content detection.
According to Google’s press release, the AI image detector launch comes with expanded compatibility.
So far, the list includes OpenAI, Nvidia, Kakao, and now, Apple.

That means any content generated with models from those companies will contain visually undetectable watermarks so users can later check whether the image is a human-made visual or something an algorithm cobbled together.
Stay up to date on news from Google headquarters…
SynthID Detector — a new portal to help identify AI-generated content
The portal provides detection capabilities across different modalities in one place and provides essential transparency in the rapidly evolving landscape of generative media.
It can also highlight which parts of the content are more likely to have been watermarked with SynthID.
SynthID not only preserves the content’s quality, it acts as a robust watermark that remains detectable even when the content is shared or undergoes a range of transformations.

While originally focused on AI-generated imagery only, we’ve since expanded SynthID to cover AI-generated text, audio and video content, including content generated by our Gemini, Imagen, Lyria and Veo models across Google.
The author would like to thank Miguel de Andrés-Clavera and the Google Partner Innovation team for their assistance in developing the SynthID Detector portal.
Content transparency remains a complex challenge.
We are starting to roll this out to early testers today, before making it available more broadly.
When you upload an image, audio track, video or piece of text created using Google's AI tools, the portal will scan the media for a SynthID watermark.

And earlier this year we took the first step in creating an ecosystem of industry partners to expand the use of the SynthID technology: We partnered with NVIDIA to watermark videos generated by their NVIDIA Cosmos™ preview NIM microservice on build.nvidia.com .
To help grow a trusted ecosystem we’ve already open sourced SynthID text watermarking , so any developer can build with this technology and incorporate it into their own models.
The tool checks images, video, and audio files for Google’s SynthID watermark , a system that embeds a near-invisible marker into AI-generated content.
Google first made its SynthID Detector available to media professionals last year, but now anyone can use it by logging into synthid.com .

sources.title: Introducing Copilot Actions, new agents, and tools to empower IT teams - Microsoft
passages: Copilot is where you interact with agents , and Copilot Studio is where you can easily create, manage, and connect agents to Copilot.
We’re introducing agents in Microsoft 365 designed to help scale individual impact and transform business processes.
These new agents complement the autonomous agents that we announced in October 2024 for sales, service, finance, and supply chain professionals—and we’re just getting started.
We’ll create many more agents in the coming year that will give customers the competitive advantage they need to future-proof their organization.
September 23 3 min read Building the system for AI at work There’s no shortage of sound and fury in AI right now.
Visit Microsoft365.com/copilot or download the Microsoft 365 app on your mobile device.
To empower every IT team to lead at scale, we’re introducing the Copilot Control System —designed for IT to confidently adopt and accelerate the business value of Copilot and agents.
Microsoft 365 Copilot is becoming a daily habit for people around the world—already, nearly 70% of Fortune 500 companies are using it.

Dow anticipates that Copilot will save it millions of dollars on shipping operations in the first year; at Bank of Queensland Group , 70% of users are saving two and a half to five hours per week; Eaton is speeding up internal documentation processes by 83%; and Accenture is going big, rolling out Copilot to 100,000 employees.

Dow anticipates that Copilot will save it millions of dollars on shipping operations in the first year; at Bank of Queensland Group , 70% of users are saving two and a half to five hours per week; Eaton is speeding up internal documentation processes by 83%; and Accenture is going big, rolling out Copilot to 100,000 employees.

Today at Microsoft Ignite 2024 , we’re accelerating our ambition to empower every employee with Copilot as a personal assistant and to transform every business process with agents built in Microsoft Copilot Studio.
These announcements build on our wave 2 momentum, including the new autonomous agent capabilities that we announced in October 2024 .

Thanks to our customers, we have the world’s best feedback loop on AI at work. We’ve dramatically improved Copilot performance—responses are two times faster on average and response satisfaction is nearly three times higher 1 —and shipped hundreds of new features. And we’re adding new value to Copilot to tackle work’s biggest pain points and help every employee scale their impact—from automating repetitive tasks to managing your calendar.

Copilot is where you interact with agents , and Copilot Studio is where you can easily create, manage, and connect agents to Copilot. We’re introducing agents in Microsoft 365 designed to help scale individual impact and transform business processes. These new agents complement the autonomous agents that we announced in October 2024 for sales, service, finance, and supply chain professionals—and we’re just getting started. We’ll create many more agents in the coming year that will give customers the competitive advantage they need to future-proof their organization.

Chief information officers and IT professionals are at the epicenter of AI transformation. To empower every IT team to lead at scale, we’re introducing the Copilot Control System —designed for IT to confidently adopt and accelerate the business value of Copilot and agents.

In today’s digital landscape, protecting your organization’s data from emerging threats and ensuring system integrity is paramount. We’re pushing the boundaries to continue making Windows the most secure and performant platform for you and your organization.

To empower every employee with Copilot as a personal assistant and transform every business process with agents built in Copilot Studio, start using Copilot today. Visit Microsoft365.com/copilot or download the Microsoft 365 app on your mobile device.

1 Blind, side-by-side human intelligence tasks conducted on behalf of Microsoft in July and August 2024, each with 9 participants (judges) to compare user satisfaction with query responses of Microsoft Copilot and a competitor. Copilot won 16% of the comparisons in July and 46% in August.
Chief Marketing Officer, AI at Work, Microsoft

Jared leads Microsoft’s AI at Work efforts, helping every organization leverage AI and agents to solve their unique business problems, reduce costs, and drive net-new value creation. His team conducts research to help predict and shape what the future of work and business will look like across industries, while also delivering new products and features within Copilot, Copilot Studio, Microsoft 365, Dynamics 365, and Power Platform.

sources.title: Microsoft is giving Copilot more control over Windows and your files
passages: At today’s Windows and Surface event, Microsoft showed off an upgrade to its Copilot AI system that will give it access to local files on your PC and the ability to take actions across the OS.
To show off how Hybrid Intelligence works, Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, walked through a video demo onstage asking Microsoft’s Autopilot tool to help with filing taxes.

Microsoft also showed off a new Windows search experience that lets you take quick actions from the search bar, like turning on dark mode, turning up your mic volume with an in-line slider, or even sending a text.
It’s part of an idea Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence,” where apps and tools rely on a mix of local and cloud AI models to accomplish tasks efficiently.
Features powered by Hybrid Intelligence will be coming to Copilot over the “next couple months,” Andreou said.

passages:
Microsoft wants its AI assistant to stop just talking about your computer and start operating it. 
 At its Windows and Surface event on October 7, 2026, the company showed off a Copilot upgrade that will let the assistant reach into local files on your PC and carry out actions across the operating system. 
 

 The upgrade falls under a concept Microsoft is calling “Hybrid Intelligence.” Under this approach, apps and tools draw on a blend of AI models: some running on the device itself, others running in the cloud, with the goal of finishing tasks efficiently. 
 Taxes, accountants, and an AI that reads your inbox 
 Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s EVP of Copilot, handled the on-stage pitch.
He then asked the agent to help get her what she was requesting. \n Advertisement \n SEARCH Searching...
Microsoft can wire its agent directly into Windows, which turns deep OS integration into its main differentiator as demand grows for AI that handles complex, multi-step work.
He walked the audience through a video demo built around a task few people enjoy: filing taxes.
The company has built in several layers of control.
AI activation is opt-in, folder access is restricted, and Copilot agents operate under separate accounts from the user.
The Microsoft 365 Copilot user base remains small, with only a limited slice of users engaging with premium features.

Microsoft announced the Surface Laptop Ultra at the event, a machine equipped with Nvidia RTX Spark silicon aimed at improved AI performance.
Microsoft has also emphasized agent workspaces and user-controlled settings, designs intended to keep privacy and security in the foreground.

sources.title: Microsoft's Hybrid Intelligence gives Copilot more control over your files
passages: Hybrid Intelligence also improves Autopilot, Microsoft's personal AI agent.
For those using Copilot for coding assistance, Microsoft says Hybrid Intelligence improves the experience in several ways.
Microsoft has unveiled Hybrid Intelligence, a set of software orchestration tools that will let your PC run AI models locally.
Microsoft says while Copilot will still rely on cloud inference for complex tasks, it can also run prompts against models running directly on your computer in cost- or privacy-sensitive scenarios.
This way, no information was sent to the cloud, further emphasizing Microsoft's focus on privacy and security in its AI advancements.
It makes writing native Windows apps directly from Copilot easier and safer with new Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) tech.

passages: Hybrid Intelligence also improves Autopilot, Microsoft's personal AI agent.
For those using Copilot for coding assistance, Microsoft says Hybrid Intelligence improves the experience in several ways.
Microsoft has unveiled Hybrid Intelligence, a set of software orchestration tools that will let your PC run AI models locally.
Microsoft says while Copilot will still rely on cloud inference for complex tasks, it can also run prompts against models running directly on your computer in cost- or privacy-sensitive scenarios.
This way, no information was sent to the cloud, further emphasizing Microsoft's focus on privacy and security in its AI advancements.
It makes writing native Windows apps directly from Copilot easier and safer with new Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) tech.

We’re introducing agents in Microsoft 365 designed to help scale individual impact and transform business processes.

September 23 3 min read Building the system for AI at work There’s no shortage of sound and fury in AI right now.

extraction.body: We'll definitely hear about the NVIDIA RTX Spark-powered Surface Laptop Ultra, but what else? It's been two years since Microsoft launched Copilot+ AI PCs , its first major attempt at fostering AI-ready hardware, and the results have been mixed , to say the least. This month, the company is again gearing up to espouse the virtues of agentic AI, the latest trendy topic in the tech world, in San Francisco on October 7 . Microsoft describes the event as "a conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC," and it will include notable guests like CEO Satya Nadella, head of Windows and Devices Pavan Davuluri and NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang. Given the PC world's lack of enthusiasm for the Copilot+ initiative , the subsequent removal of intrusive Copilot+ features in Windows 11 and the tepid response to invasive features like Recall , Microsoft is going into this event on the defensive. Can it really whip up enthusiasm for the latest buzzy AI trend? Here's what we expect to see in San Francisco next week. We'll be there liveblogging, and you can follow along with that here . NVIDIA is once again claiming it will redefine PCs with its RTX Spark , the company's first major Arm-powered chip built for massive AI models on Windows laptops and desktops. The Surface Laptop Ultra, which was announced in June , is one of the first devices powered by RTX Spark, and from the brief glimpse we got earlier this year, it appears to be a direct competitor to Apple's powerful MacBook Pro. It sports a 15-inch mini-LED screen with up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness, a massive trackpad and all the ports you want. But we still don't know how much the Surface Laptop Ultra will actually cost, and there's no concrete release date yet. I'd bet the company is saving up those crucial details for next week's event. I'd also bet it will be so expensive, only true AI diehards will want one. AMD recently launched its flagship AI desktop hardware, the Ryzen AI Halo , at $3,999, and NVIDIA's existing Linux-powered DGX Spark systems sell for $4,999 (up from $4,000 at launch). Large AI models demand gobs of RAM to run locally, which is a major reason why these AI-focused systems are so exorbitant. To recap, the NVIDIA RTX Spark will feature 6,144 Blackwell GPU cores, 20 Arm CPU cores and up to 128GB of unified memory. The RTX Spark will also be less power-hungry than existing AI hardware, drawing up to only 80 watts of power. I'm not expecting to be very surprised by the Surface Laptop Ultra. Aside from being one of the first systems with RTX Spark, it just seems to be another premium laptop. But I'm hoping to discover what inspired this poetic take on the notebook from Microsoft Corporate Vice President Brett Ostrum: "A machine like this should not sit still. It should be pushed. Taken to the edge. Used to make real what others call impossible. It belongs in the hands of world makers." Microsoft isn't really keeping this a secret: The company wants us to know it's going to have some big agentic AI news next week. That comes on the heels of Meta launching its Muse AI agent , which quickly reached 5 million downloads, but also arrived with a serious 0-day flaw . Much like it did with Recall, Microsoft could easily run into unforeseen privacy issues with a true AI agent, which would potentially be able to see all of your files, your browsing history and act on your behalf. We've already seen Microsoft's concept of an AI agent platform in the form of Project Solara , which in demos earlier this year was shown to work across a smart display and smart key badge. However, that still seems more sci-fi than reality. The company has also dabbled in some weaker agentic concepts in Windows, including Office Agent to help you build out documents, as well as an agent for dealing with settings in Copilot+ PCs . The core idea of agentic AI — letting an AI tool work on tasks with minimal input — sounds intriguing, especially to people who've already fully changed their workflows around modern AI models. But it's also not something that will easily translate to people outside of the tech world. I can see why so many programmers got excited about OpenClaw , but only a few people will want to manage an agent with an archaic command line interface.
