extraction.body: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware. It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths . It’s a sampler. It’s a synth. It has an FM radio. It will have a variety of sequencers. It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique. It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.) I got to spend some hands-on time with the current prototype of the OP-1, and hanging out with the guys from Teenage Engineering. I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design. The OP-1 is real, it’s coming, and it’s far enough along in the prototyping phase that I think we’ll see real details on getting one soon. Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing. There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating. I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real. I am surprised, though, that people are now complaining that the OP-1 is taking a long time – I think some people don’t realize how time-consuming hardware development really is, and we only just saw an under-glass prototype last spring. The fact that the OP-1 does integrate hardware and onboard software tightly and does do things in new ways is a testament to having a single, small team that works on the whole product. Teenage Engineering – OP-1 @ NAMM 2010 from Neil Bufkin on Vimeo . In the din of the NAMM hall, some people didn’t seem to “get” the OP-1. The prototypes available aren’t entirely refined in regards to the sound engine, so it’s too soon to judge sound quality, and some functionality was missing from the units on display. And it’d be easy to see this its collection of synthesis and sampling tricks as nothing new. (In fact, I get the sense that some people dialed up essentially an init preset and judged the sound quality based on that.) But look closer, and even prior to the finished product, there’s real design genius here. Some of the little touches I was able to glean: You can record backwards, an idea so simple in sampling, but also powerful, it’s a wonder it’s not widespread. Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results. It’s not hard to imagine putting an OP-1 alongside a computer, and using it alternatively as a hardware synth and a tool for resampling the output of a live computer mix. It’s a four-track virtual tape recorder, complete with virtual splicing. The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage. The OP-1 is the most convincing adaptation of that idea I’ve ever seen. A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport. But you can also cut the virtual tape – split, lift and join features are quick key shortcuts away. Just like on tape, you can change the speed during recording, not just during playback . And, so as not to be too caught in the past, the tape deck itself can be beat-synced . Let’s just reflect on that for a second: you can sample the instrument or an external source, and then speed and slow the recording like tape synced to beat, all on hardware. Sampling features are nothing new, but the implementation here really is something special. Whereas clunky hardware designs from mainstream manufacturers have typically treated tape recording as something you do to record an arrangement, the OP-1’s tape recorder is one you can play as an instrument. (See our video of one of the Teenage Engineers jamming with this feature, which I smuggled off one of their Mac laptops.) And it’s finally a sampling feature that functions on recording like tape, not just on playback. That sound you heard all around NAMM was the sound of developers and engineers collectively saying to themselves, “why didn’t I do this myself, first?” (Okay, knowing this site, I’m sure we’ll get someone on comments who has done this first, so do speak up.) Watch it in action in this video of a live jam, shot by Teenage Engineering and smuggled off one of their computers for CDM : The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly. To me, the greatest accomplishment of the OP-1 is making a small screen seem integral to a hardware design, rather than a concession to practicality. Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise. I remember synth shopping for the first time around 1990 and being frustrated by that, and things aren’t much different now. The design of the OP-1’s interface is so minimal, however, that the onboard screen seems perfect. The display itself seems like part of the hardware and the instrument, rather than being a menu system or a tacked-on indicator. It’s finally a small screen that seems ideal for its purpose – maybe even better than looking at a computer-sized screen. And that’s not just because it’s pretty; it’s because it’s functional. For a look at some of these beautiful design ideas in motion, here’s a video from a hands-on (more with sound yet to come): The synth and sampler are friendly – toy-like in the best way. In keeping with some of the most fun instruments of all time, the OP-1 is something people will want to play. Color-coded knobs and extensive graphical feedback make a reasonably sophisticated set of synthesis, envelope, and sampling options accessible. There’s nothing revolutionary in the synth or sampler; it just takes the 90% of sound-making techniques most people use and makes them more immediate. All of these things are wonderful, and clearly it’s a gorgeous little device. And it’s impossible, as always, to judge a design that isn’t finished. I have a suspicion, however, that some of the most important magic of the OP-1 lies in what the impishly-secretive Teenage Engineers aren’t saying: The OP-1 is definitely one I’ll be following; it’s at the top of my list for the year. And it’s about time we got some really significant new hardware. For more information… Teenage has a lovely set of photos on their blog – and yes, that’s me, by coincidence amidst a crew from Hispasonic: NAMM Photo Bananza And don’t miss the product page, which now has a lot of detail on it: Teenage Engineering OP-1 Among the juicy specs: how about an onboard accelerometer, Li-Ion rechargeable battery, a 60-fps display, and a powerful (for this kind of gear) 400MHz processor core? Just please, please, don’t judge the sound quality of a non-shipping synth based on YouTube videos. I’ll be sure to report back on final sound quality before you unload your hard-earned change. CDM is a home for people who make and play music and motion.

The OP-1 is definitely one I’ll be following; it’s at the top of my list for the year. And it’s about time we got some really significant new hardware. For more information…
Teenage has a lovely set of photos on their blog – and yes, that’s me, by coincidence amidst a crew from Hispasonic: NAMM Photo Bananza

Just please, please, don’t judge the sound quality of a non-shipping synth based on YouTube videos. I’ll be sure to report back on final sound quality before you unload your hard-earned change.
CDM is a home for people who make and play music and motion.

The screen isn’t just beautiful: it fits perfectly.
Since computers became commonplace in the 80s, the primitive screens on music hardware have seemed an anachronism, a compromise.

extraction.body: Teenage Engineering’s OP-1 is something unique in music hardware. It’s got a form factor inspired by the Casio VL-Tone series – you know, those cute little 80s-vintage synths . It’s a sampler. It’s a synth. It has an FM radio. It will have a variety of sequencers. It has, we’ve just learned, a multi-track tape mode that lets you do beat-synced virtual splicing as a performance technique. It is expected to integrate and interoperate with a design lifestyle including, if you like, a luxury-priced, meticulously-machined desk lamp, and according to one rumor I heard, perhaps even a specially-designed electric bicycle. (Seriously.) I got to spend some hands-on time with the current prototype of the OP-1, and hanging out with the guys from Teenage Engineering. I do mean “the guys” – I had expected to go out to dinner with the CEO and found myself with almost the entire team of 9. (One was sleeping off Sweden-to-California jetlag.) The company has a pedigree in sound engineering, including the legendary drum maker Elektron, but also in marketing, advertising, industrial and product design. The OP-1 is real, it’s coming, and it’s far enough along in the prototyping phase that I think we’ll see real details on getting one soon. Pricing will be under US$1000 – perhaps a goodly amount under, depending on the final details of manufacturing. There’s no availability date, but progress appears to be accelerating. I poked fun when the OP-1 was introduced, only because it seems like something too cool to be real. I am surprised, though, that people are now complaining that the OP-1 is taking a long time – I think some people don’t realize how time-consuming hardware development really is, and we only just saw an under-glass prototype last spring. The fact that the OP-1 does integrate hardware and onboard software tightly and does do things in new ways is a testament to having a single, small team that works on the whole product. Teenage Engineering – OP-1 @ NAMM 2010 from Neil Bufkin on Vimeo . In the din of the NAMM hall, some people didn’t seem to “get” the OP-1. The prototypes available aren’t entirely refined in regards to the sound engine, so it’s too soon to judge sound quality, and some functionality was missing from the units on display. And it’d be easy to see this its collection of synthesis and sampling tricks as nothing new. (In fact, I get the sense that some people dialed up essentially an init preset and judged the sound quality based on that.) But look closer, and even prior to the finished product, there’s real design genius here. Some of the little touches I was able to glean: You can record backwards, an idea so simple in sampling, but also powerful, it’s a wonder it’s not widespread. Go crazy with this, and you can prove some pretty out-there results. It’s not hard to imagine putting an OP-1 alongside a computer, and using it alternatively as a hardware synth and a tool for resampling the output of a live computer mix. It’s a four-track virtual tape recorder, complete with virtual splicing. The craft of early electronic music was deeply connected to the process of recording to tape, then splicing, into a finished product as a collage. The OP-1 is the most convincing adaptation of that idea I’ve ever seen. A simple, iconic on-screen representation of a reel-to-reel shows you your recording in real-time, with even some light physics simulation so it behaves like tape when you stop the transport. sources.title: Why Packaging Is Now a Frontline Issue in Pharma Supply Chains
passages: This is why packaging is now a frontline issue — not because it has become less important, but because it has become more exposed.
Pharmaceutical supply chains are being pushed into a level of coordination and control they were not originally designed to handle.
Traditional cold chain models detect issues after delivery, but modern cold chains require decisions during transit.
There are few places where that progress is more evident than in cold chain packaging.
These assumptions are breaking more frequently as variability becomes the new supply chain norm.
The shift underway in the cold chain is not about improving packaging performance; it is about redefining control.

The shift underway in the cold chain is not about improving packaging performance; it is about redefining control.

extraction.body: Pharmaceutical supply chains are being pushed into a level of coordination and control they were not originally designed to handle. At the same time, the logistics environments they move through are becoming less stable. On the surface, many of these challenges appear to be logistics problems. Protecting high-value medications, biologics and personalized medicines goes beyond packaging alone. The cold chain is no longer a controlled environment; it is a dynamic system operating under constant disruption. Packaging Is No Longer a Passive Layer — It Requires Oversight In the 100 years since the dawn of electric refrigeration, humans' ability to keep things cool has advanced significantly. There are few places where that progress is more evident than in cold chain packaging. The problem is that these systems were built on assumptions. Their success assumes that a shipment will move within a defined transit window, that exposure conditions will stay within tested ranges, or that handoffs between partners will happen as planned. These assumptions are breaking more frequently as variability becomes the new supply chain norm. Here’s what those breakdowns can look like in practice: A biologic shipment delayed at an airport transfer hub can sit on a tarmac for hours in high heat. A shipment flagged for inspection may experience temperature fluctuations that packaging was never designed to absorb. In each case, the shipment's packaging still does exactly what it was designed to do. But ultimately, packaging can only perform within its limits, and those limits are often pushed to the edge of what they can withstand. This is why packaging is now a frontline issue — not because it has become less important, but because it has become more exposed. How Are Advanced Therapies Exposing Blind Spots in Cold Chain Control? The shift in cold chain risk starts with the shipments themselves. Biologics, cell and gene therapies and personalized medicine have redefined acceptable risk in pharmaceutical logistics. Many require strict temperature control at minus 20 C, minus 80 C or below. For logistics providers handling advanced therapies at scale, this risk profile leaves no margin for error. One operator managing tens of thousands of life sciences shipments annually ultimately moved to real-time monitoring across all shipments because, in their mind, there is simply no option for failure when transporting cell and gene therapies. The difference between product loss and recovery is timing. Traditional cold chain models detect issues after delivery, but modern cold chains require decisions during transit. Packaging is designed to protect within expected conditions; it cannot adapt to compounded delays, exposure or handling variability. This assumes that what happens during shipping (and between actual checkpoints) is stable — and if it’s not, there’s no way to adapt. Continuous monitoring of temperature, location and environmental conditions enables teams to see where risk is developing, not just that it occurred. For example, when a shipment is delayed at a transfer hub, real-time data can show both the current temperature and the rate of change. Teams can estimate how much thermal protection remains and determine whether intervention is required. With visibility, teams can act while a shipment is still recoverable. One company noted that before implementing real-time tracking, “we had no real way to understand what happened” when shipments were delayed. With full visibility, teams can now trace exactly where and how disruptions occur — and intervene accordingly. When analyzed over time, shipment data reveal patterns. Addressing them often reduces risk more effectively than changing packaging alone. Why Does Control Now Depend on Visibility, Response and System Design? The shift underway in the cold chain is not about improving packaging performance; it is about redefining control. For years, protection was measured by whether packaging could hold temperature under expected conditions.

extraction.body: Pharmaceutical supply chains are being pushed into a level of coordination and control they were not originally designed to handle. At the same time, the logistics environments they move through are becoming less stable. On the surface, many of these challenges appear to be logistics problems. Protecting high-value medications, biologics and personalized medicines goes beyond packaging alone. The cold chain is no longer a controlled environment; it is a dynamic system operating under constant disruption. Packaging Is No Longer a Passive Layer — It Requires Oversight In the 100 years since the dawn of electric refrigeration, humans' ability to keep things cool has advanced significantly. There are few places where that progress is more evident than in cold chain packaging. The problem is that these systems were built on assumptions. Their success assumes that a shipment will move within a defined transit window, that exposure conditions will stay within tested ranges, or that handoffs between partners will happen as planned. These assumptions are breaking more frequently as variability becomes the new supply chain norm. Here’s what those breakdowns can look like in practice: A biologic shipment delayed at an airport transfer hub can sit on a tarmac for hours in high heat. A shipment flagged for inspection may experience temperature fluctuations that packaging was never designed to absorb. In each case, the shipment's packaging still does exactly what it was designed to do. But ultimately, packaging can only perform within its limits, and those limits are often pushed to the edge of what they can withstand. This is why packaging is now a frontline issue — not because it has become less important, but because it has become more exposed. How Are Advanced Therapies Exposing Blind Spots in Cold Chain Control? The shift in cold chain risk starts with the shipments themselves. Biologics, cell and gene therapies and personalized medicine have redefined acceptable risk in pharmaceutical logistics. Many require strict temperature control at minus 20 C, minus 80 C or below. For logistics providers handling advanced therapies at scale, this risk profile leaves no margin for error. One operator managing tens of thousands of life sciences shipments annually ultimately moved to real-time monitoring across all shipments because, in their mind, there is simply no option for failure when transporting cell and gene therapies. The difference between product loss and recovery is timing. Traditional cold chain models detect issues after delivery, but modern cold chains require decisions during transit. Packaging is designed to protect within expected conditions; it cannot adapt to compounded delays, exposure or handling variability. This assumes that what happens during shipping (and between actual checkpoints) is stable — and if it’s not, there’s no way to adapt. Continuous monitoring of temperature, location and environmental conditions enables teams to see where risk is developing, not just that it occurred. For example, when a shipment is delayed at a transfer hub, real-time data can show both the current temperature and the rate of change. Teams can estimate how much thermal protection remains and determine whether intervention is required. With visibility, teams can act while a shipment is still recoverable. One company noted that before implementing real-time tracking, “we had no real way to understand what happened” when shipments were delayed. With full visibility, teams can now trace exactly where and how disruptions occur — and intervene accordingly. When analyzed over time, shipment data reveal patterns. Addressing them often reduces risk more effectively than changing packaging alone. Why Does Control Now Depend on Visibility, Response and System Design? The shift underway in the cold chain is not about improving packaging performance; it is about redefining control. For years, protection was measured by whether packaging could hold temperature under expected conditions.

extraction.body: Staff at the Warfield say that about 15 minutes before a security guard was fatally shot, a chemical irritant was sprayed inside the venue, sending a crowd of people rushing out while coughing and struggling to breathe. The San Francisco Police Department is investigating the death of Warfield security guard Ulysses Tykee Davis, 47, who was shot outside the theater around 1 am Saturday. As KTVU reports , Davis’s wife and two of his six children witnessed the shooting. His brother-in-law, Terrance Cooper, said Davis had been helping remove a disruptive woman from the theater when she allegedly shot him in the back. The Warfield Theatre had been hosting an 18-and-over event on Friday night featuring the cast of “ Baddies USA Chapter 3 ,” which was scheduled to end at midnight. According to Mission Local , filming for the show's new season had taken place that night, and bartenders estimated that the venue was less than half full. Staff told Mission Local that a chemical irritant described as bear mace was released inside the theater at 12:45 am, sending a large crowd rushing into the lobby. Bartenders described people coughing, with red eyes and tears streaming down their faces, while others covered their faces and shouted that they could not breathe. One bartender said people were jumping over the bar as they fled, with some taking items and one person swinging at a coworker. Another bartender told the paper that a security guard pulled an attacker away before she was struck. Per Mission Local, staff were still cleaning up when two gunshots were heard near the lobby. Several workers reportedly hid in an office and locked the door. A witness who was near the box office told Mission Local that he saw a woman take a handgun from another woman before someone yelled “Gun!” He said the woman pointed the gun in his direction before he ran and heard several shots. When he looked back, he saw a security guard had been shot near the theater entrance. Police have not confirmed that account. Friends and coworkers described Davis as a longtime Bayview-Hunters Point resident who was well-liked by the people who worked alongside him, as KTVU reports. “Bear was just doing his job. He was at work, doing security,” said Terrance Silas, a friend who works next door to the theater. Police have not released information about a suspect or said whether anyone has been arrested. Per KTVU, SFPD spokesman Officer Robert Rueca said investigators are examining what happened before the shooting, including whether the Warfield had the proper permits for the event and was operating within their restrictions. passages: San Francisco police have arrested a woman in the fatal shooting of a security guard over the weekend at the Warfield on Market Street.
sources.body: San Francisco police have arrested a woman in the fatal shooting of a security guard over the weekend at the Warfield on Market Street.

extraction.body: San Francisco police have arrested a woman in the fatal shooting of a security guard over the weekend at the Warfield on Market Street. Shakia Vanderbilt of San Francisco was taken into custody Tuesday, the San Francisco Police Department said Wednesday. District Attorney Brooke Jenkins said Vanderbilt is charged with murder with a firearm enhancement, a count of intentionally discharging a firearm in an occupied building and a count of being a felon in possession of a firearm. The victim was identified by the office of the chief medical examiner as Ulysses Tykee Davis, 47. His wife and two of his six children were present at the Mid-Market theater when he was gunned down, according to reports . Davis had been working at the Warfield, which was hosting the “Baddies USA: Chapter Three” tour, a reality TV series known for arguing, shouting, and fighting. Police Chief Derrick Lew said Vanderbilt was escorted outside the Warfield following a disruption and that a dispute ensued, culminating in the shooting at approximately 1 a.m Saturday. Lew declined to say if Vanderbilt targeted Davis, but added that there is footage of the shooting. Vanderbilt possibly brought a gun inside the Warfield despite their screening process for attendees, Jenkins said. “Nobody should worry that if they go watch a show at a venue that somebody is armed inside,” Jenkins said. “We want to hold those accountable who think that gun violence is okay in our city.” Davis died in a hospital, police said. Prosecutors will seek to have her held without bail, Jenkins said. According to Mission Local , Warfield staffers said Davis, nicknamed “Bear,” was working at the event as a security guard. Bartenders told Mission Local that during the event, a chemical irritant, possibly bear mace, was released, sending a swarm of panicked attendees toward the exits. The Warfield’s management did not respond to requests for comment. There have been 21 homicides in San Francisco this year through Sunday, according to police statistics . “We have made great strides as a city in reducing gun violence and homicides, and we will continue to devote resources into preventing violence of this kind,” Lew said.

extraction.body: San Francisco police have arrested a woman in the fatal shooting of a security guard over the weekend at the Warfield on Market Street. Shakia Vanderbilt of San Francisco was taken into custody Tuesday, the San Francisco Police Department said Wednesday. District Attorney Brooke Jenkins said Vanderbilt is charged with murder with a firearm enhancement, a count of intentionally discharging a firearm in an occupied building and a count of being a felon in possession of a firearm. The victim was identified by the office of the chief medical examiner as Ulysses Tykee Davis, 47. His wife and two of his six children were present at the Mid-Market theater when he was gunned down, according to reports . Davis had been working at the Warfield, which was hosting the “Baddies USA: Chapter Three” tour, a reality TV series known for arguing, shouting, and fighting. Police Chief Derrick Lew said Vanderbilt was escorted outside the Warfield following a disruption and that a dispute ensued, culminating in the shooting at approximately 1 a.m Saturday. Lew declined to say if Vanderbilt targeted Davis, but added that there is footage of the shooting. Vanderbilt possibly brought a gun inside the Warfield despite their screening process for attendees, Jenkins said. “Nobody should worry that if they go watch a show at a venue that somebody is armed inside,” Jenkins said. “We want to hold those accountable who think that gun violence is okay in our city.” Davis died in a hospital, police said. Prosecutors will seek to have her held without bail, Jenkins said. According to Mission Local , Warfield staffers said Davis, nicknamed “Bear,” was working at the event as a security guard. Bartenders told Mission Local that during the event, a chemical irritant, possibly bear mace, was released, sending a swarm of panicked attendees toward the exits. The Warfield’s management did not respond to requests for comment. There have been 21 homicides in San Francisco this year through Sunday, according to police statistics . “We have made great strides as a city in reducing gun violence and homicides, and we will continue to devote resources into preventing violence of this kind,” Lew said.

passages: Bitmine's Relentless Ethereum Buying Is About to End, Tom Lee Says

Bitmine Immersion Technologies is about to take its foot off the gas. Chairman Tom Lee said the company will halt its Ethereum buying once its holdings reach 5% of the token's circulating supply, drawing a hard line under one of the market's steadiest sources of demand.

Speaking Wednesday at the Token2049 conference in Singapore, Lee said the company is roughly 100,000 ETH away from the threshold. At last week's pace, that's about six to seven more weeks of accumulation before Bitmine stops.
"We thought this would take five years," Lee said on stage. "It took us a little over a year. More importantly, we did this all in the middle of a bear market,” he said. “Now we’re going to stop.”

The NYSE-listed firm is the world's largest Ethereum treasury company, holding 6,016,414 ETH, or about 4.9% of supply, as of its latest disclosure. Bitmine added roughly $41 million in ETH just last week as it closed in on the goal it brands the " Alchemy of 5% ." (Disclosure: Tom Lee is one of several investors in Dastan, Decrypt ’s parent company.)
🚨BREAKING: Tom Lee says BitMine will "STOP" buying ETH at 5% "hard cap."
"We only need to get another 100,000 ETH to get to 5%," Lee said on stage at Token2049.
Lee called 5% BitMine’s “hard cap,” saying it optimizes shareholder value. pic.twitter.com/mm0WYnv4Z0
The company has bought Ethereum every week since launching its treasury strategy in June 2025, providing a reliable bid that helped underpin the token through a choppy stretch.

That makes the coming stop notable for the broader market. Bitmine's weekly purchases have been a persistent source of demand, and their end removes a buyer that has absorbed a steady stream of ETH for more than a year.
Lee has previously signaled the company could even sell Ethereum earned through staking to keep its share of supply from drifting above the 5% cap.

The milestone arrives with Bitmine deep underwater on paper. Because much of its accumulation happened last year at higher prices during the bull market, the firm's ETH holdings carry roughly $4.5 billion in unrealized losses, according to tracking data, with Ethereum trading near $2,570 on Wednesday.
Ethereum is down 5.5% today, outpacing losses across most major crypto assets, dropping sharply during Asia trading hours, coinciding with Lee’s remarks.

Still, Lee framed the achievement as a point of pride, having compressed a five-year plan into just over a year. Once the 5% ceiling is reached, Bitmine's defining buying spree, and the market demand it generated, will come to a close.

The NYSE-listed firm is the world's largest Ethereum treasury company, holding 6,016,414 ETH, or about 4.9% of supply, as of its latest disclosure.

Still, Lee framed the achievement as a point of pride, having compressed a five-year plan into just over a year.
Once the 5% ceiling is reached, Bitmine's defining buying spree, and the market demand it generated, will come to a close.

Speaking Wednesday at the Token2049 conference in Singapore, Lee said the company is roughly 100,000 ETH away from the threshold.
At last week's pace, that's about six to seven more weeks of accumulation before Bitmine stops.
That makes the coming stop notable for the broader market.
Bitmine's weekly purchases have been a persistent source of demand, and their end removes a buyer that has absorbed a steady stream of ETH for more than a year.

passages: Bitmine's Relentless Ethereum Buying Is About to End, Tom Lee Says

Bitmine Immersion Technologies is about to take its foot off the gas. Chairman Tom Lee said the company will halt its Ethereum buying once its holdings reach 5% of the token's circulating supply, drawing a hard line under one of the market's steadiest sources of demand.

Speaking Wednesday at the Token2049 conference in Singapore, Lee said the company is roughly 100,000 ETH away from the threshold. At last week's pace, that's about six to seven more weeks of accumulation before Bitmine stops.
"We thought this would take five years," Lee said on stage. "It took us a little over a year. More importantly, we did this all in the middle of a bear market,” he said. “Now we’re going to stop.”

The NYSE-listed firm is the world's largest Ethereum treasury company, holding 6,016,414 ETH, or about 4.9% of supply, as of its latest disclosure. Bitmine added roughly $41 million in ETH just last week as it closed in on the goal it brands the " Alchemy of 5% ." (Disclosure: Tom Lee is one of several investors in Dastan, Decrypt ’s parent company.)
🚨BREAKING: Tom Lee says BitMine will "STOP" buying ETH at 5% "hard cap."
"We only need to get another 100,000 ETH to get to 5%," Lee said on stage at Token2049.
Lee called 5% BitMine’s “hard cap,” saying it optimizes shareholder value. pic.twitter.com/mm0WYnv4Z0
The company has bought Ethereum every week since launching its treasury strategy in June 2025, providing a reliable bid that helped underpin the token through a choppy stretch.

That makes the coming stop notable for the broader market. Bitmine's weekly purchases have been a persistent source of demand, and their end removes a buyer that has absorbed a steady stream of ETH for more than a year.
Lee has previously signaled the company could even sell Ethereum earned through staking to keep its share of supply from drifting above the 5% cap.

The milestone arrives with Bitmine deep underwater on paper. Because much of its accumulation happened last year at higher prices during the bull market, the firm's ETH holdings carry roughly $4.5 billion in unrealized losses, according to tracking data, with Ethereum trading near $2,570 on Wednesday.
Ethereum is down 5.5% today, outpacing losses across most major crypto assets, dropping sharply during Asia trading hours, coinciding with Lee’s remarks.

Still, Lee framed the achievement as a point of pride, having compressed a five-year plan into just over a year. Once the 5% ceiling is reached, Bitmine's defining buying spree, and the market demand it generated, will come to a close.

Markus Thielen of 10x Research made two forecasts about a potential Bitcoin bottom during the summer of 2026, but Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) never dipped to those levels. On June 24, he suggested that Bitcoin could drop to $55,000 between late August and October. Just ten days later, on July 4, he revised his forecast, calling for a fall to between $46,000 and $47,000 before anticipating a 30% bounce back to $60,000 to $65,000 by year-end.

However, Bitcoin hit its 2026 low at $57,717 on June 30, just six days after the first forecast and four days before the second. Since then, it has surged nearly 49%, trading around $86,000 as of October 7—significantly above the $55,000 target and 85% higher than the middle of the lower range Thielen proposed.

The current rally does have its limitations. Bitcoin has risen about 8% in the past month but is still down roughly 30% from the previous year and trades about 32% below its record high of $126,080 from October 2025. So, where did Thielen's bear case go wrong?

A stronger dollar makes Bitcoin more expensive for investors using other currencies, while higher interest rates can make cash and bonds more appealing to investors. At the time, traders debated whether the Fed's next move under Chair Kevin Warsh would be a rate hike rather than a cut.

In July, Thielen expanded his analysis by incorporating Elliott Wave theory, which interprets price charts as repeating wave patterns. He identified a first wave down to around $63,000 in February, followed by a rebound to between $82,000 and $83,000, and concluded with a final wave (Wave C) that would see prices drop to $46,000 to $47,000.

Market evidence supported his earlier claims. Between mid-May and July, US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw around $7 billion in net outflows, and Strategy, the year's largest buyer with about $13 billion in purchases, slowed its buying. As Thielen noted in July, "there's no real buyer in the market right now."

However, that claim about a lack of buyers was the one aspect of the forecast that was quickly tested, and the data soon contradicted it. Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which allow everyday investors to gain exposure to Bitcoin through regular brokerage accounts, attracted about $6.3 billion in the third quarter, including $2.3 billion in just four days at the end of September.

This influx of funds correlated directly with Bitcoin's performance. Thielen had forecast that the bottom would occur between late August and October, but instead, Bitcoin rose from its June low during that timeframe.

On the macroeconomic side, we still need to evaluate Thielen's calls about the dollar and the Federal Reserve. Bitcoin's price rise alone doesn't conclusively indicate whether his analysis of these factors was accurate. The Fed's decision on rates during its September meeting was held on September 16, with another meeting slated for October 27 and 28. These outcomes will clarify whether rates have moved in line with Thielen's expectations.

Moreover, his end-of-year range now looks different. Initially, Thielen projected Bitcoin would rebound to $60,000 to $65,000 from $46,000. If Bitcoin drops below its 2026 low of $57,717 before December 31, and if ETF outflows resume in the fourth quarter, Thielen's lower price targets could come back into play. As long as Bitcoin stays above that critical level and demand from fund buyers remains strong, the assertion that there is "no real buyer" will continue to prove incorrect.

Thielen's June forecast was based on a strong US dollar and a hawkish Federal Reserve, which was expected to keep interest rates high to combat inflation. A stronger dollar makes Bitcoin more expensive for investors using other currencies, while higher interest rates can make cash and bonds more appealing to investors. At the time, traders debated whether the Fed's next move under Chair Kevin Warsh would be a rate hike rather than a cut.

In July, Thielen expanded his analysis by incorporating Elliott Wave theory, which interprets price charts as repeating wave patterns. He identified a first wave down to around $63,000 in February, followed by a rebound to between $82,000 and $83,000, and concluded with a final wave (Wave C) that would see prices drop to $46,000 to $47,000.

Market evidence supported his earlier claims. Between mid-May and July, US spot Bitcoin ETFs saw around $7 billion in net outflows, and Strategy, the year's largest buyer with about $13 billion in purchases, slowed its buying. As Thielen noted in July, "there's no real buyer in the market right now."

However, that claim about a lack of buyers was the one aspect of the forecast that was quickly tested, and the data soon contradicted it. Bitcoin exchange-traded funds, which allow everyday investors to gain exposure to Bitcoin through regular brokerage accounts, attracted about $6.3 billion in the third quarter, including $2.3 billion in just four days at the end of September.

On the macroeconomic side, we still need to evaluate Thielen's calls about the dollar and the Federal Reserve. Bitcoin's price rise alone doesn't conclusively indicate whether his analysis of these factors was accurate. The Fed's decision on rates during its September meeting was held on September 16, with another meeting slated for October 27 and 28. These outcomes will clarify whether rates have moved in line with Thielen's expectations.

Moreover, his end-of-year range now looks different. Initially, Thielen projected Bitcoin would rebound to $60,000 to $65,000 from $46,000. Investors in Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ), and Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) often hear predictions that their coins could 10x by 2030. However, what a 10x increase means varies greatly between these cryptocurrencies. For Solana, it would mean growing from a market cap of approximately $70 billion to $700 billion. For Bitcoin, it would need to rise from $1.69 trillion to nearly $17 trillion—almost three times the value of Nvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ), currently around $6 trillion.
So which crypto stands the best chance of achieving a 10x increase by 2030, and what would each need to do to make that leap?

A coin’s price alone doesn’t provide much information, especially since these four cryptocurrencies have different token supplies. Market cap is the key metric here. It calculates a cryptocurrency’s total value by multiplying the price of one coin by the number of coins in circulation. This figure determines how much new investment is required for a 10x increase. Investors must be willing to pay the higher price for every circulating coin, so a larger starting market cap requires significantly more total investment.
Here’s a table comparing the four cryptocurrencies, ranked by their targets for a 10x increase as of October 7, 2026:

Solana and XRP have the smallest market cap targets for achieving a 10x increase. For instance, reaching $700 billion for Solana and $930 billion for XRP would not require the creation of a new market, as these values are comparable to some of the largest U.S. tech companies.

However, both cryptocurrencies do have increasing supplies. Solana rewards holders (stakers) with new tokens for helping secure its network, while Ripple can release up to 1 billion XRP each month from an escrow account. If their supplies increase significantly, the same market values could result in lower prices than expected.

Bitcoin and Ethereum benefit from greater demand. They have larger investor bases, more established ETF markets , and better access for institutional investors like banks and pension funds, making them more attractive for big-money investments.

Nevertheless, their targets are quite high. For Ethereum to reach a 10x increase, it would need a market cap of about $3.2 trillion, corresponding to a price per coin of $26,000. That would place it among the few assets valued over $3 trillion. Bitcoin, on the other hand, would need to surge to about $16.9 trillion or roughly $842,000 per coin. This equates to nearly 60% of the total value of all gold ever mined, estimated around $29 trillion at a price of $4,133 per ounce.

Supply dynamics could work in Bitcoin and Ethereum’s favor. Bitcoin’s maximum supply is capped at 21 million coins , while Ethereum’s protocol burns a portion of its transaction fees, which offsets much of its new issuance over time.

Based on our analysis, Solana appears to have the highest chance of achieving a 10x increase by 2030, primarily because it has the smallest target. However, its demand must outpace the growth of its token supply. XRP follows closely, though potential escrow releases could add more coins as prices rise. Ethereum ranks third, while Bitcoin sits at the bottom of the list, needing to grow nearly three times as much as Nvidia for a successful 10x.

This ranking has important implications. The cryptocurrency with the easiest math—Solana—has a smaller pool of large buyers . Solana’s market cap would first need to surpass XRP’s $93 billion, then Ethereum’s $320 billion. If Solana’s price exceeds $1,189 before Ethereum reaches $26,169, the ranking holds. But if Ethereum hits its target first, it suggests larger investors’ buying power outweighs starting size, making the order potentially inaccurate.

Investors in Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ), Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ), XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ), and Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) often hear predictions that their coins could 10x by 2030. However, what a 10x increase means varies greatly between these cryptocurrencies. For Solana, it would mean growing from a market cap of approximately $70 billion to $700 billion. For Bitcoin, it would need to rise from $1.69 trillion to nearly $17 trillion—almost three times the value of Nvidia ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ), currently around $6 trillion.
So which crypto stands the best chance of achieving a 10x increase by 2030, and what would each need to do to make that leap?

A coin’s price alone doesn’t provide much information, especially since these four cryptocurrencies have different token supplies. Market cap is the key metric here. It calculates a cryptocurrency’s total value by multiplying the price of one coin by the number of coins in circulation. This figure determines how much new investment is required for a 10x increase. Investors must be willing to pay the higher price for every circulating coin, so a larger starting market cap requires significantly more total investment.
Here’s a table comparing the four cryptocurrencies, ranked by their targets for a 10x increase as of October 7, 2026:

Solana and XRP have the smallest market cap targets for achieving a 10x increase. For instance, reaching $700 billion for Solana and $930 billion for XRP would not require the creation of a new market, as these values are comparable to some of the largest U.S. tech companies.

However, both cryptocurrencies do have increasing supplies. Solana rewards holders (stakers) with new tokens for helping secure its network, while Ripple can release up to 1 billion XRP each month from an escrow account. If their supplies increase significantly, the same market values could result in lower prices than expected.

Bitcoin and Ethereum benefit from greater demand. They have larger investor bases, more established ETF markets , and better access for institutional investors like banks and pension funds, making them more attractive for big-money investments.

Nevertheless, their targets are quite high. For Ethereum to reach a 10x increase, it would need a market cap of about $3.2 trillion, corresponding to a price per coin of $26,000. That would place it among the few assets valued over $3 trillion. Bitcoin, on the other hand, would need to surge to about $16.9 trillion or roughly $842,000 per coin. This equates to nearly 60% of the total value of all gold ever mined, estimated around $29 trillion at a price of $4,133 per ounce.

Supply dynamics could work in Bitcoin and Ethereum’s favor. Bitcoin’s maximum supply is capped at 21 million coins , while Ethereum’s protocol burns a portion of its transaction fees, which offsets much of its new issuance over time.

Based on our analysis, Solana appears to have the highest chance of achieving a 10x increase by 2030, primarily because it has the smallest target. However, its demand must outpace the growth of its token supply. XRP follows closely, though potential escrow releases could add more coins as prices rise. Ethereum ranks third, while Bitcoin sits at the bottom of the list, needing to grow nearly three times as much as Nvidia for a successful 10x.

This ranking has important implications. The cryptocurrency with the easiest math—Solana—has a smaller pool of large buyers . Solana’s market cap would first need to surpass XRP’s $93 billion, then Ethereum’s $320 billion. If Solana’s price exceeds $1,189 before Ethereum reaches $26,169, the ranking holds. But if Ethereum hits its target first, it suggests larger investors’ buying power outweighs starting size, making the order potentially inaccurate.

You can also ask ChatGPT to generate tools for different tasks, such as a retirement savings calculator, retro game, or bill splitter. It will then generate the tool in-line with its response. In addition to enabling Intelligent UI, OpenAI says its GPT-6 allows ChatGPT to perform better web searches and provide quicker, partial answers to users while it gathers information. integrityPreflight.title: Bloom raises $3.6M to become the ‘Alibaba’ of American manufacturing

sources.pageTitle: Bloom raises $3.6M to become the 'Alibaba' of American manufacturing | TechCrunch

sources.title: Bloom raises $3.6M to become the ‘Alibaba’ of American manufacturing
passages: The reinvention slowed Bloom’s fundraising plans.
But the company has now made over 2,000 matches for more than 140 companies, and it wants to grow faster.
That was an opportunity for Bloom, which is based in Detroit, but to tackle it, the startup had to partially reinvent itself.
Instead of performing some of those harder, behind-the-scenes tasks, which was a big part of the original plan, Bloom shifted to a pure marketplace model, in which it connects buyers and sellers.
Some customers use the platform to post contract opportunities, while others use it to bid on those opportunities.

Bloom handles quoting, booking, and payment all on its platform, and it now helps match companies with suppliers that can do contract manufacturing, assembly, design and engineering, freight, warehousing, repairs, and even hazardous-materials shipping.
A lot of that was public data — how a company describes itself on its website, for instance.
But around 30-40% of that data is coming directly from the companies, Kosmides said.
When Justin Kosmides co-founded Bloom in 2023, his goal was to create a savior for the mobility industry .
He wanted to convince survivors and new entrants to let Bloom handle that work for them.
SNAK first met with Bloom in April of last year, in the early stages of this reinvention.
So early, in fact, that the firm passed on the chance to invest in the startup’s pre-seed round.
Kosmides believes this is all a better way to strike up supplier relationships, and that it also makes it easier for startups to get off the ground.
“The ability to discover, and the ability to do matchmaking, that is what I think is truly missing” from U.S. manufacturing, he said. “That just doesn’t exist electronically.”
Bloom kept in touch with SNAK as it worked through becoming a more software-focused startup.
By May of this year, Bloom had made as much revenue in five months as it did in all of 2025.
Bloom did court other term sheets, Kosmides said.

But SNAK, which was founded by longtime retail executive Sonia Nagar, is “who you want in your camp” to “build a hopefully category-defining marketplace for mobility, and drones, and all this hardware.”
On Wednesday, Bloom announced a $3.6 million seed round led by SNAK Venture Partners , a marketplace-focused investment firm.
Also joining were Flyover Capital (an early-stage investor that focuses on flyover states), and deep tech firm Mana Ventures.
Local backers include Detroit Venture Partners, Invest Detroit Ventures, and the Michigan Outdoor Innovation Fund.

“Our friends at the parts marketplaces like Fictiv, Xometry, MacroFab, and others are really good yesteryear marketplaces for finding one particular part,” Kosmides said. “But when you’re XYZ Drone Company, or an electric motorcycle company, and you need to find a provider that meets all these requirements, have them all bid on this opportunity, that’s a lot more complicated than finding a CNC part.”
Kosmides said the fundraising scene has been a bit ruthless for startups like Bloom.

He gave an example of one Michigan-based contract manufacturer that, until it started working with Bloom, was taking on odd jobs like refurbishing Nest thermostats and Bird scooters, or working with Chick-fil-A displays.
That same company is now bidding on drone assembly contracts.

extraction.body: When Justin Kosmides co-founded Bloom in 2023, his goal was to create a savior for the mobility industry . He had seen many e-bike and e-scooter companies fail because of an inability — or an unwillingness — to outsource some of the hardest problems, like logistics, manufacturing, or building a supply chain. He wanted to convince survivors and new entrants to let Bloom handle that work for them. Some customers use the platform to post contract opportunities, while others use it to bid on those opportunities.

On Wednesday, Bloom announced a $3.6 million seed round led by SNAK Venture Partners , a marketplace-focused investment firm.
Also joining were Flyover Capital (an early-stage investor that focuses on flyover states), and deep tech firm Mana Ventures.
Local backers include Detroit Venture Partners, Invest Detroit Ventures, and the Michigan Outdoor Innovation Fund.

Kosmides said the fundraising scene has been a bit ruthless for startups like Bloom.

He gave an example of one Michigan-based contract manufacturer that, until it started working with Bloom, was taking on odd jobs like refurbishing Nest thermostats and Bird scooters, or working with Chick-fil-A displays.

extraction.body: When Justin Kosmides co-founded Bloom in 2023, his goal was to create a savior for the mobility industry . He had seen many e-bike and e-scooter companies fail because of an inability — or an unwillingness — to outsource some of the hardest problems, like logistics, manufacturing, or building a supply chain. He wanted to convince survivors and new entrants to let Bloom handle that work for them. Then Donald Trump got re-elected and started shotgun-blasting tariffs on dozens of countries, partially to jump-start U.S. manufacturing. This accelerated a hardware scene that was already heating up in this country and, suddenly, it was more than just mobility companies looking to beef up their domestic supply chain. Robotics startups, drone-makers, and many more started to pop up. That was an opportunity for Bloom, which is based in Detroit, but to tackle it, the startup had to partially reinvent itself. Instead of performing some of those harder, behind-the-scenes tasks, which was a big part of the original plan, Bloom shifted to a pure marketplace model, in which it connects buyers and sellers. It’s now focused on making, essentially, supply chain AI agents that Bloom’s customers use to find specific types of suppliers, parts, or manufacturing and engineering services. The reinvention slowed Bloom’s fundraising plans. But the company has now made over 2,000 matches for more than 140 companies, and it wants to grow faster. In an interview earlier this year, Kosmides, who is Bloom’s CEO, said his startup is like what an AI-driven version of Alibaba did in China, where it created a marketplace for contract manufacturers. Investors are finally buying in. On Wednesday, Bloom announced a $3.6 million seed round led by SNAK Venture Partners , a marketplace-focused investment firm. Also joining were Flyover Capital (an early-stage investor that focuses on flyover states), and deep tech firm Mana Ventures. Local backers include Detroit Venture Partners, Invest Detroit Ventures, and the Michigan Outdoor Innovation Fund. Kosmides, sounding relieved, said in the interview that he’s “excited to be done with fundraising and get back to building.” SNAK first met with Bloom in April of last year, in the early stages of this reinvention. So early, in fact, that the firm passed on the chance to invest in the startup’s pre-seed round. “We liked the founder and the thesis and passed anyway: we wanted to see more traction,” the firm wrote in a blog post. “We said so plainly and kept tracking the company.” Bloom kept in touch with SNAK as it worked through becoming a more software-focused startup. By May of this year, Bloom had made as much revenue in five months as it did in all of 2025. SNAK also said the number of memberships on its platform had grown fivefold “with low churn,” meaning few customers were canceling. “This is meant to reiterate that for us, a pass on pre-seed is not always a pass forever. We are fortunate to have a super focused thesis that allows us to track a small set of interesting early stage companies and build a relationship over time,” the firm wrote. Kosmides said the fundraising scene has been a bit ruthless for startups like Bloom. Proving your value to investors in a world where the leading AI models keep improving can be an uphill battle. “To find investors to actually write a term sheet, not follow one, is getting harder and harder,” he said. “That’s just this new era that we’re in, with everyone trying to figure out what’s real and what’s not, what to invest in.” Bloom did court other term sheets, Kosmides said. But SNAK, which was founded by longtime retail executive Sonia Nagar, is “who you want in your camp” to “build a hopefully category-defining marketplace for mobility, and drones, and all this hardware.” Bloom’s platform handles both sides of a supplier relationship. Some customers use the platform to post contract opportunities, while others use it to bid on those opportunities. Bloom handles quoting, booking, and payment all on its platform, and it now helps match companies with suppliers that can do contract manufacturing, assembly, design and engineering, freight, warehousing, repairs, and even hazardous-materials shipping. “Our friends at the parts marketplaces like Fictiv, Xometry, MacroFab, and others are really good yesteryear marketplaces for finding one particular part,” Kosmides said. “But when you’re XYZ Drone Company, or an electric motorcycle company, and you need to find a provider that meets all these requirements, have them all bid on this opportunity, that’s a lot more complicated than finding a CNC part.” Making this system work well is a big part of Bloom’s reinvention, and it involved ingesting a lot of data about each provider on the platform. A lot of that was public data — how a company describes itself on its website, for instance. But around 30-40% of that data is coming directly from the companies, Kosmides said. Add in the data being generated as the startup onboards more customers and makes more matches, and you have Bloom’s edge, he said. “You can build the craziest model for scraping data but you would never get to that accuracy,” he said. “We started with manually booking services, and then built in layers and pieces and understanding as we built up the provider network, as we built out more and more transactions, and so it’s only getting better and better.” Kosmides believes this is all a better way to strike up supplier relationships, and that it also makes it easier for startups to get off the ground. But he also thinks Bloom’s platform will help create opportunities for small manufacturers who may not have big marketing budgets or sales teams. He gave an example of one Michigan-based contract manufacturer that, until it started working with Bloom, was taking on odd jobs like refurbishing Nest thermostats and Bird scooters, or working with Chick-fil-A displays. That same company is now bidding on drone assembly contracts. “The ability to discover, and the ability to do matchmaking, that is what I think is truly missing” from U.S. manufacturing, he said. “That just doesn’t exist electronically.” Sean O’Kane is a reporter who has spent a decade covering the rapidly-evolving business and technology of the transportation industry, including Tesla and the many startups chasing Elon Musk. Most recently, he was a reporter at Bloomberg News where he helped break stories about some of the most notorious EV SPAC flops. He previously worked at The Verge, where he also covered consumer technology, hosted many short- and long-form videos, performed product and editorial photography, and once nearly passed out in a Red Bull Air Race plane. sources.title: X expands its ‘Gametime’ sports hub beyond the NFL, starting with MLB
passages: X is doubling down on sports, with Wednesday’s news that it’s expanding its “Gametime” feature on the social media site to go beyond tracking the NFL alone.

“In just six weeks, Gametime has evolved from a football-focused product into a scalable destination for sports, attracting strong demand across major advertisers from payments to consumer goods looking to engage highly attentive fans from the pregame conversation through the biggest moments of the game,” said SpaceXAI’s head of Global Advertising, Monique Pintarelli, in an announcement.
First announced in August, NFL Gametime is X’s new project that offers a single hub for tracking live scores, getting play-by-play updates, tuning into game feeds, and more.
The move wasn’t meant to be useful only to X users who like to congregate on the platform to discuss live sporting events, but to woo brands and advertisers looking to reach passionate sports fans.
At Advertising Week New York, X said Gametime will become a year-round destination spanning “all professional sports.”
However, that full expansion isn’t yet live as of today.
Instead, X announced its second league partnership with Major League Baseball (MLB).

Arriving this month, the new MLB experience will allow baseball fans to follow and engage in postseason discussions and will organize things like scores and stats, team and league content, plus news, creator content, and real-time discussions.

The expansion of the Gametime feature comes as X continues its efforts to win back advertisers — in this case by leveraging live sports and their highly engaged fans as a way to draw brands back to X.

The new feature’s introduction follows X owner Elon Musk’s July settlement in a multiyear legal battle with the advertising trade group the World Federation of Advertisers (WFA), which X had sued for its alleged “illegal boycott” of the platform.
Musk believed the WFA’s guidelines had steered brands and ad agencies away from X, suggesting it was a place where their ads could appear next to harmful online content.

integrityPreflight.title: Google’s new SynthID website can identify AI-generated media

sources.pageTitle: Google's new SynthID website can identify AI-generated media | TechCrunch

sources.title: Google’s new SynthID website can identify AI-generated media
passages: Google is using SynthID, which it introduced in 2023 , to identify whether media is AI-generated.
The company’s Nano Banana, Veo, and Lyria models, as well as tools with generation capabilities, like Gemini, Flow, ProducerAI, and Vids, all use SynthID to watermark any media they generate.
Google has baked SynthID verification into the Gemini app and Google Chrome.
The company said people currently make 1 million requests to verify content every day.
Google on Tuesday launched a new site that lets anyone verify whether a piece of media, be it an image, a video, or an audio clip, is generated using AI.
Microsoft and Meta have their own standards for watermarking and verifying content.
However, these tools are not infallible, often failing to identify content created by their makers’ models.
OpenAI, Nvidia, and Kakao also support SynthID, and OpenAI maintains its own site for checking content.
Apple is said to be adding support soon, too.

Perhaps more importantly, the app is where you can browse past ones. Siri AI is more conversational than the old assistant, and keeps a record of past queries across all your devices. So the Siri app in watchOS 27 shows you conversations not just from your Apple Watch, but from your iPhone, Mac, and more. Joining iOS 27’s new features for the Find My app , Apple has rethought the Find My experience in watchOS this year too. In watchOS 26, Find My was split up into three separate apps: Find Devices, Find Items, and Find People. But in watchOS 27, Apple has streamlined all finding features into a new, unified ‘Find My’ app. Find My on Apple Watch provides all the functionality of the previous three apps, but in a condensed experience so you can easily locate anything or anyone on a map-centric view. You can switch between different things you’re looking for via a menu in the top-left corner, but otherwise you’ll see a consistent interface. That’s the question Tanvi Thombre and Lakshya Saraf began investigating when they were engineering students who worked in their university makerspace. In fact, Thombre said via email that, while working in the space, they were “unknowingly exposed to toxic fumes from laser cutters, 3D printers, and soldering irons,” but they didn’t realize it until Thombre’s best friend fainted and had to go to the hospital. After that, Thombre said, “We began investigating indoor air pollution and realized it was an invisible but dangerous health risk — especially in schools, offices, hotels, salons, and any commercial buildings where air-conditioning prevents windows from being opened.” Those issues persist even when a building is equipped with air purifiers, as their makerspace was. The problem, according to Saraf, is that although purifiers are good at cleaning out particulate matter like dust and pollen, they are less effective at removing toxic gases such as carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, and benzine (many of which are classified as volatile organic compounds, or VOCs — chemicals that evaporate easily into the air). Thombre said that VOCs are linked to chronic disease and “ sick building syndrome ,” a condition in which occupants experience health effects and discomfort after spending time in a building, even though no specific cause or illness has been identified. She also pointed to Harvard research showing that improving indoor air quality improved cognitive function and productivity as well. That’s why the pair is targeting toxic gases in the workplace with their startup Greenairy , which will be part of Startup Battlefield 200 at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt . Greenairy’s approach centers on building plant towers that are supposed to draw in air, break down toxic gases, and then release the purified air. As Saraf put it, “A plant in a pot cleans air slowly. But, when we change the conditions around the plant, it cleans air much faster and better than these conventional methods.” Saraf also said that while some air purifier filters can remove “a narrow range of VOCs,” those filters need to be changed frequently to be effective. In contrast, plants are “a natural solution, no harmful by-products are formed, and no filter replacement is required.” Greenairy has already conducted short-term pilots at locations around Singapore. Saraf said that in the startup’s own testing using RESET-certified air monitors, it compared three offices: one with Greenairy plant towers, one that had a medical-grade ionizer (a device that uses an electrical charge to make dust and other particles clump together and fall out of the air), and a third with a HEPA air purifier that traps very small particles. “Our tower had the lowest VOC levels and removed VOCs the fastest,” she said. “The office staff also grew fond of the natural ‘fresh’ aroma of the tower and the natural vibe it brought.” Thombre added that they saw an “immediate” improvement within regular office hours, with a 50% reduction in both the daily VOC average and peak levels. She said the results improved even more “as the plants and microbes mature and the gases are prevented from accumulating.” Greenairy has also had its results validated by the German testing and certification firm TÜV SÜD and will be publishing them soon. (Results are available upon request in the meantime.) The pair plans to begin large-scale manufacturing after the results are certified. The startup’s founders are currently based on opposite sides of the world, with Saraf in Berkeley, California, and Thombre in Singapore. It’s an arrangement that Saraf said “works well at this stage,” allowing one founder to focus on testing in Singapore while the other can fundraise in the Bay Area. “If things go to plan, both of us will be in Singapore by the first half of 2027,” she added. “That’s when we expect to launch our first mass-produced towers and install them for our first customers” in Singapore. How clean is the air in your workplace? That’s the question Tanvi Thombre and Lakshya Saraf began investigating when they were engineering students who worked in their university makerspace.

In fact, Thombre said via email that, while working in the space, they were “unknowingly exposed to toxic fumes from laser cutters, 3D printers, and soldering irons,” but they didn’t realize it until Thombre’s best friend fainted and had to go to the hospital.

After that, Thombre said, “We began investigating indoor air pollution and realized it was an invisible but dangerous health risk — especially in schools, offices, hotels, salons, and any commercial buildings where air-conditioning prevents windows from being opened.”

Those issues persist even when a building is equipped with air purifiers, as their makerspace was. The problem, according to Saraf, is that although purifiers are good at cleaning out particulate matter like dust and pollen, they are less effective at removing toxic gases such as carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, and benzine (many of which are classified as volatile organic compounds, or VOCs — chemicals that evaporate easily into the air).

Thombre said that VOCs are linked to chronic disease and “ sick building syndrome ,” a condition in which occupants experience health effects and discomfort after spending time in a building, even though no specific cause or illness has been identified. She also pointed to Harvard research showing that improving indoor air quality improved cognitive function and productivity as well.
That’s why the pair is targeting toxic gases in the workplace with their startup Greenairy , which will be part of Startup Battlefield 200 at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt .

Greenairy’s approach centers on building plant towers that are supposed to draw in air, break down toxic gases, and then release the purified air. As Saraf put it, “A plant in a pot cleans air slowly. But, when we change the conditions around the plant, it cleans air much faster and better than these conventional methods.”

Saraf also said that while some air purifier filters can remove “a narrow range of VOCs,” those filters need to be changed frequently to be effective. In contrast, plants are “a natural solution, no harmful by-products are formed, and no filter replacement is required.”

Greenairy has already conducted short-term pilots at locations around Singapore. Saraf said that in the startup’s own testing using RESET-certified air monitors, it compared three offices: one with Greenairy plant towers, one that had a medical-grade ionizer (a device that uses an electrical charge to make dust and other particles clump together and fall out of the air), and a third with a HEPA air purifier that traps very small particles.
“Our tower had the lowest VOC levels and removed VOCs the fastest,” she said. “The office staff also grew fond of the natural ‘fresh’ aroma of the tower and the natural vibe it brought.”

Thombre added that they saw an “immediate” improvement within regular office hours, with a 50% reduction in both the daily VOC average and peak levels. She said the results improved even more “as the plants and microbes mature and the gases are prevented from accumulating.”

Greenairy has also had its results validated by the German testing and certification firm TÜV SÜD and will be publishing them soon. (Results are available upon request in the meantime.) The pair plans to begin large-scale manufacturing after the results are certified.

The startup’s founders are currently based on opposite sides of the world, with Saraf in Berkeley, California, and Thombre in Singapore. It’s an arrangement that Saraf said “works well at this stage,” allowing one founder to focus on testing in Singapore while the other can fundraise in the Bay Area.

“If things go to plan, both of us will be in Singapore by the first half of 2027,” she added. “That’s when we expect to launch our first mass-produced towers and install them for our first customers” in Singapore.

How clean is the air in your workplace? That’s the question Tanvi Thombre and Lakshya Saraf began investigating when they were engineering students who worked in their university makerspace.

In fact, Thombre said via email that, while working in the space, they were “unknowingly exposed to toxic fumes from laser cutters, 3D printers, and soldering irons,” but they didn’t realize it until Thombre’s best friend fainted and had to go to the hospital.

After that, Thombre said, “We began investigating indoor air pollution and realized it was an invisible but dangerous health risk — especially in schools, offices, hotels, salons, and any commercial buildings where air-conditioning prevents windows from being opened.”

Those issues persist even when a building is equipped with air purifiers, as their makerspace was. The problem, according to Saraf, is that although purifiers are good at cleaning out particulate matter like dust and pollen, they are less effective at removing toxic gases such as carbon dioxide, formaldehyde, and benzine (many of which are classified as volatile organic compounds, or VOCs — chemicals that evaporate easily into the air).

Thombre said that VOCs are linked to chronic disease and “ sick building syndrome ,” a condition in which occupants experience health effects and discomfort after spending time in a building, even though no specific cause or illness has been identified. She also pointed to Harvard research showing that improving indoor air quality improved cognitive function and productivity as well.
That’s why the pair is targeting toxic gases in the workplace with their startup Greenairy , which will be part of Startup Battlefield 200 at this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt .

Greenairy’s approach centers on building plant towers that are supposed to draw in air, break down toxic gases, and then release the purified air. As Saraf put it, “A plant in a pot cleans air slowly. But, when we change the conditions around the plant, it cleans air much faster and better than these conventional methods.”

Saraf also said that while some air purifier filters can remove “a narrow range of VOCs,” those filters need to be changed frequently to be effective. In contrast, plants are “a natural solution, no harmful by-products are formed, and no filter replacement is required.”

Greenairy has already conducted short-term pilots at locations around Singapore. Saraf said that in the startup’s own testing using RESET-certified air monitors, it compared three offices: one with Greenairy plant towers, one that had a medical-grade ionizer (a device that uses an electrical charge to make dust and other particles clump together and fall out of the air), and a third with a HEPA air purifier that traps very small particles.
“Our tower had the lowest VOC levels and removed VOCs the fastest,” she said. “The office staff also grew fond of the natural ‘fresh’ aroma of the tower and the natural vibe it brought.”

Thombre added that they saw an “immediate” improvement within regular office hours, with a 50% reduction in both the daily VOC average and peak levels. She said the results improved even more “as the plants and microbes mature and the gases are prevented from accumulating.”

Greenairy has also had its results validated by the German testing and certification firm TÜV SÜD and will be publishing them soon. (Results are available upon request in the meantime.) The pair plans to begin large-scale manufacturing after the results are certified.

The startup’s founders are currently based on opposite sides of the world, with Saraf in Berkeley, California, and Thombre in Singapore. It’s an arrangement that Saraf said “works well at this stage,” allowing one founder to focus on testing in Singapore while the other can fundraise in the Bay Area.

“If things go to plan, both of us will be in Singapore by the first half of 2027,” she added. “That’s when we expect to launch our first mass-produced towers and install them for our first customers” in Singapore.
